By the Yangtze at Xunyang, I bid my guest farewell at night;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn chill.
The host dismounted, the guest stepped onto his boat;
We raised our cups to drink, but no music played.
Drunk yet joyless, we faced the sorrow of parting;
As we said goodbye, the vast river bathed the moon.
Suddenly, from across the water, came the sound of a pipa!
The host forgot to go home, the guest delayed his departure.
Following the sound, I asked softly who was playing;
The pipa stopped, as if she hesitated to speak.
I moved my boat closer and invited her to meet;
We added more wine, turned up the lamps, and resumed the feast.
After many calls and entreaties, she finally appeared,
Still holding her pipa, half-covering her face.
She turned the pegs and plucked the strings two or three times;
Before the melody formed, emotion already poured forth.
Each string suppressed, each note full of thought,
Seeming to tell of lifelong frustration and unfulfilled dreams.
Head lowered, fingers moving confidently, she continued to play,
Expressing endless affairs hidden within her heart.
Light gathering, slow twisting, wiping, then plucking—
First playing *Ni Shang*, then *Liu Yao*.
The thick strings rumbled like sudden heavy rain,
The thin strings whispered like intimate confidences.
Rumbling and whispering interwoven in chaotic play,
Like large and small pearls falling into a jade plate.
Smoothly flowing like orioles singing among flowers,
Muffled and choked like spring water freezing under ice.
Ice-cold, sluggish, the strings seemed to snap in silence;
Silence halted, no sound for a moment.
Then arose new dark sorrows and hidden resentments;
At this moment, silence surpassed even sound.
Suddenly, like a silver vase bursting, water splashed out;
Like iron cavalry charging, swords and spears clashed and rang.
As the song ended, she drew her plectrum across the center;
The four strings sounded once, like tearing silk.
Boats on the east and west fell silent, saying nothing;
Only the white autumn moon shone upon the river’s heart.
Lost in thought, she placed her plectrum between the strings,
Straightened her clothes, rose, and composed her expression.
She spoke of herself: "I was originally a girl from the capital,
My home living near Shama Ling (Frog Mound).
At thirteen I mastered the pipa,
And my name belonged to the first division of the Imperial Music Bureau.
After finishing a tune, even great masters would admire me;
When I put on makeup, every beautiful woman envied me.
Young men from the Five Tombs competed to give me gifts,
For one song, I received countless bolts of red silk.
Gold hairpins and silver combs broke keeping time,
Blood-red skirts were stained with spilled wine.
Year after year passed in laughter and joy,
Idly spending the autumn moons and spring breezes.
My brother went off to war, my aunt died;
Day by day, morning by evening, my beauty faded.
Before my door, life grew cold, horses and carriages rare;
Aging, I married a merchant’s wife.
Merchants value profit over love, and care little for separation;
Last month he left for Fuliang to buy tea.
He left, and I waited alone at the river mouth guarding an empty boat;
Around the boat, bright moonlight, the river water cold.
Deep in the night, I suddenly dreamed of youth’s affairs;
I woke crying, tears staining my rouge-covered cheeks red.
I listened to the pipa and sighed already deeply,
And hearing these words, I sobbed anew.
Both of us are wanderers lost at the end of the world;
Since we’ve met, why must we have known each other before?
I left the Imperial Capital last year,
Banished and bedridden with illness in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, without music;
All year long, I hear not the sounds of silk and bamboo.
Living near the Pen River where the land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboos grow around my house.
What do I hear there, morning and evening?
Cuckoos bleaking blood, monkeys wailing mournfully.
On spring river blooms’ mornings and autumn moon nights,
I often take wine and pour it alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
They are harsh, discordant, and unbearable to listen to.
Tonight I heard your pipa’s language,
It was like hearing celestial music, my ears suddenly clear.
Please, don’t refuse to sit again and play one more tune;
For your sake, I shall compose *The Ballad of the Pipa*.
Moved by my words, she stood for a long while,
Then sat down again, tightening the strings, which now played faster.
Sorrowful, unlike the previous sound,
Those seated again listened and all covered their faces, weeping.
Who among the guests shed the most tears?
The Sima of Jiangzhou, whose blue robe was soaked through."}

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "**The Ballad of the Pipa**

By the Yangtze at Xunyang, I bid my guest farewell at night;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn chill.
The host dismounted, the guest stepped onto his boat;
We raised our cups to drink, but no music played.
Drunk yet joyless, we faced the sorrow of parting;
As we said goodbye, the vast river bathed the moon.
Suddenly, from across the water, came the sound of a pipa!
The host forgot to go home, the guest delayed his departure.
Following the sound, I asked softly who was playing;
The pipa stopped, as if she hesitated to speak.
I moved my boat closer and invited her to meet;
We added more wine, turned up the lamps, and resumed the feast.
After many calls and entreaties, she finally appeared,
Still holding her pipa, half-covering her face.
She turned the pegs and plucked the strings two or three times;
Before the melody formed, emotion already poured forth.
Each string suppressed, each note full of thought,
Seeming to tell of lifelong frustration and unfulfilled dreams.
Head lowered, fingers moving confidently, she continued to play,
Expressing endless affairs hidden within her heart.
Light gathering, slow twisting, wiping, then plucking—
First playing *Ni Shang*, then *Liu Yao*.
The thick strings rumbled like sudden heavy rain,
The thin strings whispered like intimate confidences.
Rumbling and whispering interwoven in chaotic play,
Like large and small pearls falling into a jade plate.
Smoothly flowing like orioles singing among flowers,
Muffled and choked like spring water freezing under ice.
Ice-cold, sluggish, the strings seemed to snap in silence;
Silence halted, no sound for a moment.
Then arose new dark sorrows and hidden resentments;
At this moment, silence surpassed even sound.
Suddenly, like a silver vase bursting, water splashed out;
Like iron cavalry charging, swords and spears clashed and rang.
As the song ended, she drew her plectrum across the center;
The four strings sounded once, like tearing silk.
Boats on the east and west fell silent, saying nothing;
Only the white autumn moon shone upon the river’s heart.
Lost in thought, she placed her plectrum between the strings,
Straightened her clothes, rose, and composed her expression.
She spoke of herself: "I was originally a girl from the capital,
My home living near Shama Ling (Frog Mound).
At thirteen I mastered the pipa,
And my name belonged to the first division of the Imperial Music Bureau.
After finishing a tune, even great masters would admire me;
When I put on makeup, every beautiful woman envied me.
Young men from the Five Tombs competed to give me gifts,
For one song, I received countless bolts of red silk.
Gold hairpins and silver combs broke keeping time,
Blood-red skirts were stained with spilled wine.
Year after year passed in laughter and joy,
Idly spending the autumn moons and spring breezes.
My brother went off to war, my aunt died;
Day by day, morning by evening, my beauty faded.
Before my door, life grew cold, horses and carriages rare;
Aging, I married a merchant’s wife.
Merchants value profit over love, and care little for separation;
Last month he left for Fuliang to buy tea.
He left, and I waited alone at the river mouth guarding an empty boat;
Around the boat, bright moonlight, the river water cold.
Deep in the night, I suddenly dreamed of youth’s affairs;
I woke crying, tears staining my rouge-covered cheeks red.
I listened to the pipa and sighed already deeply,
And hearing these words, I sobbed anew.
Both of us are wanderers lost at the end of the world;
Since we’ve met, why must we have known each other before?
I left the Imperial Capital last year,
Banished and bedridden with illness in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, without music;
All year long, I hear not the sounds of silk and bamboo.
Living near the Pen River where the land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboos grow around my house.
What do I hear there, morning and evening?
Cuckoos bleaking blood, monkeys wailing mournfully.
On spring river blooms’ mornings and autumn moon nights,
I often take wine and pour it alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
They are harsh, discordant, and unbearable to listen to.
Tonight I heard your pipa’s language,
It was like hearing celestial music, my ears suddenly clear.
Please, don’t refuse to sit again and play one more tune;
For your sake, I shall compose *The Ballad of the Pipa*.
Moved by my words, she stood for a long while,
Then sat down again, tightening the strings, which now played faster.
Sorrowful, unlike the previous sound,
Those seated again listened and all covered their faces, weeping.
Who among the guests shed the most tears?
The Sima of Jiangzhou, whose blue robe was soaked through."}

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "**The Song of the Pipa**

By the Xunyang River, at night, I bid farewell to a guest;
Maple leaves and reed blossoms shiver in the autumn breeze.
I dismounted my horse while my guest remained on his boat;
We raised our cups intending to drink, but had no music to play.
Though drunk, joy eluded us as we faced parting’s sorrow;
At the moment of departure, the vast river submerged the moon in its depths.

Suddenly, from across the water, came the sound of pipa strings;
The host forgot to return home, the guest delayed his departure.
Following the sound, I asked softly who was playing;
The pipa notes ceased, hesitating, as if wishing to speak but holding back.
I moved my boat closer to invite her to meet me;
More wine was served, lamps were relit, and the feast resumed.
Called upon time and again, she finally emerged,
Still holding her pipa before her face, half-concealing herself.

She turned the tuning pegs and plucked a few preliminary strings;
Before the melody formed, emotion already filled the air.
Each string murmured with suppressed feeling, each note carrying deep thought,
Seeming to recount a lifetime of unfulfilled ambitions.
Head bowed low, fingers moving deftly, she played on continuously,
Expressing the boundless sorrows within her heart.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, sweeping then plucking,
First she played "Rainbow Robes," then followed with "Six Strings."

The thick strings clattered loudly like sudden rain,
The thin strings whispered softly like private confidences.
Loud and soft notes intermingled in complex harmony,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Sweet and smooth, like orioles singing beneath flowers,
Then choked and muffled, like spring water struggling under ice.
The cold, stagnant spring froze the strings into silence,
The blocked flow caused the sound to pause briefly.
A hidden sorrow and secret resentment arose within this quietude;
In such moments, silence surpasses even the most eloquent speech.

Then suddenly, like a silver vase bursting open, water sprang forth;
Like armored cavalry charging out, blades and spears clashed.
As the song ended, she drew the plectrum sharply across the center strings,
All four strings sounded together, tearing like silk being ripped apart.
Eastward boats and westward ships fell silent, listening intently;
Only the white autumn moon remained visible over the river’s center.

Lost in reflection, she paused, placed the plectrum among the strings,
Straightened her clothes, rose, and composed her expression.
She spoke: "Originally, I was a daughter of the capital city,
My home once stood below Xiama Ridge.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa art,
My name ranked first among the Imperial Music Bureau's performers.
After finishing a piece, even great masters would bow in admiration;
Once made up, other beautiful women often envied my charm.
Young men from the Five Mausoleums competed to offer me red silk scarves;
For one song alone, I received countless lengths of crimson gauze.
Gold-inlaid hairpins and silver combs broke keeping time to the beat,
Blood-red skirts stained by spilled wine during revelry.
Year after year, laughter and joy continued endlessly,
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed by carelessly.
But then my brother went off to join the army, and my aunt died;
Days faded into nights, and my youthful beauty began to wane.
The carriage traffic before my door grew sparse and cold,
And so, growing old, I married a merchant as his wife.
Merchants prize profit lightly regarding separation;
Last month, he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He left, and I stayed guarding an empty boat at the river mouth,
Surrounded only by bright moonlight and cold river waters.
Late at night, I suddenly dreamed of affairs from my youth;
Waking from tears, my rouge-stained makeup trailed down my cheeks in streams."

Hearing the pipa, I had already sighed deeply;
Listening to these words, I felt even heavier grief.
We are both people adrift at the edge of heaven, lost and fallen;
Since we have met, does it matter that we did not know each other before?

I myself parted from the imperial capital last year,
Exiled here to lie ill in the town of Xunyang.
Xunyang is remote, devoid of music;
Throughout the entire year, no sounds of silk and bamboo reach my ears.
Living near Pen River where the land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my dwelling.
What can one hear here, morning or evening?
Cuckoos crying blood and apes wailing in their grief.
On spring rivers, flower mornings, and autumn moonlit nights,
Often I take wine and pour it alone for myself.
Are there truly no mountain songs or village flutes?
Their harsh, discordant tones are too painful to endure.

Tonight, hearing your pipa melodies,
It is like listening to immortal music; my ears are suddenly clear.
Please do not refuse to sit and play another piece;
For you, I shall compose a new ballad: *The Song of the Pipa*.

Moved by my words, she stood for a long while in silence,
Then sat back down, tightening her grip on the strings, which now sounded more urgent.
Her mournful notes differed greatly from those played just now;
Everyone seated there listened again, hiding their faces in tears.
Among all present, whose tears flowed most abundantly?
The Magistrate of Jiangzhou—his blue robe wet through."}

Roaring and whispering mix together,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
The melody glides like orioles singing under blossoms,
Sobs like a spring trapped beneath ice.
Ice-cold and sluggish, the strings seem to freeze;
Frozen and blocked, the sound briefly pauses.
New hidden sorrows and resentments arise;
Now silence speaks louder than sound.
Then suddenly, like a silver bottle bursting, water sprays,
Like iron cavalry charging, swords clang.
When the song ends, she draws the plectrum across the center,
Four strings snap once, like silk tearing.
Boats east and west fall silent;
Only in the river's heart does the autumn moon shine white.
She sighs, places the plectrum between the strings,
Straightens her clothes, rises with composed grace.
She says she was originally a woman of the capital,
Living near Shama Ridge.
By thirteen, she mastered the pipa,
Her name listed first among the imperial musicians.
Her songs left skilled masters amazed,
Her makeup made even the beautiful Qiuniang jealous.
Young men from the Five Tombs vied to give her gifts,
For one song, countless bolts of red silk.
Gold-ornamented combs snapped as she kept time,
Blood-red skirts stained with spilling wine.
Year after year of laughter and joy,
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed idly by.
Then her brother joined the army, her aunt died,
Day and night went by, her beauty faded.
Fewer horses came before her door,
Growing old, she married a merchant.
The merchant values profit over farewell;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
Leaving her to guard an empty boat at the river mouth,
Surrounded by bright moonlight and cold water.
Late at night she dreams of her youth,
Waking weeps, tears staining her rouge.
Hearing her pipa, I already sighed,
And hearing her story, I am deeply moved.
Both lost souls wandering the ends of the earth,
Meeting now—why need we have known each other before?
Since last year I left the Imperial City,
Banished and ill, living in Xunyang Town.
Xunyang is remote, without music,
All year long I hear no strings or pipes.
My home near Pen River is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around.
What do I hear day and night here?
Cuckoos crying blood, gibbons wailing sadly.
In spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn nights,
I often take wine and drink alone.
Are there mountain songs and village flutes?
Crude and discordant, hard to listen to.
Tonight I hear your pipa words,
Like heavenly music, my ears are cleared.
Do not refuse to sit and play another tune;
For you, I will compose this "Song of the Pipa."
Moved by my words, she stands for a long time,
Then sits again, playing faster, strings urgent.
The melancholy differs from earlier sounds;
Everyone present listens anew, covering faces in tears.
Who sheds the most tears in this gathering?

Maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in the autumn chill.
The host dismounts, the guest is already on board;
We raise our cups to drink, but lack the music of pipes and strings.
Drunken yet joyless, we grieve as parting approaches;
In the moment of leaving, the vast river soaks the moon.
Suddenly, from across the water, the sound of a pipa rises;
The host forgets to return home, and the guest delays his departure.
Following the sound, I ask softly who plays;
The pipa falls silent, as if the player wishes to speak but hesitates.
I move my boat closer to invite her out;
More wine is added, lamps are brought back, and the feast resumes.
After a thousand calls and ten thousand summons, she finally appears,
Still holding the pipa before her, half-hiding her face.
She turns the pegs and plucks the strings a few times;
Before the tune begins, emotion already flows.
Each string murmurs in suppressed tones, each note laden with sorrowful longing,
As if telling of a life frustrated by fate.
Eyes lowered, fingers moving freely, she plays on,
Expressing all the endless sorrow within her heart.
Fingers lightly press, slowly twist, sweep down, then flick up—
First "Rainbow Shirt," then "Six Melodies."
The thick strings rumble like a sudden downpour,
The thin strings whisper like private talk.
Rumbling and whispering intertwine,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Smooth as orioles singing beneath blossoms,
Then choking like springs trapped under ice.
Ice-cold and stagnant, the strings seem to freeze;
Frozen and blocked, the sound abruptly stops.
Yet another kind of hidden grief and secret resentment stirs within;
Here, silence surpasses all sound.
Then suddenly, like a silver vase breaking with water bursting forth,
Like iron cavalry charging with swords clashing loud.
At the tune’s end, her pick sweeps forcefully across the middle strings;
All four strings strike together, tearing silk with a sharp snap.
Boats to the east and west fall silent;
Only the white autumn moon reflects in the river’s heart.
Musing softly, she sets the pick aside among the strings,
Straightens her clothes and stands up, composing her expression.
She tells me, "I was originally a maiden from the imperial capital,
My home lay near Shama Ling.
By thirteen, I had mastered the pipa;
My name belonged to the first troupe of the imperial academy.
When I finished a piece, even the great musicians bowed in admiration;
When I dressed, every courtesan grew jealous.
Nobles’ sons vied to reward me with rolls of silken head-wraps,
For one song, countless bolts of red silk were given.
Gold-inlaid combs snapped in time to the beat,
Blood-red skirts stained by spilling wine.
Year after year passed in laughter and joy,
Autumn moons and spring winds were passed in idle ease.
Then my brother went off to war, and my aunt died;
With days turning into nights, my looks grew old and worn.
My doorway grew desolate, few horses came;
Too old now, I married a merchant as his wife.
Merchants prize profit above all, caring little for partings;
Last month he bought tea and left for Fuliang.
He comes and goes, leaving me alone guarding an empty boat,
Surrounded only by bright moonlight and chilling river waters.
Deep in the night, I dream suddenly of youthful days,
Crying in my sleep, makeup streaked red with tears.
Hearing the pipa, I sighed long ago;
Now hearing these words, again I lament deeply.
"Both of us are exiles wandering to the ends of the earth;
Since we meet here, why must we have known each other before?
"I left the imperial capital last year,
Banished to lie sick in the city of Xunyang.
This place is remote, without any music;
All year round, I never hear the sound of strings or flutes.
Living near the Pen River, where land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear there day and night?
Cuckoos bleeding from their cries, monkeys wailing in grief.
On spring rivers’ flowering mornings and autumn nights beneath the moon,
Often I take wine and pour it alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
They are harsh and jarring, painful to listen to.
Tonight, hearing your pipa speech,
It is like listening to celestial music; my ears are suddenly clear.
Please, sit again and play another tune;
For you, I will compose this 'Song of the Pipa.'"
Moved by my words, she stood for a long time,
Then sat down again, tightening the strings, playing faster.
Sorrowful sounds, unlike those heard before;
Everyone in the room, hearing them anew, covered faces and wept.
Who shed the most tears among those seated?

五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。

门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。

夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。

Thick, thin intertwined, they crash and mingle in the air,

Day fading into dawn, her youth’s vibrant hue grew pale,
The doorstep lonely now, few horses pass along the trail.
Aged beyond her prime, she wed a merchant man,
Who values profit high, disregards love’s tender span.
Last month to Fuliang Town he went, tea trading far away,
She guards this empty boat alone where waters cold display.
At night’s deep hour, old memories flood back in dreams,
Crying awake, makeup tears stream, leaving red streaks gleams.
Hearing her pipa sighs had stirred my soul with pain,
But hearing these words now makes my grief return again.
Both are exiled souls drifting at world’s vast edge, meeting true!
Why need we have known each other when hearts resonate so?
Since last year I left the imperial city’s grandeur bright,
Demoted here to Xunyang, sick, enduring endless night.
This place remote lacks music entirely throughout the year,
No strings or bamboo flutes reach my ear’s hollow sphere.
Living near Pen River, land low and damp surrounds,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboos enclose my dwelling grounds.
What do I hear from dusk till dawn in this desolate place?
Cuckoos bleeding cries, apes wailing in mournful case.
On spring river banks under blooming flowers, autumn nights serene,
I often take my wine alone, drinking amidst the scene.
Are there no mountain songs, nor village pipes’ rough tone?
Harsh and jarring, painful to the ear, they grate and moan.
Tonight I hear your pipa’s voice, celestial it seems,
My ears awakened fresh, washed clean by heavenly beams.

For you, I’ll compose a new ballad, titled 'The Ballad of the Pipa'.
Moved by my words, she stood a while in thoughtful pause,
Sat down again, tightened strings, letting tempo draw.
Melancholy filled the air, different from sounds before,
The whole assembly wept, tears streaming on the floor.
Who shed the most tears among those listening guests?
The Jiangzhou Sima's blue robe is soaked with grief."}

By the Yangtze at Xunyang, in the night I saw off a guest,
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn chill.
I dismounted; he was already on his boat.
We raised our cups to drink, but there were no winds or strings.
Drunk yet joyless, sad at parting,
As we parted, only the vast river bathed in moonlight remained.
Suddenly, from over the water, came the sound of pipa music.
I forgot to go home; my guest forgot to set sail.

Following the sound, I asked softly who was playing,
But the pipa stopped, as if hesitant to speak.
I moved my boat closer to invite her out,
Added more wine, trimmed the lamp, and reopened the feast.
After countless calls and entreaties she finally appeared,
Still holding the pipa, half-covering her face.

She turned the pegs and plucked the strings two or three times,
Before any melody formed, emotion was already present.
Each string was suppressed, each note full of thought,
Seeming to tell of a life unfulfilled.
She lowered her brows and casually continued to play,
Expressing all the infinite sorrows within her heart.

Lightly gathered, slowly twisted, swept and then picked—
First "Rainbow Robes," then later the "Six Strings."
The thick strings rumbled like driving rain,
The thin strings whispered like private talk.
Rumble and whisper intertwined in complex play,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Smooth and clear, like orioles singing under blossoms,
Low and choked, like spring water struggling beneath ice.
Ice-cold and sluggish, the strings seemed to freeze and stop,
Frozen and blocked, the sound momentarily ceased.

Yet another hidden sorrow and dark resentment arose,
At this moment, silence surpassed speech.
Then suddenly, like a silver vase bursting, water splashed forth,
Like iron cavalry charging, swords and spears clanging.
When the piece ended, she drew the pick across the center,
And with one strike of the four strings, it sounded like tearing silk.

East boats and west barges stood silent,
Only the autumn moon’s white light shone upon the river’s heart.
She pondered, put down the pick among the strings,
Straightened her clothes, rose, and composed her face.

She said: "I was originally a girl from the capital,
My home near Xiama Ling (Shrimp Hill Tomb).
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa,
My name listed first in the Imperial Academy.
After finishing a tune, even master musicians admired me;
When fully made up, even beautiful singers grew jealous.
Young men of the Five Mausoleums vied to offer gifts,
For one song, they gave countless bolts of red gauze.
Jeweled hairpins and silver combs broke keeping time,
Blood-red silk skirts stained by spilled wine.
Year after year filled with laughter and delight,
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed carelessly by.

Then my brother went off to soldiering, and my aunt died,
Evenings faded into mornings, and my beauty waned.
My doorstep grew cold, horse riders scarce,
Aging, I married a merchant for a wife.
Merchants value profit above all, indifferent to parting,
Last month he left for Fuliang to buy tea.
Leaving me alone to guard an empty boat at the river mouth,
Surrounded by bright moonlight and cold river waters.
In the deep night, I suddenly dreamed of youthful days,
Waking tearfully, my makeup streaked red down my cheeks."

Hearing her pipa, I had already sighed,
Hearing these words, I sighed again deeply.
Both of us are those fallen from grace at heaven’s edge,
Having met, why must we have known each other before?

Since last year I left the Emperor’s Capital,
Demoted and sick, I lay idle in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, without music,
All year long, not a single sound of silk or bamboo reaches the ear.
Living near the Pen River where land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboos grow around my house.
What do I hear here morning and evening?
Cuckoos crying blood and gibbons wailing in grief.
On spring river nights with blossoms, or autumn moonlit evenings,
Often I take wine and pour myself alone.

Is there no mountain song or village flute?
Their harsh, jarring sounds are painful to hear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa language,
It is like listening to celestial music; my ears are suddenly clear.
Do not refuse to sit again and play one more tune,
For you, I shall compose this "Ballad of the Pipa."

Moved by my words, she stood for a long while,
Then sat back down and tightened the strings, which played faster.
Mournful, unlike the previous sounds,
Everyone present heard and covered their faces in tears.
Who among them shed the most tears?
The Simajiang Prefect of Jiangzhou, whose blue robe was wet."}

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "**The Ballad of the Pipa**

By the Yangtze at Xunyang, in the night I saw off a guest,
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn chill.
I dismounted; he was already on his boat.
We raised our cups to drink, but there were no winds or strings.
Drunk yet joyless, sad at parting,
As we parted, only the vast river bathed in moonlight remained.
Suddenly, from over the water, came the sound of pipa music.
I forgot to go home; my guest forgot to set sail.

Following the sound, I asked softly who was playing,
But the pipa stopped, as if hesitant to speak.
I moved my boat closer to invite her out,
Added more wine, trimmed the lamp, and reopened the feast.
After countless calls and entreaties she finally appeared,
Still holding the pipa, half-covering her face.

She turned the pegs and plucked the strings two or three times,
Before any melody formed, emotion was already present.
Each string was suppressed, each note full of thought,
Seeming to tell of a life unfulfilled.
She lowered her brows and casually continued to play,
Expressing all the infinite sorrows within her heart.

Lightly gathered, slowly twisted, swept and then picked—
First "Rainbow Robes," then later the "Six Strings."
The thick strings rumbled like driving rain,
The thin strings whispered like private talk.
Rumble and whisper intertwined in complex play,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Smooth and clear, like orioles singing under blossoms,
Low and choked, like spring water struggling beneath ice.
Ice-cold and sluggish, the strings seemed to freeze and stop,
Frozen and blocked, the sound momentarily ceased.

Yet another hidden sorrow and dark resentment arose,
At this moment, silence surpassed speech.
Then suddenly, like a silver vase bursting, water splashed forth,
Like iron cavalry charging, swords and spears clanging.
When the piece ended, she drew the pick across the center,
And with one strike of the four strings, it sounded like tearing silk.

East boats and west barges stood silent,
Only the autumn moon’s white light shone upon the river’s heart.
She pondered, put down the pick among the strings,
Straightened her clothes, rose, and composed her face.

She said: "I was originally a girl from the capital,
My home near Xiama Ling (Shrimp Hill Tomb).
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa,
My name listed first in the Imperial Academy.
After finishing a tune, even master musicians admired me;
When fully made up, even beautiful singers grew jealous.
Young men of the Five Mausoleums vied to offer gifts,
For one song, they gave countless bolts of red gauze.
Jeweled hairpins and silver combs broke keeping time,
Blood-red silk skirts stained by spilled wine.
Year after year filled with laughter and delight,
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed carelessly by.

Then my brother went off to soldiering, and my aunt died,
Evenings faded into mornings, and my beauty waned.
My doorstep grew cold, horse riders scarce,
Aging, I married a merchant for a wife.
Merchants value profit above all, indifferent to parting,
Last month he left for Fuliang to buy tea.
Leaving me alone to guard an empty boat at the river mouth,
Surrounded by bright moonlight and cold river waters.
In the deep night, I suddenly dreamed of youthful days,
Waking tearfully, my makeup streaked red down my cheeks."

Hearing her pipa, I had already sighed,
Hearing these words, I sighed again deeply.
Both of us are those fallen from grace at heaven’s edge,
Having met, why must we have known each other before?

Since last year I left the Emperor’s Capital,
Demoted and sick, I lay idle in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, without music,
All year long, not a single sound of silk or bamboo reaches the ear.
Living near the Pen River where land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboos grow around my house.
What do I hear here morning and evening?
Cuckoos crying blood and gibbons wailing in grief.
On spring river nights with blossoms, or autumn moonlit evenings,
Often I take wine and pour myself alone.

Is there no mountain song or village flute?
Their harsh, jarring sounds are painful to hear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa language,
It is like listening to celestial music; my ears are suddenly clear.
Do not refuse to sit again and play one more tune,
For you, I shall compose this "Ballad of the Pipa."

Moved by my words, she stood for a long while,
Then sat back down and tightened the strings, which played faster.
Mournful, unlike the previous sounds,
Everyone present heard and covered their faces in tears.
Who among them shed the most tears?
The Simajiang Prefect of Jiangzhou, whose blue robe was wet."}

低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。

座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "**The Ballad of the Pipa**

By the Yangtze at Xunyang, in the night I saw off a guest,
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn chill.
I dismounted; he was already on his boat.
We raised our cups to drink, but there were no winds or strings.
Drunk yet joyless, sad at parting,
As we parted, only the vast river bathed in moonlight remained.
Suddenly, from over the water, came the sound of pipa music.
I forgot to go home; my guest forgot to set sail.

Following the sound, I asked softly who was playing,
But the pipa stopped, as if hesitant to speak.
I moved my boat closer to invite her out,
Added more wine, trimmed the lamp, and reopened the feast.
After countless calls and entreaties she finally appeared,
Still holding the pipa, half-covering her face.

She turned the pegs and plucked the strings two or three times,
Before any melody formed, emotion was already present.
Each string was suppressed, each note full of thought,
Seeming to tell of a life unfulfilled.
She lowered her brows and casually continued to play,
Expressing all the infinite sorrows within her heart.

Lightly gathered, slowly twisted, swept and then picked—
First "Rainbow Robes," then later the "Six Strings."
The thick strings rumbled like driving rain,
The thin strings whispered like private talk.
Rumble and whisper intertwined in complex play,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Smooth and clear, like orioles singing under blossoms,
Low and choked, like spring water struggling beneath ice.
Ice-cold and sluggish, the strings seemed to freeze and stop,
Frozen and blocked, the sound momentarily ceased.

Yet another hidden sorrow and dark resentment arose,
At this moment, silence surpassed speech.
Then suddenly, like a silver vase bursting, water splashed forth,
Like iron cavalry charging, swords and spears clanging.
When the piece ended, she drew the pick across the center,
And with one strike of the four strings, it sounded like tearing silk.

East boats and west barges stood silent,
Only the autumn moon’s white light shone upon the river’s heart.
She pondered, put down the pick among the strings,
Straightened her clothes, rose, and composed her face.

She said: "I was originally a girl from the capital,
My home near Xiama Ling (Shrimp Hill Tomb).
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa,
My name listed first in the Imperial Academy.
After finishing a tune, even master musicians admired me;
When fully made up, even beautiful singers grew jealous.
Young men of the Five Mausoleums vied to offer gifts,
For one song, they gave countless bolts of red gauze.
Jeweled hairpins and silver combs broke keeping time,
Blood-red silk skirts stained by spilled wine.
Year after year filled with laughter and delight,
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed carelessly by.

Then my brother went off to soldiering, and my aunt died,
Evenings faded into mornings, and my beauty waned.
My doorstep grew cold, horse riders scarce,
Aging, I married a merchant for a wife.
Merchants value profit above all, indifferent to parting,
Last month he left for Fuliang to buy tea.
Leaving me alone to guard an empty boat at the river mouth,
Surrounded by bright moonlight and cold river waters.
In the deep night, I suddenly dreamed of youthful days,
Waking tearfully, my makeup streaked red down my cheeks."

Hearing her pipa, I had already sighed,
Hearing these words, I sighed again deeply.
Both of us are those fallen from grace at heaven’s edge,
Having met, why must we have known each other before?

Since last year I left the Emperor’s Capital,
Demoted and sick, I lay idle in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, without music,
All year long, not a single sound of silk or bamboo reaches the ear.
Living near the Pen River where land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboos grow around my house.
What do I hear here morning and evening?
Cuckoos crying blood and gibbons wailing in grief.
On spring river nights with blossoms, or autumn moonlit evenings,
Often I take wine and pour myself alone.

Is there no mountain song or village flute?
Their harsh, jarring sounds are painful to hear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa language,
It is like listening to celestial music; my ears are suddenly clear.
Do not refuse to sit again and play one more tune,
For you, I shall compose this "Ballad of the Pipa."

Moved by my words, she stood for a long while,
Then sat back down and tightened the strings, which played faster.
Mournful, unlike the previous sounds,
Everyone present heard and covered their faces in tears.
Who among them shed the most tears?
The Simajiang Prefect of Jiangzhou, whose blue robe was wet."}

Ice-bound springs grew cold and sluggish, strings seeming frozen,
The flow halted completely, sound momentarily stilled.

Like iron cavalry charging out, clashing swords ringing loud.

A single sharp crack like tearing silk cut through the air.

Only the white autumn moon reflected on the river’s heart remained.
Lost in thought, she placed the plectrum among the strings,
Straightened her clothes, stood up, composing her solemn face.

She told how she was originally a girl from the capital,

By thirteen, she had mastered the pipa technique,
Enrolled in the first troupe of the Imperial Music Academy.

After performances, even master musicians bowed to her skill,
When made up, courtesans often envied her beauty.
Young nobles from Five Tombs competed to offer gifts,
For one tune, countless rolls of red silk were given.

Jeweled hairpins snapped while marking time’s beat,
Blood-red skirts stained by overturned wine cups.
Year after year passed in laughter and revelry,
Autumn moons and spring breezes spent carelessly away.

Then her brother joined the army, her aunt died,
Days and nights flew by until her youth faded.
Her door grew lonely, horsemen scarce outside,
Aging, she married a merchant as his wife.

He valued profit high, caring little for partings,
Last month leaving for Fuliang to trade in tea.
Gone and gone, she guards this empty boat at the mouth of the river,
Bathed in bright moonlight, chilled by the cold river waters.

Deep in night, suddenly dreaming of youthful days,
She wakes weeping, tears staining makeup down cheekbones.

And upon hearing these words, my grief intensified.
Both are wanderers fallen far from home,
Meeting here, need we ask if we knew each other before?

Demoted and sick, dwelling in Xunyang City.

Then sat back quickly, tightening strings, playing faster now.

Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn chill.
The host dismounted, while the guest remained aboard his boat;
We raised our cups to drink, but there were no pipes or strings to play.
Drunk yet joyless, we parted in sorrow;
As we left, the vast river was steeped in moonlight.

Suddenly, from over the water, came the sound of a pipa;
The host forgot to return home, and the guest delayed his departure.
Tracing the sound, I asked discreetly who was playing;
The music ceased, as if she wished to speak but hesitated.
I moved my boat closer to invite her out;
More wine was poured, lamps were lit, and the feast resumed.

After countless calls and entreaties, she finally emerged,
Still holding her pipa, half-concealing her face.
She turned the pegs and plucked the strings two or three times;
Before forming any melody, her emotion was already present.

Every string concealed restraint, every note harbored thought,
Seeming to tell of a life unfulfilled and ambitions thwarted.
With lowered brows, she played on without pause,
Expressing all the infinite affairs within her heart.

Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, brushing then picking—
First "Rainbow Robes," then "Six Flutes" followed.
The thick strings sounded loud like sudden rain;
The thin strings whispered soft like private talk.
Loud and soft intertwined in complex harmony,
Like large and small pearls falling into a plate of jade.

Now smooth as orioles singing through flowers below,
Now choked as springs struggling beneath ice.
Ice-cold waters slowed, strings seemed frozen still;
When music failed to flow, sound momentarily ceased.

Then arose hidden sorrow and secret resentment;
In that silence, quiet spoke louder than words.
Silver bottles burst with gushing spray;
Iron cavalry surged forth, swords and spears clashing.

The song ended; she drew the pick across the center strings;
One sharp sound ripped like tearing silk.
Boats to the east and ships to the west fell silent;
Only the white autumn moon hung over the river’s heart.

Lost in deep thought, she inserted her pick among the strings,
Straightened her clothes and rose, composing her features.
She said: "Once I was a woman of the capital city,
My home lay near Shrimp Mound Ridge.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa;
My name belonged to the First Division of the Imperial Troupe.
When I finished a piece, even skilled masters admired me;
When dressed up, beautiful courtesans envied my grace.

Young men of the Five Tombs competed to toss me red silk scarves;
For a single song, I received countless bolts of fine fabric.
Jeweled hairpins broke keeping time to the beat;
Blood-red skirts spilled with stains of wine.
Year after year passed in laughter and revelry;
Autumn moons and spring winds were spent idly away.

Then my brother went off to join the army, and my aunt died;
Day by day, youth faded from my face.
The door before me grew cold; horses and carriages became scarce;
Aging, I married a merchant for a wife’s status.

He values profit above all else, indifferent to separation;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
Gone and gone, I guard an empty boat at the river mouth;
Around the vessel, bright moonlight reflects on chilling waters.

Deep in the night, I suddenly dreamt of youthful days;
Crying in my dreams, tears stained my makeup red."

Hearing the pipa, I had already sighed deeply;
Listening to these words, I moaned again in grief.
We are both down-and-out wanderers under heaven’s wide sky;
Meeting now, why bother wondering if we knew each other before?

Since last year, having left the Emperor’s capital,
I have been exiled, lying ill in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, devoid of music;
All year long, I hear not the sound of strings and flutes.
Living near the Pen River, where land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my dwelling.

What do I hear here, morning and evening?
Dusky cuckoos crying blood, apes wailing mournfully.
On spring river mornings, flower-filled dawns, autumn moonlit nights,
Often I take wine and pour it down alone.

Are there no mountain songs and village whistles?
Their harsh, grating sounds are painful to the ear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa melodies,
It is like listening to celestial music; my ears are temporarily cleared.

Please do not refuse to sit again and play one more tune;
For your sake, I shall compose the *Song of the Pipa*.

Moved by my words, she stood for a long time;
Then sat down, tightened the strings, which grew urgent once more.
Sorrowful tones unlike those heard before;
Everyone in the room listened again, covering their faces in tears.

Who among us shed the most tears?
The Blue-Robed Magistrate of Jiangzhou, whose robe was wet."}

Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn chill.
The host dismounted, while the guest remained aboard his boat;
We raised our cups to drink, but there were no pipes or strings to play.
Drunk yet joyless, we parted in sorrow;
As we left, the vast river was steeped in moonlight.

Suddenly, from over the water, came the sound of a pipa;
The host forgot to return home, and the guest delayed his departure.
Tracing the sound, I asked discreetly who was playing;
The music ceased, as if she wished to speak but hesitated.
I moved my boat closer to invite her out;
More wine was poured, lamps were lit, and the feast resumed.

After countless calls and entreaties, she finally emerged,
Still holding her pipa, half-concealing her face.
She turned the pegs and plucked the strings two or three times;
Before forming any melody, her emotion was already present.

Every string concealed restraint, every note harbored thought,
Seeming to tell of a life unfulfilled and ambitions thwarted.
With lowered brows, she played on without pause,
Expressing all the infinite affairs within her heart.

Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, brushing then picking—
First "Rainbow Robes," then "Six Flutes" followed.
The thick strings sounded loud like sudden rain;
The thin strings whispered soft like private talk.
Loud and soft intertwined in complex harmony,
Like large and small pearls falling into a plate of jade.

Now smooth as orioles singing through flowers below,
Now choked as springs struggling beneath ice.
Ice-cold waters slowed, strings seemed frozen still;
When music failed to flow, sound momentarily ceased.

Then arose hidden sorrow and secret resentment;
In that silence, quiet spoke louder than words.
Silver bottles burst with gushing spray;
Iron cavalry surged forth, swords and spears clashing.

The song ended; she drew the pick across the center strings;
One sharp sound ripped like tearing silk.
Boats to the east and ships to the west fell silent;
Only the white autumn moon hung over the river’s heart.

Lost in deep thought, she inserted her pick among the strings,
Straightened her clothes and rose, composing her features.

My home lay near Xiamaling.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa;
My name belonged to the First Division of the Imperial Troupe.
When I finished a piece, even skilled masters admired me;
When dressed up, beautiful courtesans envied my grace.

Young men of the Five Tombs competed to toss me red silk scarves;
For a single song, I received countless bolts of fine fabric.
Jeweled hairpins broke keeping time to the beat;
Blood-red skirts spilled with stains of wine.
Year after year passed in laughter and revelry;
Autumn moons and spring winds were spent idly away.

Then my brother went off to join the army, and my aunt died;
Day by day, youth faded from my face.
The door before me grew cold; horses and carriages became scarce;
Aging, I married a merchant for a wife’s status.

He values profit above all else, indifferent to separation;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
Gone and gone, I guard an empty boat at the river mouth;
Around the vessel, bright moonlight reflects on chilling waters.

Deep in the night, I suddenly dreamt of youthful days;
Crying in my dreams, tears stained my makeup red."

Listening to these words, I moaned again in grief.
Both of us are castaways drifting from the ends of the earth;
Meeting now, why bother wondering if we knew each other before?

I have been exiled, lying ill in Xunyang City.

All year long, I hear no sound of strings or pipes.

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "At the head of Xunyang River, I bid a guest farewell at night;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn chill.
The host dismounted, the guest was on board;
We raised our wine cups, longing to drink, but lacked music—no flutes or strings.
Drunkenness brought no joy, only sorrow before parting;
As we parted, the vast river immersed the moon in its depths.

Suddenly, the sound of a pipa drifted over the water;
The host forgot to return home, the guest delayed setting sail.
Following the sound, I quietly asked who was playing;
The pipa paused, and the player hesitated to speak.
I moved my boat closer to invite her out,
Refilled the wine, relit the lamps, and reopened the feast.
After countless calls and entreaties, she finally emerged,
Still holding the pipa, half-covering her face.

She turned the pegs and plucked the strings two or three times,
And though the melody had not yet begun, emotion was already there.
Each string was suppressed, each note full of thought,
As if telling of a lifetime spent unfulfilled.
With downcast eyes, she played with flowing ease,
Expressing all the endless matters within her heart.
Lightly pressing, slowly twisting, sweeping and plucking again,
First playing *Ni Chang*, then *Liu Yao*.

The thick strings rumbled like heavy rain,
The thin strings whispered like intimate murmurs.
Rumbling and whispering intertwined in mixed play,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Bird-like chirps slid smoothly beneath flowers,
Trickling springs choked difficultly under ice.
The cold, sticky spring froze, and the strings seemed to break;
When broken and blocked, the sound momentarily ceased.

But another secret sorrow and hidden resentment arose,
At this moment, silence surpassed sound.
Suddenly, silver bottles burst, water splashing forth,
Iron cavalry charged, swords and spears clashing loudly.
As the tune ended, she drew the pick across the center,
The four strings struck together, tearing like silk cloth.

East boats and west ships fell silent,
Only the white moon in the heart of the river remained visible.
She pondered, set down the pick among the strings,
Straightened her clothes, rose, and arranged her expression.

She said herself that she was originally a girl from the capital,
Living near Shama Ling.
By thirteen, she had mastered the pipa,
Her name listed in the first rank of the Imperial Music Bureau.
After finishing songs, even skilled masters would admire her;
Once made up, every beauty envied her.
Young men from the Five Mausoleums fought to give her gifts,
One song earned her unknown quantities of crimson silk.
Gold-inlaid combs were shattered keeping time,
Blood-red skirts stained by overturned wine.

This year laughter and merriment, next year too,
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed casually.
Her brother enlisted in the army, her aunt died,
Evenings pass, mornings come, and her beauty fades.
Before her gate, visitors became few, horses sparse,
Aging, she married a merchant as his wife.
That merchant values profit lightly regarding separation,
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He left, and she guards the empty boat at the river mouth,
Surrounded by bright moonlight and cold river waters.

Deep in the night, she suddenly dreams of youthful days,
Waking crying, makeup tears stain the red railings.

Hearing the pipa, I sighed deeply,
Then hearing these words, I lamented anew.
Both are people fallen into wandering fate beyond the sky’s edge,
Meeting now, why must we have known each other before?

Since last year, I left the imperial capital,
Banished to lie ill in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, without music,
All year long, no sound of silk and bamboo is heard.
My dwelling is near Pen River, low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboos grow around my house.
What do I hear here morning and evening?
Cuckoos bleeding cries and apes wailing sadly.
On spring rivers’ flower mornings and autumn moon nights,
Often I take wine and pour it alone.

Is there no mountain song and village flute?
They are hoarse, harsh, and unbearable to listen to.
Tonight, hearing your pipa speech,
It is like hearing celestial music; my ears clear for a moment.
Do not refuse to sit again and play one more tune,
For you, I shall compose the Song of the Pipa.

Moved by my words, she stood for a long while,
Then sat back, tightened the strings, which grew faster.
Sorrowful sounds unlike those before,
The whole audience listened again, covering their faces and weeping.
Who among the guests wept the most?
The Sima of Jiangzhou, whose green robe was wet."}

千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。

曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。

钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。

弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。

By the Xunyang River, I bid a guest farewell one night,
Beneath autumn’s chill, maple leaves and reed flowers sighed in the breeze.
I dismounted from my horse while he waited on his boat;
We raised our cups to drink, but lacked the music of flutes and strings.
Though drunk, joy failed us, and sorrow marked our parting;
Looking away, we saw nothing but the river soaking the moonlight.

Suddenly, sounds of a pipa drifted across the water,
And both host and guest forgot their duties: I stayed, he did not depart.
Tracing the sound, I asked softly who was playing,
But the pipa ceased, and the player hesitated to speak.
I moved my ship closer and invited her to come out,
Adding more wine, trimming the lamps, and resuming the feast.
After much calling and urging, she finally appeared,
Still holding her pipa, half hiding her face behind it.

She turned the pegs and plucked the strings a few times,
Before any melody formed, emotion already flowed.
Each string suppressed a sigh, each note carried longing,
As if narrating a lifetime of unfulfilled ambitions.
Head bowed low, fingers moving with ease,
Voicing all the endless sorrows within her heart.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, sweeping then picking,
First she played "Rainbow Robe," then followed with "Six Strings."

The big strings thundered like a sudden downpour,
The small strings whispered like hushed private talk.
Loud and soft notes intermingled,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Melodies slid smooth as orioles singing among blooming branches,
Then choked like spring streams struggling through ice beneath.
Ice-cold water stiffened, strings froze into silence,
The flow blocked, the sound momentarily ceased.

Yet hidden grief and deep resentment were born anew—
At this moment, silence spoke louder than words.
Then suddenly, like a silver vase bursting open, water spewed forth,
Or iron cavalry charging, swords and spears clashing loud.
As the song ended, she drew the plectrum sharply across the center,
The four strings sounded once, like silk tearing apart.

Boats to the east and west fell silent, no word spoken,
Only the white autumn moon reflected in the river’s heart.
Lost in thought, she placed the plectrum between the strings,
Straightened her clothes, rose, and composed her features.

She said herself: "Originally, I was a woman of the capital,
My home lay near Shama Ridge.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa,
My name ranked first among the courtesans of the Imperial Music Bureau.
After finishing a piece, even great masters would admire me;
When made up, every beauty envied my charm.
Young nobles from Five Tombs vied to toss silks at my feet,
For one song, they gave countless bundles of red silk.
Gold hairpins and silver combs broke keeping time,
Blood-red skirts stained by spilled wine.
Years of laughter passed into other years,
Autumn moons and spring winds spent carelessly.
Then my brother joined the army, my aunt died,
Time stole my youth, fading my beauty day by day.
Front gate grew cold, fewer horses visited,
Aged now, I married a merchant man.
He values profits over affection, parting lightly,
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
Now he is gone, leaving me alone guarding an empty boat,
Surrounded by bright moonlight and the chill river waters.
Late at night, I often dream of youthful days,
Waking with tears that ruin my makeup, running down my face."

Hearing her pipa, I had already sighed,
Now hearing her story, I grieved even more.
We are both fallen souls drifting at the world's edge,
Why must we have known each other before meeting today?

"Since last year I left the imperial capital,
Exiled here, sick in bed in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, devoid of music,
All year long, I hear neither silk nor bamboo instruments.
Living near the Pen River, in low, damp land,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo surround my house.
What do I hear morning and evening here?
Cuckoos crying blood, monkeys wailing mournfully.
On spring evenings with flowers, under autumn moons,
Often I take wine and pour it out alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village pipes?
Their coarse and harsh tones are painful to hear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa’s voice,
It is like listening to celestial music; my ears clear for a moment.
Do not refuse to sit again and play another tune;
For you, I will compose this 'Song of the Pipa.'"

Moved by my words, she stood for a long time,
Then sat back down, tightened the strings, which played faster now.
Melancholy, unlike the previous tunes,
As everyone present listened again, all covered their faces and wept.
Who shed the most tears in the room?
The Prefect of Jiangzhou, his blue robe soaked wet."}

Maple leaves and reed flowers rustle in the autumn wind.
I dismount; my guest is already on board;
We raise our cups to drink, but lack the music of pipes and strings.
Drunken yet joyless, we grieve as parting approaches;
In the moment of leaving, the vast river soaks the moon.
Suddenly, from across the water, the sound of a pipa rises;
The host forgets to return home, and the guest delays his departure.
Following the sound, I ask softly who plays;
The pipa falls silent, as if the player wishes to speak but hesitates.
I move my boat closer to invite her out;
More wine is added, lamps are brought back, and the feast resumes.
After a thousand calls and ten thousand summons, she finally appears,
Embracing the pipa, she covers half her face.
She turns the pegs and plucks the strings a few times;
Before the tune begins, emotion already flows.
Every string is suppressed, every note carries deep sorrow,
As if recounting a lifetime of unfulfilled ambition.
Eyes lowered, fingers moving freely, she plays on,
Expressing all the endless sorrow within her heart.
Light chords, slow twists, sweeping strokes, then picks—
First "Rainbow Shirt," then "Six Melodies."
The thick strings rumble like a sudden downpour,
The thin strings whisper like private talk.
Rumbling and whispering intertwine,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.

Then choking like springs trapped under ice.

Frozen and blocked, the sound abruptly stops.

Then suddenly, like a silver vase breaking with water bursting forth,
Like iron cavalry charging with swords clashing loud.

All four strings strike together, tearing silk with a sharp snap.

Only the white autumn moon reflects in the river’s heart.

Straightens her clothes and stands up, composing her expression.

My home lay near Shama Ling.

I was ranked first in the Imperial Music Bureau.

When I dressed, every courtesan grew jealous.

For one song, countless bolts of red silk were given.

Blood-red skirts stained by spilling wine.

Autumn moons and spring breezes treated casually.

My brother went off to war, and my aunt died.
The front gate became cold, horsemen rare;

Maple leaves and reed flowers rustle in the autumn wind.
I dismount; my guest is already on board;
We raise our cups to drink, but lack the music of pipes and strings.
Drunken yet joyless, we grieve as parting approaches;
In the moment of leaving, the vast river soaks the moon.
Suddenly, from across the water, the sound of a pipa rises;
The host forgets to return home, and the guest delays his departure.
Following the sound, I ask softly who plays;
The pipa falls silent, as if the player wishes to speak but hesitates.
I move my boat closer to invite her out;
More wine is added, lamps are brought back, and the feast resumes.
After a thousand calls and ten thousand summons, she finally appears,
Embracing the pipa, she covers half her face.
She turns the pegs and plucks the strings a few times;
Before the tune begins, emotion already flows.
Every string is suppressed, every sound holds sorrow,
As if recounting a lifetime of unfulfilled ambition.
Eyes lowered, fingers moving freely, she plays on,
Expressing all the endless sorrow within her heart.
Light chords, slow twists, sweeping strokes, then picks—
First "Rainbow Shirt," then "Six Melodies."
The thick strings rumble like a sudden downpour,
The thin strings whisper like private talk.
Rumbling and whispering intertwine,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Smooth as orioles singing beneath blossoms,
Then choking like springs trapped under ice.
Ice-cold and stagnant, the strings seem to freeze;
Frozen and blocked, the sound abruptly stops.
A new sadness and hidden resentment arise;
Here, silence surpasses all sound.
Then suddenly, like a silver vase breaking with water bursting forth,
Like iron cavalry charging with swords clashing loud.
When the song ends, she draws the pick across the center;
All four strings strike together, tearing silk with a sharp snap.
Boats to the east and west fall silent;
Only the white autumn moon reflects in the river’s heart.
Pondering deeply, she places the pick among the strings,
Straightens her clothes and stands up, composing her expression.
She says, "Once I was a girl from the capital city,
My home lay near Shama Ling.
By thirteen, I had mastered the pipa;
I was ranked first in the Imperial Music Bureau.
Even master players were convinced by my skill;
When I dressed, every courtesan grew jealous.
The young nobles of the Five Mausoleums vied to bestow silks upon me,
For one song, countless bolts of red silk were given.
Gold-inlaid combs snapped in time to the beat,
Blood-red skirts stained by spilling wine.
Year after year passed in laughter and joy,
Autumn moons and spring breezes treated casually.
As evenings fade and mornings rise, my beauty waned;
My brother went off to war, and my aunt died.
The front gate became cold, horsemen rare;
Too old now, I married a merchant as his wife.
The merchant cares only for profit, disregarding partings;
Last month he bought tea and left for Fuliang.
He comes and goes, leaving me alone guarding an empty boat,
Surrounded only by bright moonlight and chilling river waters.
Deep in the night, I dream suddenly of youthful days,
Crying in my sleep, makeup streaked red with tears.
I had already sighed at the pipa's tune;
Now hearing her story, my grief doubles.
"We are both exiles drifting to the world's end;
Meeting thus, what need had we to know each other before?
"I left the imperial capital last year,
Banished to lie sick in the city of Xunyang.
This place is remote, without any music;
All year round, I never hear the sound of strings or flutes.

Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.

We raise our cups to drink, yet lack the strings and pipes.
Drunk but not joyful, grief awaits our parting soon,
Parting time: vast waters drown the moon's reflection.
Suddenly, from across the water, pipa sounds arise,
The host forgets to go; the guest delays departure.
Seeking the source, I whisper, asking who is playing;
The pipa music stops, the player seems slow to speak.
I move my boat close by, inviting her to meet me,
Add more wine, trim the lamps, resume the feast anew.
Called again and again, she finally comes out,
Still holding her pipa, half hiding her face.
She turns the pegs, plucks two or three strings,
Before a tune forms, emotion already flows.
String after string, muted notes convey longing,
As if telling of a life unfulfilled and thwarted.
Brow lowered, fingers moving with ease, playing on,
Expressing endless matters within her heart.
Lightly pressing, slowly twisting, sweeping, then picking,
First playing "Rainbow Robe," then "Six Strings" melodies.

The thin strings murmur as private whispers do.

Like big and small pearls dropping onto a jade plate.

Choked and low as a spring flowing beneath ice.

Stopped and blocked, the sound briefly rests.
Hidden sorrows and secret grievances arise,
This silence speaks louder than any sound could.

Iron cavalry charges, swords and spears clashing loudly.
The song ends; she draws the plectrum across the center,
One final note from four strings, like tearing silk.
Boats east and west are silent, speechless all around,
Only seeing the white autumn moon upon the river center.
Lost in thought, she puts her plectrum between the strings,
Adjusts her clothes, rises, composing her demeanor.
She says she was originally a girl from the capital city,
Her home lived near Xiama Ridge below.
At thirteen, she mastered the pipa art,
Her name listed first among the imperial instructors.
After songs, even skilled masters would admire her skill,
When made up, courtesans like Qiuniang often envied her.
Young men from Five Mausoleums competed to give gifts,
For one song, bolts of red silk received beyond count.
Jeweled hairpins and silver combs broke keeping time,
Blood-red skirts stained by spilled wine during revelry.
Joy this year, joy next year passed casually away,
Autumn moons and spring breezes spent without care.
Her brother joined the army; her aunt died; time flew by,
Day and night changed, her beauty faded.
Before her door grew cold, horsemen rarely came,
Aging, she married a merchant who valued profit over love.
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea, leaving her alone.
She waits at the river mouth guarding an empty boat,
Around the ship, bright moonlight; the river water is cold.
Deep in night, she suddenly dreams of youth's events,
Waking weeping, her makeup tears streak red down her cheeks.

Now hearing these words, I sigh again heavily.
Both of us are fallen souls drifting far from home,
Meeting now—why must we have known each other before?

Exiled and sick, lying idle in Xunyang City.

All year round, no sound of strings or flutes is heard.

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "At night I bid farewell to a guest by the Xunyang River bank,
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn chill.
The host dismounted; the guest remained on the boat;
We raised our wine cups, yet lacked pipes and strings.
Drunkenness brought no joy as we faced parting’s sorrow,
Only the vast river, immersed in moonlight, greeted our farewell.

Suddenly, from over the water, came the sound of a pipa;
The host forgot to return home, the guest delayed his departure.
Following the melody, I asked softly who was playing,
But the pipa paused, hesitant before answering.
I moved my boat closer, inviting her to meet me,
Refilled the wine, lit the lamps, and resumed the feast.
After many calls and entreaties, she finally emerged,
Still holding the pipa, half-concealing her face.

She turned the pegs and plucked the strings a few times;
Before the tune took form, emotion already spoke.
Each string was muffled with sighs, every note laden with thought,
As if telling the story of a life unfulfilled.
With downcast eyes, fingers moving naturally, she played on,
Expressing all the boundless secrets of her heart.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, sweeping then picking,
First the 'Rainbow Robes,' then the rapid 'Six Melodies.'
The thick strings thundered like sudden heavy rain,
The thin strings whispered like private conversations.
Thundering and whispering intertwined in complex play,
Like large and small pearls clattering upon a jade plate.
The oriole’s song winds smoothly beneath flowers,
Then choked sounds struggle through springs under ice.
Ice-cold springs slowed the strings to stillness,
When silence fell and the voice ceased for a moment.
A new hidden sorrow and dark resentment arose—
In that instant, silence surpassed any sound.
Then, like a silver vase bursting open, water splashed forth,
Like iron cavalry charging, swords and spears clangored.
Ending the piece, she swept the plectrum across the center,
One final cry from the four strings, like tearing silk.
East and west boats lay quiet, speechless alike,
Seeing only the pale autumn moon reflected in the river’s heart.

She pondered deeply, inserted the plectrum among the strings,
Straightened her clothes, rose, and composed her expression.
She said: “I was originally a girl from the capital city,
Living near Shrimp Hill, in the old quarter.
By thirteen, I had mastered the pipa,
My name inscribed in the First Hall of the Music Academy.
After finishing a song, even great masters would admire,
And after makeup, peers often envied my beauty.
Young nobles from Five Mausoleums vied to gift me brocade,
For one performance, countless bolts of red silk were presented.
Gold-inlaid combs snapped keeping time,
Crimson skirts stained with spilled wine.
Year after year, laughter repeated itself,
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed casually by.
My brother joined the army, my aunt died,
Days turned to nights, and my youth faded away.
Before my gate, visitors grew scarce, horses rare,
So when old, I married a merchant man.
Merchants prize profit over affection, leaving easily,
Last month he went to Fuliang to trade tea.
He left, and I waited alone by the river mouth,
Surrounded by bright moonlight, the river water cold.
Deep in the night, I suddenly dreamed of my younger days,
Waking with tears staining my makeup red.”

Hearing the pipa, I had already sighed,
Now hearing these words, my grief deepened further.
“Both of us are wanderers fallen from grace,
Meeting here, why should previous acquaintance matter?
Since last year I left the Imperial Capital,
Banished to lie ill in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, devoid of music,
All year long, I hear not a single string or pipe.
Near the Pen River, where land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my home.
What do I hear there, morning and evening?
Cuckoos crying blood, monkeys wailing in sorrow.
Spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moonlit nights—
Often I pour wine, drinking alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
Their harsh, discordant tones are hard to bear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa’s language,
It is like listening to celestial music, clearing my ears.
Do not refuse to sit and play another tune,
For you, I will compose ‘The Ballad of the Pipa.’”

Moved by my words, she stood for a long while,
Then returned to sit, tightening the strings, playing faster.
Her mournful notes differed from those before,
To the full audience, each covered their faces and wept.
Who shed the most tears in the room?
The Jiangzhou Sima, his blue robe soaked."}

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。

醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。

春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
