Small strings whisper like private talk.
Thunder and whisper intermingle,
Like large and small pearls falling into a jade plate.

A new hidden sorrow, a dark regret arises;

Iron cavalry charges, swords and spears clang.

Straightens her clothes, rises with composed dignity.

My home lived below Shama Ridge.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa,
My name belonged to the first rank of the Imperial Academy.
When I finished playing, even great masters admired me;
When made up, other beauties envied me.
Young men of Five Tombs competed for my favors,
One song earned bolts of red silk beyond counting.
Jeweled hairpins and silver combs broke keeping time,
Blood-red skirts stained by spilled wine.
This year laughter, next year again,
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed idly away.
Brother went to army, aunt died,
Dusk passes, dawn comes, beauty fades.
Front gate desolate, horses sparse,
Aged, I married as a merchant's wife.

Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He left, I guard the empty boat at the river mouth,

Ugly clatter, hard to bear hearing.

Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn heart.
The host dismounted, guest on board; we raised our cups of wine,
But lacked the pipes and strings to make the mood divine.
Though drunk, no joy remained as parting drew near,
And moonlight drowned in misty waters, bleak and drear.
Suddenly across the water came pipa's strains,
I forgot my return, my guest held back his lanes.
Following the sound, I asked who played so shyly there,
The music stopped, as if hesitant to declare.
I moved my boat close by, invited her to meet,
Refilled the wine, trimmed lamps, renewed the feast's retreat.
After many calls she finally emerged with grace,
Holding her pipa still, half covering her face.
She turned the pegs and plucked two, three tentative notes,
Before the tune began, her feeling overflowed.
Each string suppressed a sigh, each note conveyed deep thought,
As if telling all the life that fortune had not brought.
With lowered brows she played on fingers free and light,
Expressing boundless sorrows hidden in her plight.
With gentle sweeps and slow twists, flicks both up and down,
First *Rainbow Robes*, then *Six Strings'* mournful sound.
The thick strings boomed like sudden rain in torrents fierce,
The thin ones whispered soft, as lovers could rehearse.
Thick, thin intertwined, they crashed and mingled clear,
Like large pearls falling, small pearls skipping, jade tray near.
Birdsong glided smooth through floral shadows sweet,
Muffled sobs flowed hard beneath ice-bound feet.
The cold spring froze stiff, strings seemed severed tight,
In silence choked, the song paused, losing flight.
Deeper grief and hidden hate began to stir within,
This void of sound spoke louder than any noise could win.
Then silver vases broke, water burst apart,
Iron cavalry charged, blades clashed, spears impart shock.
The tune ended; she drew pick across center line,
Four strings snapped once—like silk tearing—to make them mine.
East boats and west barges fell into hushed repose,
Only white autumn moon reflected on river's flow.
She paused, inserted pick among the strings with care,
Adjusted garments, rose, composed countenance fair.
She said she was a girl from capital’s bright core,
Her home below Shama Ling ancient door.
At thirteen mastered pipa, skill attained its peak,
Named first among teaching guilds where talents seek.
After songs, even masters bowed in awe,
When dressed, rival courtesans envied flaw.
Young nobles contended for her favor’s prize,
For one song, countless red silks given as dues.
Gold combs broken keeping time’s beat,
Blood skirts stained by spilled wine’s heat.
Year after year laughter, spring winds, autumn moons idly spent,
Until brother joined army, aunt departed silent.
Day fading into dawn, youth’s hue grew pale,
Doorstep lonely, few horses pass along trail.
Aged beyond prime, she wed merchant man,
Who valued profit high, disregarded love’s span.
Last month to Fuliang he went, tea trading far,
She guarded empty boat where waters cold are.
Night’s deep hour, old memories flooded dreams,
Crying awake, makeup tears left red streaks gleams.
Hearing pipa sighed stirred soul with pain,
Hearing these words made grief return again.
Both exiled souls drifting world’s vast edge, meeting true!
Why need we have known each other when hearts resonate so?

Demoted here to Xunyang, sick, enduring endless night.

No strings or bamboo flutes reach ear’s hollow sphere.

Yellow reeds and bitter bamboos enclose dwelling grounds.

Sat down, tightened strings, tempo draw.

The host dismounts from his horse while the guest stands on the boat; We raise our wine cups, but there is no music to accompany us. Drunk yet without joy, we face the sorrow of parting; As we leave, the vast river is submerged in moonlight. Suddenly, from over the water, comes the sound of a pipa; The host forgets to return home, and the guest delays departure. Turning the pegs and plucking the strings, two or three notes— Before the tune forms, emotion is already present. Each string suppressed, each note full of longing, Seeming to tell of a lifetime of unfulfilled aspirations. With lowered brows, she plays casually yet continuously, Expressing all the infinite matters within her heart. Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, stroking and then picking, First 'Rainbow Robe', then later 'Six Strings'. The thick strings rumble like sudden rain, The thin strings whisper like private talk. Cold, sticky, and涩 (astringent), the strings seem frozen; Frozen and blocked, the sound halts momentarily. Yet another hidden sorrow and secret hate are born; At this moment, silence surpasses speech. Suddenly a silver vase bursts, water spurting forth; Like iron cavalry charging, with swords and spears clashing. At the end of the piece, she draws the plectrum across the center; One strike from four strings sounds like tearing silk. East and west boats fall silent, no one speaks; Only seeing the autumn moon white in the middle of the river. She meditates deeply, inserts the plectrum into the strings, Straightens her clothes, rises, and composes herself. She says she was originally a girl from the capital city, Her family lived near Shama Mound. At thirteen years old she mastered the pipa, Her name listed in the first troupe of the imperial academy. Young men of Five Tombs vied to offer gifts; For one song, red silk was received beyond count. Ornate hairpins and silver combs shattered keeping time; Blood-red skirts were stained by spilled wine. This year laughter and joy followed last year's, Autumn moons and spring breezes passed idly by. Then her brother joined the army, her aunt died, Days and months slipped away, and her beauty faded. Few cars and horses came to her door anymore, So in old age she married a merchant's wife. But merchants value profit and disdain separation, Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea. Since then she guards an empty boat at the river mouth, Surrounded by bright moonlight and cold river water. Deep at night she suddenly dreams of youth's affairs, Waking crying, tears stain her rouge, running down her face. Hearing her pipa, I sighed deeply, And hearing these words, my sighs grew heavier still. Both are lost wanderers at the end of the world, Meeting here, why need have known each other before? Even on spring rivers, flower mornings, or autumn moon nights, Often I take wine and pour alone. Are there not mountain songs and village flutes? Their harsh, confused noises are unbearable to listen. Tonight hearing your pipa speech, It is like listening to celestial music, making my ears clear once again. Do not refuse to sit and play another piece; For you, I shall compose this 'Song of the Pipa'. Moved by my words, she stood for a long time, Then sat back down, tightening the strings, which played faster. Sorrowful sounds unlike those before, Everyone present covered their faces and wept anew. Who among the guests shed the most tears? The Jiangzhou Sima, whose blue robe is soaked wet."}

Maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in autumn's chill.
The host dismounts, his guest remains aboard the boat;
We raise our cups to drink, but lack the music’s note.
In drunkenness no joy; we part with heavy hearts,
As moonlight spreads across the misty river’s waters.
Suddenly, from the water, pipa sounds arise,
And both my host forgets to go, my guest delays.
I seek the source, ask softly who is playing there,
The pipa stops, the player hesitates to speak or stare.
I move my boat closer, invite her to appear,
Add wine, relight the lamp, refresh the banquet here.
After ten thousand calls, she finally comes forth,
Still holding her pipa half-covering her face.
She tightens strings and plucks two, three notes so faint,
Before the tune begins, emotion fills the air.
Each string suppresses sorrow, each sound holds deep thought,
Seeming to tell of life’s disappointments wrought.

Expressing endless things that weigh upon her day.

First 'Nishang Yuyi', then 'Liuyao'’s refrain.

That silence speaks more than any sound could fill.

The four strings snap once, tearing silk with sharp design.

Only the white moon over middle river saw.

Named first in teaching quarters, known for excellence.

My makeup made rivals jealous, causing bitter deeds.

One song earned bolts of red silk beyond control.

Blood-red skirts stained by spilled wine, careless sweet.

Autumn moons and spring winds passed without our sights.

At leaving, vast and dim, the river soaks the moon.
Suddenly, from over the water, comes the sound of a pipa;
The host forgets to return; the guest does not depart.
Following the sound, I ask softly who plays;

More wine is poured, lamps turned back, the feast begins again.

She turns the pegs and plucks two or three strings;
Before the tune forms, feeling already flows.
Every string conceals restraint, every note carries longing,

With lowered brows, she plays on without pause,
Saying all the endless affairs within her heart.
Lightly pressing, slowly twisting, brushing then picking—
First “Rainbow Robes,” then “Six Flutes” follow.

Large pearls and small ones fall into a jade plate.

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。

寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。

五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。

春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。

座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "Ballad of the Pipa

By the Xunyang River at night, I bid my friend goodbye,
Maple leaves and reed flowers tremble in the autumn chill.
I dismount from my horse; he is already aboard his boat,
We raise our wine cups, but there are no flutes or strings to play.
Though drunk, we cannot find joy, and sorrow hangs as we part;
At the moment of farewell, the vast river holds the moon.
Suddenly, from across the water comes the sound of a pipa,
The host forgets to return; the guest delays his departure.
Following the music, I whisper, "Who plays so well?"
The pipa stops, and the player seems hesitant to speak.
I move my boat closer to invite her out,
Refill my wine, trim the lamps, and restart the feast.
After much calling and pleading, she finally appears,
Still holding her pipa, half hiding her face.
She turns the pegs and plucks a few notes,
Before the melody forms, the emotion is already there.
Each string is suppressed, each note laden with thought,
As if telling of a lifetime of unfulfilled ambition.
With lowered brow, she casually continues to play,
Expressing all the infinite affairs of her heart.
Lightly pressing, slowly twisting, strumming and picking,
First playing 'Rainbow Skirt,' then 'Six One.'
The thick strings churn like sudden rain,
The thin strings whisper like private talk.
Churning and whispering intertwined and mixed,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
The melody flows smooth as an oriole singing among flowers,
Then sobs low like a spring flowing under ice.
The cold spring stagnates, the strings seem frozen,
When they cease to flow, the sound momentarily halts.
Another hidden sorrow and secret resentment arise,
In this silence, quietness surpasses sound.
Then, like a silver vase suddenly bursting with splashing water,
Or iron cavalry charging out with clashing swords.
As the song ends, she sweeps the plectrum across the center,
One final chord tears like silk being ripped.
To the east and west, boats fall silent, not a word is spoken,
Only the white autumn moon shines upon the river's heart.
She pauses, inserts the plectrum into the strings,
Adjusts her clothes, stands up, composing her expression.
She says she was originally a girl from the capital,
Her home near Xia Ma Ling.
At thirteen, she mastered the pipa,
Her name recorded first in the Imperial Music Academy.
After performing, even great masters were impressed,
When dressed up, courtesans would envy her beauty.
Young men of the Five Tombs vied to give her gifts,
For one song, red silk pieces counted without end.
Jeweled combs broke in rhythm,
Blood-red skirts stained by spilled wine.
Year after year of laughter and joy,
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed idly.
Her brother went to join the army, her aunt died,
Day by day, her youth faded away.
The front gate grew lonely, fewer horses visited,
Too old to stay single, she married a merchant’s wife.
The merchant values profit more than love,
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He left, and she guards the empty boat at the river mouth,
Moonlight surrounds the boat, the river water is cold.
Late at night, she suddenly dreams of her youthful days,
Waking crying, red makeup stains tearfully wet her cheeks.
Hearing her pipa, I have long sighed,
And hearing these words, I sigh again deeply.
Both of us are drifters lost in the world,
Why must we have known each other before meeting?
Since last year I left the imperial capital,
Demoted and ill, I lie in Xunyang city.
Xunyang is remote, devoid of music,
All year round, I hear no strings or flutes.
Living near the Pen River, the land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear here morning and evening?
Cuckoos bleeding cries, apes wailing mournfully.
On spring river nights with flowers, on autumn moonlit evenings,
Often I take my wine and drink it alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
Their rough cacophony is hard to bear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa's voice,
It is like listening to celestial music, my ears clear anew.
Please do not refuse to sit down and play one more piece,
I will compose for you this 'Ballad of the Pipa.'
Touched by my words, she stood for a long time,
Then sat back, tightened the strings, playing faster.
The melancholy was unlike the previous sounds,
The whole audience covered their faces and wept again.
Who among the guests shed the most tears?
The Prefect of Jiangzhou, whose blue robe was soaked."}

By Bai Juyi

At Xunyang River's head, I bid a guest goodbye at night;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustle in the autumn chill.
The host dismounts; his guest is on the boat.
We raise our wine to drink, but lack the pipes and strings.
Though drunk, no joy remains; sad parting looms ahead.
At separation time, the vast river soaks the moon.
Suddenly, from the water, pipa notes are heard.
The host forgets to go; the guest delays his start.
Following the sound, we ask who plays: the music stops,
And she hesitates, afraid to speak her name.
We move our boats close by and invite her forth.
More wine is poured; lamps turned up; the feast resumes.
After a thousand calls, ten thousand cries, she comes.
Pipa held close, half her face still veiled.
She turns the pegs and flicks three or two strings.
Before the tune begins, emotion fills the air.
Each string suppresses sigh; each note conveys deep thought,
As if telling of a life unfulfilled.
Brows lowered, fingers moving continuously,
She speaks all boundless matters in her heart.
Lightly pressing, slowly twisting, sweeping then picking—
First 'Rainbow Garment', then 'Six Strings' follows.
The thick strings rumble like a sudden rainstorm;
The thin strings whisper soft as private talk.
Rumbling and whispering intermingle:
Large and small pearls falling into jade plates.
Flowers beneath, the warbling oriole flows smooth.
Deeply choked, the spring under ice struggles hard.
The ice-cold spring turns sluggish; strings freeze solid.
Frozen, blocked—the sound pauses briefly.
A different sorrow, hidden hate arises here.
This silence surpasses any spoken word.
Like silver vases bursting, water gushes out;
Like iron cavalry charging, blades clash loudly.
The song ends; she draws the plectrum across the center.
One final strum sounds like tearing silk.
East and west boats fall silent, speechless all.
Only the white moon shines upon the river's heart.
Thoughtfully, she puts the plectrum between the strings,
Adjusts her clothes, rises, composing her face.
She says herself once was a city girl,
Home lived below Xiama Ridge.
At thirteen, learned to master the pipa well;
Her name listed first among imperial schools.
When songs were done, skilled masters praised her art.
When dressed, rivals envied beauty and charm.
Young nobles from Five Mausoleums fought for gifts;
One song earned countless bolts of red gauze.
Jeweled combs broke keeping rhythm;
Blood-red skirts stained with spilled wine.
This year laughter, next year too;
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed lightly away.
Brother went to army; aunt died. Day and night pass.
Beauty fades; door grows cold, few horses come.
In old age, married to a merchant wife.
Merchants prize profit, treat partings lightly.
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
Left me alone at river mouth guarding empty boat.
Moonlight surrounds ship; river water cold.
Late at night, dream suddenly of youth's affairs.
Tears stain makeup red down cheeks.
Hearing this pipa, I already sighed.
Hearing these words, my grief doubles again.
Both we are wanderers lost at world's end.
Meeting now, need not have known before.
Since last year I left Emperor's Capital City,
Banished to live sick in Xunyang Town.
Xunyang remote, no music exists.
All year long never hear pipes or strings.
Dwelling near Fen River, land low and damp.
Yellow reeds, bitter bamboo grow around house.
What do we hear morning and evening here?
Cuckoos bleed tears; gibbons cry in agony.
Spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moon nights,
Often take wine, pour alone.
Are there none mountain songs and village flutes?
Hoarse noises harsh, difficult to listen to.
Tonight hearing you play pipa language,
Like listening to fairy music, ears clear momentarily.
Do not refuse to sit further, play one more song.
For you, I will compose Ballad of the Pipa.
Moved by my words, she stands long time.
Sits back, tightens strings; playing becomes urgent.
Mournful tones unlike earlier ones.
Full room hears again, wipes tears openly.
Who weeps most heavily in the audience?
The blue robe of Jiangzhou Prefect is wet."}

She says she was originally a girl from the capital city,
Living near Xiama Ridge.
At thirteen, she mastered the pipa,
Her name enrolled in the first section of the Imperial Music Bureau.
After finishing a tune, even skilled musicians admired her;
Once made up, often envied by beauty queens.
Young men of the Five Tombs vied to wrap gifts around her head,
For one song, red silk ribbons were countless.
Gold-inlaid hairpins snapped when beating time,
Crimson skirts stained with spilled wine.
Laughter and joy this year, again next year,
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed idly by.
Her brother went off to war, her aunt died;
Days pass, nights come, her beauty fades.
The door grows cold, horses rare;
Aging, she married a merchant's wife.
The merchant values profit over separation;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
Upon returning, she guards an empty boat at the river mouth,
Surrounded by bright moonlight and cold river waters.
Late at night, she suddenly dreams of youthful days,
Waking to find tears staining her makeup red.
Hearing the pipa, I already sighed,
And hearing these words, I sigh heavily again.
Both of us are castaways wandering afar;
Meeting now, why need we have known each other before?

I was demoted here, lying ill in Xunyang City.

All year round, no sound of silk and bamboo is heard.

Yellow reeds and bitter bamboos grow around the house.

Blood-crying cuckoos and mournful-gibbing apes.

Often I take wine and pour it alone.

It seems like celestial tune, clarifying my ears momentarily.
Please do not refuse to sit down and play once more;
For you, I shall compose "The Ballad of the Pipa."
Moved by my words, she stood for a long time,
Then sat back, tightening the strings, which played faster.

The whole audience listened again, covering their faces weeping.

Bright birdsong glides smoothly under blossoms;
Muffled sobs struggle through ice beneath springs.
When cold springs freeze and strings seem to cease,
And silence halts the flow, no sound remains.

At this moment, no sound speaks louder than sound.
Suddenly, a silver bottle breaks and liquid bursts forth;
Iron cavalry charge with the clash of blades.
At the song's end, she gathers her plectrum for one final stroke;
One strike of the four strings tears silk apart.
Boats east and west fall silent without word;
Only the white moon shines upon the river’s heart.
She pauses, places her pick among the strings,
Straightens her clothes, and composes her face.
She says she was originally a girl of the capital,
Living near the Xiamaoling district.
By thirteen, she mastered the pipa;
Her name belonged to the top tier of the Imperial Music Bureau.
After finishing a tune, even skilled masters would admire her;
Once made up, every beauty grew envious of her looks.
Young men of noble families vied to give gifts;
One single song earned countless bolts of crimson gauze.
Jeweled hairpins broke keeping time;
Blood-red skirts were stained by spilled wine.
Year after year passed in laughter and merriment;
Autumn moons and spring breezes were taken lightly.
Her brother joined the army; her aunt died;
Days turned into nights until age faded her charm.
The door became desolate, rare visitors came;
In old age, she married a merchant wife.
The merchant values profit over farewells;
Last month, he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He left her alone guarding an empty boat at the river mouth;
Surrounding the ship, bright moonlight chills the river waters.
Late at night, she suddenly dreams of youthful days;
Waking in sorrow, tears ruin her makeup.
Hearing the pipa, I sighed deeply;
Hearing these words, I lamented once more.
Both of us are wanderers fallen far from home;
Why must we have known each other before meeting?

Demoted and ill, lying idle in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, devoid of music;
All year long, not a flute nor string is heard.
My home near the Pen River lies low and damp,

By Bai Juyi

At night by the Xunyang River I saw off a guest;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn chill.
The host dismounted, my guest was aboard his boat;
We raised our cups to drink but had no music.
Drunk yet joyless, we faced the sorrow of parting,
As the vast river submerged the moon in its depths.
Suddenly, from over the water, came the sound of a pipa;
The host forgot to return, the guest delayed setting sail.
Following the sound, I asked who played; the pipa paused,
The player hesitated, shy to speak. We moved our boats close,
Invited her to come out, added wine, relit the lamps,
And reopened the feast. After countless calls and pleas,
she finally emerged, still holding the pipa to half-conceal her face.
She turned the pegs and plucked the strings a few times,
Before forming a tune, melody already brimming with feeling.
Each string suppressed sighs, each note carried longing,
As if telling of a life thwarted by fate. Head bowed, fingers moving effortlessly,
she poured out endless tales within her heart. Lightly gathering, slowly twisting,
plucking and sweeping, she first played "Rainbow Robes," then "Six Strings." The thick strings rumbled like sudden rain,
The thin strings whispered like private conversation. Rumbling and whispering, confused together,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Birds chirping smoothly under blossoms, muffled waters struggling beneath ice.
When icy springs froze stiff, the strings ceased their flow,
Silence held sway, and sound briefly died away.
Yet another hidden sorrow, a dark resentment arose:
In such moments, silence speaks louder than sound.
Silver vials bursting, water splashing forth;
Iron cavalry charging, swords and spears clanging.
When the song ended, she drew her plectrum across the center,
All four strings sounded once, tearing silk apart.
East and west boats fell silent, not a word spoken;
Only the white autumn moon remained in the river's heart.
She pondered for a moment, placed her plectrum among the strings,
Straightened her clothes, rose, and composed her expression. She said herself: originally a girl from the capital city,
Her home lay below Xiama Ling (Toad Tomb).
At thirteen she mastered the pipa, named among the first rank of the Imperial Music Bureau.
After playing, even expert musicians admired her skill;
When adorned, other beauties grew envious. Young men from Wuling fought to give her gifts,
One song earned countless red silks. Gold-inlaid hairpins snapped keeping time;
Blood-red skirts stained with spilled wine. This year’s laughter gave way to next year’s;
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed casually away.
Her brother went to war, her aunt died; day after day, youth faded.
Visitors dwindled at her door, horse and carriage rare;
Aging, she married a merchant as his wife.
The merchant values profit above all else, cares little for parting;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea. He left; she guarded an empty boat at the river mouth,
Surrounded by bright moonlight, the river water cold. Deep in the night she suddenly dreamed of her youthful days,
Waking from dreams, tears streaming, makeup running down flushed cheeks.
I heard the pipa and sighed; hearing these words made me groan anew.
Both are persons adrift far from home—what need to know each other before meeting?
I left the imperial capital last year,
Banished, ill, living in Xunyang City. A remote place, devoid of music;
All year long I hear no string or wind instruments. My dwelling near Pen River is low and damp;
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo surround my house.
What do I hear there, morning and evening? Cuckoos bleeding cries, apes wailing mournfully.
On spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moonlit nights,
Often I take wine and pour it alone. Are there no mountain songs and village flutes?
They are harsh, grating, unpleasant to listen to.
Tonight I hear your pipa speech; like celestial music, my ears brighten momentarily.
Please don’t refuse to sit again and play one more piece;
For you, I will compose this Ballad of the Pipa.
Moved by my words, she stood for a long while, then returned to sit,
Plucked the strings faster, growing urgent. Sorrowful sounds unlike those before;
The whole audience listened again and covered faces while crying.
Who among us shed most tears? The Sima of Jiangzhou, his blue robe soaked."}

座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "Night by night I bid farewell to a friend at the head of the Xunyang River,
Maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in the autumn wind.
The host dismounts while the guest is already on the boat;
We raise our cups to drink, but there are no pipes or strings.
Drunken yet joyless, we grieve as parting approaches;
At the moment of separation, the vast river soaks the moon.
Suddenly I hear the sound of a pipa across the water;
The host forgets to return home, and the guest delays departure.
I follow the sound and ask softly who plays;
The pipa stops, as if she wishes to speak but hesitates.
I move my boat closer to invite her out;
More wine is added, lamps are brought back, and the feast resumes.
After a thousand calls and ten thousand summons, she finally emerges,
Still holding the pipa before her, half-hiding her face.
She turns the pegs and plucks the strings a few times;
Before the tune begins, emotion already flows.
Each string sighs and restrains, every note carries deep thought,
As if telling of a life frustrated by fate.
Eyes lowered, fingers moving freely, she plays continuously,
Expressing all the endless sorrow within her heart.
Light gathering, slow rolling, sweeping strokes, then picking—
First playing 'Rainbow Garment,' then 'Six Melodies.'
The thick strings rumble like sudden rain,
The thin strings whisper like private talk.
Rumbling and whispering intertwine in complex play,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Smooth as orioles singing beneath blossoms,
Then choking like springs trapped under ice.
Ice-cold and stagnant, the strings seem to freeze;
Frozen and blocked, the sound abruptly stops.
A new sadness and hidden resentment arise;
Here, silence surpasses all sound.
Suddenly, like a silver vase breaking with water bursting forth,
Like iron cavalry charging with swords clashing loud.
When the song ends, she draws the pick across the center;
All four strings strike together, tearing silk with a sharp snap.
Boats to the east and west fall silent;
Only the white autumn moon reflects in the river's heart.
Pondering deeply, she places the pick among the strings,
Straightens her clothes and stands up, composing her expression.

My home lay near Shama Ling.
By thirteen, I had mastered the pipa;
My name belonged to the first troupe of the imperial academy.
When I finished a piece, even master musicians bowed in admiration;
When I dressed, every Qiu Niang grew jealous.
Young men of the Five Tombs vied to wrap me in brocade;
For one song, countless bolts of red silk were given.
Gold-inlaid combs snapped in time to the beat,
Blood-red skirts stained by spilling wine.
Year after year passed in laughter and joy,
Autumn moons and spring breezes treated casually.
Then my brother went off to war, and my aunt died;
Days turned to nights, and my beauty faded away.
The front gate became cold, horsemen rare;
Too old now, I married a merchant as his wife.
Merchants value profit over love, indifferent to separation;
Last month he bought tea and left for Fuliang.
He comes and goes, leaving me alone guarding an empty boat,
Surrounded only by bright moonlight and chilling river waters.
Deep in the night, I dream suddenly of youthful days,
Crying in my sleep, makeup streaked red with tears.
Hearing the pipa, I sighed long ago;
Now hearing these words, again I lament deeply.
"Both of us are exiles wandering to the ends of the earth;
Since we meet here, why must we have known each other before?
I left the imperial capital last year,
Banished to lie sick in the city of Xunyang.
This place is remote, without any music;
All year round, I never hear the sound of strings or flutes.
Living near the Pen River, where land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear there day and night?
Cuckoos bleeding from their cries, monkeys wailing in grief.
On spring rivers' flowering mornings and autumn nights beneath the moon,
Often I take wine and pour it alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
They are harsh and jarring, painful to listen to.
Tonight, hearing your pipa speech,
It is like listening to celestial music; my ears are suddenly clear.
Please, sit again and play another tune;
For you, I will compose this 'Song of the Pipa.'"
Moved by my words, she stood for a long time,
Then sat down again, tightening the strings, playing faster.
Sorrowful sounds, unlike those heard before;
Everyone in the room, hearing them anew, covered faces and wept.
Who shed the most tears among those seated?
The Magistrate of Jiangzhou, his blue robe soaked wet."}

座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "At the mouth of the Xunyang River by night I bid a guest farewell;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustle in the autumn chill.
The host alights from horse while the guest stays aboard his boat;
We raise our cups to drink, but there are no pipes or strings.
Drunk yet joyless, we part in bitter sorrow;
As we leave, the vast river is steeped in moonlight.
Suddenly, over the water, comes the sound of a pipa;
The host forgets to return home, the guest delays departure.
Seeking the voice, I ask quietly who plays;
The pipa stops, she wishes to speak but hesitates.
I move my boat closer to invite her out;
More wine is poured, lamps lit, the feast resumed.
After countless calls and summonings, she finally emerges,
Still holding her pipa, half-concealing her face.
She turns the pegs and plucks two or three notes;
Before forming any tune, emotion is already present.
Every string conceals restraint, every note harbors thought,
Seeming to tell of a life unfulfilled and ambitions thwarted.
With lowered brows, she plays on without pause,
Expressing all the infinite affairs within her heart.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, brushing then picking—
First 'Rainbow Robes', then 'Six Flutes' follow.
The thick strings roar like sudden rain;
The thin strings whisper like private talk.
Loud and soft, mixed together in play,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Smooth as orioles singing beneath flowers;
Choked as springs flowing with difficulty beneath ice.
Ice-cold waters sluggish, strings seem frozen still;
When music fails to flow, sound momentarily ceases.
Then arise hidden sorrows and secret resentments;
In that silence, quiet speaks louder than words.
Silver bottles burst with gushing spray;
Iron cavalry surge forth, swords and spears clashing.
The song ends; she draws the pick across the center strings;
One sharp sound rips like tearing silk.
Boats to the east and ships to the west fall silent;
Only the white autumn moon hangs over the river's heart.
Lost in deep thought, she inserts her pick among the strings,
Straightens her clothes and rises, composing her features.
She says: 'Once I was a woman of the capital city,
My home lay near Shrimp Mound Ridge.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa;
My name belonged to the First Division of the Imperial Troupe.
When I finished a piece, even skilled masters admired me;
When dressed up, beautiful courtesans envied my grace.
Young men of the Five Tombs competed to toss me red silk scarves;
For a single song, I received countless bolts of fine fabric.
Jeweled hairpins broke keeping time to the beat;
Blood-red skirts spilled with stains of wine.
Year after year passed in laughter and revelry;
Autumn moons and spring winds were spent idly away.
Then my brother went off to join the army, and my aunt died;
Day by day, youth faded from my face.
The door before me grew cold; horses and carriages became scarce;
Aging, I married a merchant for a wife’s status.
He values profit above all else, indifferent to separation;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
Gone and gone, I guard an empty boat at the river mouth;
Around the vessel, bright moonlight reflects on chilling waters.
Deep in the night, I suddenly dreamt of youthful days;
Crying in my dreams, tears stained my makeup red.'
Hearing the pipa, I had already sighed deeply;
Listening to these words, I moan again in grief.
We are both down-and-out wanderers under heaven’s wide sky;
Meeting now, why bother wondering if we knew each other before?
Since last year, having left the Emperor’s capital,
I have been exiled, lying ill in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, devoid of music;
All year long, I hear not the sound of strings and flutes.
Living near the Pen River, where land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my dwelling.
What do I hear here, morning and evening?
Dusky cuckoos crying blood, apes wailing mournfully.
On spring river mornings, flower-filled dawns, autumn moonlit nights,
Often I take wine and pour it down alone.
Are there no mountain songs and village whistles?
Their harsh, grating sounds are painful to the ear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa melodies,
It is like listening to celestial music; my ears are temporarily cleared.
Please do not refuse to sit again and play one more tune;
For your sake, I shall compose the Song of the Pipa.
Moved by my words, she stood for a long time;
Then sat down, tightened the strings, which grew urgent once more.
Sorrowful tones unlike those heard before;
Everyone in the room listened again, covering their faces in tears.
Who among us shed the most tears?
The Blue-Robed Magistrate of Jiangzhou, whose robe was wet."}

by Bai Juyi

At night I saw off my guest by the Xunyang River,
Where maple leaves and reed flowers shivered in autumn's chill.
The host dismounted, his guest aboard the boat;
They raised their cups to drink, but there was no music.
Drunken yet joyless, they grieved at parting,
While moonlight shimmered on the vast, misty river.
Suddenly, from the water, came the sound of a pipa,
So the host forgot to go home, and the guest did not depart.
I followed the sound and asked who played it;
The pipa stopped, and she hesitated before speaking.
We moved our boats closer and invited her to see us,
Added wine, lit the lamps, and began the feast again.
After many calls and pleas, she finally appeared,
Still holding the pipa close, half hiding her face.
She turned the pegs and plucked the strings lightly,
Before any melody formed, emotion was already present.
Each string suppressed sighs; each note carried longing,
As if telling of a life thwarted in its ambitions.
With downcast eyes, she played with casual ease,
Expressing all the boundless matters within her heart.
Her fingers gathered slowly, twisted, swept, then picked;
First 'Rainbow Robe Dance,' then 'Six Strings Melody.'
The thick strings thundered like a sudden rainstorm,
The thin strings whispered like private confidences.
Thunders and whispers mingled in complex play,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Sweetly clear as orioles singing beneath blossoms,
Then choked and low, like springs freezing under ice.
Cold and stagnant, the strings froze tight;
Frozen tight and blocked, the sound momentarily ceased.
A hidden sorrow and secret resentment arose;
In this silence, sound surpassed all sounds.
Suddenly, like a silver jar bursting open, water splashed forth,
Or armored cavalry charging out, swords clashing loudly.
The song ended; she drew the plectrum across the center,
The four strings struck together like tearing silk.
Boats east and west fell silent, no one spoke;
All that remained was the white autumn moon over the river.
Lost in thought, she placed the plectrum among the strings,
Straightened her clothes and stood up with composed dignity.
She said she had been a girl from the capital city,
Living near Shama Ridge in Xi'an.
At thirteen, she mastered the pipa,
And was ranked first among the imperial entertainment troupe.
When songs were finished, even great musicians praised her skill;
When made up, even beautiful courtesans envied her.
Young men from the Five Tombs competed to give gifts;
For one performance, countless rolls of red silk were won.
Gold-hairpins and silver combs broke keeping time;
Silk skirts stained crimson by spilled wine.
Year after year brought laughter and merriment;
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed casually away.
Then her brother joined the army, and her aunt died;
Days and nights changed, and her beauty faded.
Her door became desolate, few horses came to call;
Aging, she married a merchant as his wife.
The merchant valued profit over love of companionship;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He left her alone guarding an empty boat at the river mouth,
Surrounded by bright moonlight and cold yellow waters.
Late at night, she dreamed of youthful days,
Waking weeping with tears staining her rouge.
Hearing the pipa, I sighed deeply already;
Hearing her tale, I lamented anew.
Both are wanderers fallen from grace far from home;
Why must we have known each other before meeting?
Since last year I left the Imperial Capital,
Exiled to bed-ridden Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, without music;
All year long, I hear not a single string or flute.
My dwelling near the Pen River is damp and low,
Surrounded by yellow reeds and bitter bamboo.
What do I hear here morning and evening?
Cuckoos bleeding cries, monkeys wailing mournfully.
On spring nights with flowers, on autumn full-moon evenings,
Often I take wine and pour it out alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
Their crude and harsh sounds are unbearable to listen to.
Tonight hearing your pipasong,
It feels like celestial music sharpening my ears.
Do not refuse; sit again and play another tune—
I will compose for you this 'Ballad of the Pipa.'
Moved by my words, she stood for a long while,
Then returned to her seat, tightening the strings faster.
Melancholy now unlike the previous sound;
Everyone present listened again and covered their faces weeping.
Who shed the most tears in the room?
The Jiangzhou Prefect, whose blue robe was soaked through."}

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "By the Xunyang River, I bid farewell to friends at night;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustle in autumn’s chill.
I dismount from my horse while my guest stays in his boat;
We raise our cups to drink, yet have no music to fill the air.
Drunk though we are, joy is absent before this sad parting;
At separation, the vast river soaks a solitary moon.

Suddenly, pipas’ notes drift over the water’s surface;
The host forgets to return home, the guest delays departure.
Following the sound, I ask softly who plays so well;
The pipa stops, as if she hesitates to speak aloud.
We move our boats closer, invite her to come out;
Add wine, trim the lamp, begin again the feast anew.
After many calls, she finally appears, shy and slow, 
Still holding her pipa half-hidden behind her face.

She turns the pegs and plucks the strings two or three times;
Before the melody forms, emotion already lingers deep.
Each string muffles sorrow, each note conveys longing—
As if telling of a life unfulfilled, frustrations suppressed.
Head bowed, fingers moving steadily one by one,
Expressing all the endless stories locked within her heart.
Lightly pressing, slowly twisting, sweeping then picking—
First playing “Rainbow Garments,” then “Six Strings” next.

The thick strings rumble loud like sudden heavy rain;
The thin strings whisper softly like private confessions.
Loud murmurs and soft whispers intermingle freely;
Big pearls and small pearls tumble onto plates of jade.
Smooth as oriole songs flowing under blooming blossoms;
Stifled sobs like springs struggling beneath frozen ice.
Cold, viscous spring water freezes; the strings cease their song;
Blocked and unable to flow, the sounds pause for a moment.

Then arise hidden sorrows and silent resentments;
In this silence, meaning surpasses any spoken word.
A silver vase suddenly breaks, splashing forth its liquid;
Iron cavalry charges out, swords and spears clash loudly.
When the tune ends, she draws her pick across the center;
Four strings strike together, tearing silk in sharp rupture.

East and west ships fall quiet, not a word remains;
Only seeing the white autumn moon upon the river’s heart.
Lost in thought, she puts down her pick among the strings;
Adjusting her clothes, she rises, composing her demeanor.
She says herself: “Born a girl in the capital city,
My home lay near the Shrimp Frog Hill district.”
At thirteen years old, mastery of pipa was won;
Her name ranked first among the Imperial Music Bureau’s ranks.

Even great masters were impressed when tunes concluded;
Every time makeup was done, Qiu Niang grew envious.
Young nobles of Five Tombs vied to give red scarves;
One song earned countless lengths of silken threads.
Jeweled combs snapped keeping time with beats;
Blood-red skirts stained with spilling wine.
Year after year laughter continued endlessly;
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed casually away.

Brothers went off to war, aunties died one by one;
Evenings came, mornings returned, beauty faded away.
Before my door, cold emptiness, few horses remain;
Growing older, I became a merchant’s wife instead.
Merchants value profit heavily, disregard farewells lightly;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea far away.
Since then alone guarding empty boat at river mouth;
Surrounding ship bright moon, chilling river waters cold.

Late at night suddenly dreaming youthful days past;
Waking tears stain rouge running down cheeks in red lines.
Hearing the pipa makes me sigh deeply once more;
Listening to these words weighs heavily on my sighs too.
Both wanderers cast adrift at world’s edge alike;
Meeting here, what need to have known each other before?
Since last year leaving imperial capital behind me,
Demoted here, sick bedridden in Xunyang town.

Xunyang remote place without proper musical arts;
All year round never hearing string instruments play.
Living near Pen River where land low damp persists;
Yellow rushes bitter bamboo grow surrounding home.
Between dawn dusk hear only cuckoos crying blood;
And gibbons wailing mournfully through mists unclear.
Spring rivers flower mornings autumn moonlit nights often;
Take cup drink alone pour oneself sorrow inside.

Have I truly got no folk songs village flutes?
Harsh rough discordant noise difficult to endure.
Tonight hearing your pipa voice speaks eloquently clear;
Like celestial music ears momentarily awakened bright.
Do not refuse sit again play another piece;
For you compose poem titled Ballad of Pipa.

Moved by my words stood long contemplative still;
Returned seating tightened strings speed increased rapidly.
Melancholy unlike previous sounds previously heard;
Full audience listening again covered faces weeping.
Who shed most tears seated within gathering hall?
Prefect Jiangzhou official’s blue robe soaked wet completely."}

By the Xun River at night I saw off a guest;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in autumn's chill.
I dismounted, my guest was boarding his boat,
We raised our cups but had no music to drink to.
Drunkenness brought no joy; sad was parting soon,
When we bade farewell, only moonlight soaked the vast river.
Suddenly from the water came the sound of a pipa;
Forgetting to return, neither host nor guest set sail.
Following the sound, I asked softly who was playing;
The pipa paused, as if hesitant to speak.
We moved our boats close by and invited her out,
Refilled the wine, trimmed the lamp, and reopened the feast.
Called many times, she finally emerged,
Still holding the pipa half-covering her face.
She turned the pegs and plucked a few strings;
Before the tune began, feelings were already there.
Each string suppressed, each note full of thought,
As if telling a life of thwarted ambition.
Head lowered, fingers moving freely on and on,
Expressing endless matters within her heart.
Lightly pressing, slowly twisting, brushing then picking,
First "Rainbow Feather," then later "Six Strings."
The big strings thunder like sudden rain;
The small strings whisper like private talk.
Thundering and whispering mingled together,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Bird calls, smooth beneath blossoms;
A sobbing stream struggling under ice.
Ice-cold, sluggish, the strings seem frozen still;
Frozen still, unconnected, the sound briefly ceases.
Then arise hidden sorrows and secret regrets;
At this moment, silence surpasses sound.
As if a silver vase suddenly bursts, liquid spraying;
As if iron cavalry charge forth, swords and spears clashing.
The song ends; she draws the plectrum across the center,
All four strings strike once, like tearing silk.
Boats east and west fall silent without word,
Only seeing the white autumn moon in the river's heart.
She hesitates, puts down the plectrum among the strings,
Straightens her clothes, rises with composed grace.
She says: "Originally I was a girl from the capital,
My home near Shama Ling below.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa,
My name was listed in the first troupe of the Music Bureau.
After finishing songs, even master players admired me;
When dressed up, I was often envied by beautiful women.
Young nobles from the Five Tombs competed to give gifts,
One song earned countless scarlet silks.
Inlaid combs broke keeping time,
Blood-red skirts stained by spilled wine.
Laughing year after year,
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed idly away.
Brothers went off to war, aunties died;
Evenings depart, mornings come, beauty fades.
Front door grown cold, horse riders rare;
Getting older, I married a merchant’s wife.
The merchant values profit over separation,
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He left; I guard an empty boat at the river mouth,
Surrounded by bright moon, cold river water.
Deep in the night I suddenly dream of youthful days,
Waking crying, makeup tears run red down my face.
Hearing the pipa, I sighed,
Hearing these words, I lamented further.
Both are people lost far from home;
Meeting now, what need has passed acquaintance?
Since last year I left the Imperial Capital,
Exiled, bedridden in Xunyang City.
This place is remote, devoid of music;
All year long I hear no strings or pipes.
Living near Pen River where land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear here dawn and dusk?
Cuckoos bleeding cries, gibbons wailing mournfully.
Spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moon nights,
Often take wine and pour it alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
Their hoarse, discordant notes are hard to bear hearing.
Tonight hearing your pipa speech,
It is like listening to immortal music; ears clear momentarily.
Do not refuse to sit again and play one more tune;
For you, I shall write this Ballad of the Pipa.
Moved by my words, she stood for a long time,
Returned to sit, tightened the strings, which grew urgent.
Sorrowful sounds unlike those before,
The whole audience heard again and wiped their tears.
Who among them shed the most tears?
The Blue-robed Sima of Jiangzhou."}

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "By the Xunyang River, at night, I bid my guest farewell,
Amid maple leaves and reed flowers, autumn winds swirl.
The host dismounts; the guest is on his boat already there,
We raise our cups to drink, but lack the music’s air.
Though drunk, no joy remains before our parting tears,
When we must leave, the moonlight drowns in misty spheres.
Suddenly, from across the water, pipa notes arise,
Forgetting home, I linger; guests delay their departure’s ties.
I follow the sound, asking softly who might play,
The strings fall silent, as if shy to speak or stay.
I move my vessel close, inviting her to show her face,
Refill the wine, trim lamps anew, resume the banquet’s grace.
After a thousand calls, she finally emerges slow,
Still holding near her pipa, half her beauty’s glow.
She turns the pegs, then plucks two, three tentative sounds,
Before the melody begins, emotion floods the grounds.
Each string suppresses sighs, each note conveys deep thought,
As if recounting all the dreams that life has not brought forth.
Her brows lowered low, she plays with fingers free and light,
Expressing boundless sorrows hidden in her heart’s retreat.
With gentle sweeps, slow twists, and flicks both up and down,
First playing *Rainbow Robes*, then *Six Strings’* mournful frown.
The thick strings boom like sudden rain in torrents fierce,
The thin ones whisper secrets soft, as lovers rehearse.
Thick, thin intertwined, they crash and mingle in the air,
Like large pearls falling, small pearls skipping, on jade trays rare.
Clear birdsong glides through floral shadows, smooth and sweet,
Then muffled sobbing flows beneath the ice-bound street.
The cold spring freezes stiff, the strings seem severed tight,
In silence choked, the song pauses, losing its flight.
But deeper grief and hidden hate begin to stir within,
This void of sound speaks louder than any noise can win.
Then suddenly, silver vases break, water bursts apart,
Iron cavalry charge forward, blades clash, spears impart shock.
The tune concludes; she draws her pick across the center line,
Four strings snap once—like silk tearing—to make them mine.
East boats and west barges fall into hushed repose,
Only the white autumn moon reflects upon the river’s flow.
She pauses, inserts the pick among the strings with care,
Adjusts her garments, rises, composing countenance fair.
She states she was a girl from the Imperial Capital’s core,
Her home resided below Shama Ling’s ancient door.
At thirteen, mastering the pipa, skill attained its peak,
Named first among the teaching guilds, where talents seek.
After songs ended, even master musicians bowed in awe,
When dressed, her beauty caused rival courtesans’ envy’s flaw.
Young nobles of Five Tombs contended for her favor’s prize,
For one song played, countless red silks were given as dues.
Gold-inlaid combs broken keeping time’s rhythmic beat,
Blood-colored skirts stained by spilled wine’s crimson heat.
Year after year passed laughter, spring winds and autumn moons spent idly,
Until her brother joined the army, aunt departed silently.
Day fading into dawn, her youth’s vibrant hue grew pale,
The doorstep lonely now, few horses pass along the trail.
Aged beyond her prime, she wed a merchant man,
Who values profit high, disregards love’s tender span.
Last month to Fuliang Town he went, tea trading far away,
She guards this empty boat alone where waters cold display.
At night’s deep hour, old memories flood back in dreams,
Crying awake, makeup tears stream, leaving red streaks gleams.
Hearing her pipa sighs had stirred my soul with pain,
But hearing these words now makes my grief return again.
Both are exiled souls drifting at world’s vast edge, meeting true!
Why need we have known each other when hearts resonate so?
Since last year I left the imperial city’s grandeur bright,
Demoted here to Xunyang, sick, enduring endless night.
This place remote lacks music entirely throughout the year,
No strings or bamboo flutes reach my ear’s hollow sphere.
Living near Pen River, land low and damp surrounds,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboos enclose my dwelling grounds.
What do I hear from dusk till dawn in this desolate place?
Cuckoos bleeding cries, apes wailing in mournful case.
On spring river banks under blooming flowers, autumn nights serene,
I often take my wine alone, drinking amidst the scene.
Are there no mountain songs, nor village pipes’ rough tone?
Their grating cacophony is hard for ears to own.
Tonight I hear your pipa’s voice, celestial it seems,
My ears awakened fresh, washed clean by heavenly beams.
Please do not refuse to sit again and play another song,
For you, I’ll rewrite this ballad, long and strong.
Moved by my words, she stood a while in thoughtful pause,
Sat down again, tightened strings, letting tempo draw.
Melancholy filled the air, different from sounds before,
The whole assembly wept, tears streaming on the floor.
Who shed the most tears among those listening guests?
The Sima of Jiangzhou, whose blue robe stains wettest."}

She pauses, inserts the pick among the strings with care,
Adjusts her garments, rises, composing countenance fair.
She states she was a girl from the Imperial Capital’s core,
Her home resided below Shama Ling’s ancient door.
At thirteen, mastering the pipa, skill attained its peak,
Named first among the teaching guilds, where talents seek.
After songs ended, even master musicians bowed in awe,
When dressed, her beauty caused rival courtesans’ envy’s flaw.
Young nobles of Five Tombs contended for her favor’s prize,
For one song played, countless red silks were given as dues.
Gold-inlaid combs broken keeping time’s rhythmic beat,
Blood-colored skirts stained by spilled wine’s crimson heat.
Year after year passed laughter, spring winds and autumn moons spent idly,
Until her brother joined the army, aunt departed silently.
Day fading into dawn, her youth’s vibrant hue grew pale,
The doorstep lonely now, few horses pass along the trail.
Aged beyond her prime, she wed a merchant man,
Who values profit high, disregards love’s tender span.
Last month to Fuliang Town he went, tea trading far away,
She guards this empty boat alone where waters cold display.
At night’s deep hour, old memories flood back in dreams,
Crying awake, makeup tears stream, leaving red streaks gleams.
Hearing her pipa sighs had stirred my soul with pain,
But hearing these words now makes my grief return again.
Both are exiled souls drifting at world’s vast edge, meeting true!
Why need we have known each other when hearts resonate so?
Since last year I left the imperial city’s grandeur bright,
Demoted here to Xunyang, sick, enduring endless night.
This place remote lacks music entirely throughout the year,
No strings or bamboo flutes reach my ear’s hollow sphere.
Living near Pen River, land low and damp surrounds,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboos enclose my dwelling grounds.

Cuckoos bleeding cries, apes wailing in mournful case.
On spring river banks under blooming flowers, autumn nights serene,

Their grating cacophony is hard for ears to own.
Tonight I hear your pipa’s voice, celestial it seems,
My ears awakened fresh, washed clean by heavenly beams.

For you, I’ll rewrite this ballad, long and strong.

Sat down again, tightened strings, letting tempo draw.

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "At the mouth of the Xunyang River, I bid farewell to a guest by night;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn chill.
The host dismounted, while the guest remained aboard his boat;
We raised our cups to drink, but there were no pipes or strings.
Drunk yet joyless, we parted in sorrow;
As we left, the vast river was steeped in moonlight.

Suddenly, from over the water, came the sound of a pipa;
The host forgot to return home, and the guest delayed his departure.
Tracing the sound, I asked discreetly who was playing;
The music ceased, as if she wished to speak but hesitated.
I moved my boat closer to invite her out;
More wine was poured, lamps were lit, and the feast resumed.
After countless calls and entreaties, she finally emerged,
Still holding her pipa, half-concealing her face.
She turned the pegs and plucked the strings two or three times;
Before forming any melody, her emotion was already present.

Every string concealed restraint, every note harbored thought,
Seeming to tell of a life unfulfilled and ambitions thwarted.
With lowered brows, she played on without pause,
Expressing all the infinite affairs within her heart.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, brushing then picking—
First "Rainbow Robes," then "Six Flutes" followed.
The thick strings sounded loud like sudden rain;
The thin strings whispered soft like private talk.
Loud and soft intertwined in complex harmony,
Like large and small pearls falling into a plate of jade.
Now smooth as orioles singing through flowers below,
Now choked as springs struggling beneath ice.
Ice-cold waters slowed, strings seemed frozen still;
When music failed to flow, sound momentarily ceased.
Then arose hidden sorrow and secret resentment;
In that silence, quiet spoke louder than words.
A silver flask burst, its contents gushing forth;
Iron cavalry surged, swords and spears clashing.

The song ended; she drew the pick across the center strings;
One sharp sound ripped like tearing silk.
Boats to the east and ships to the west fell silent;
Only the white autumn moon hung over the river’s heart.

Lost in deep thought, she inserted her pick among the strings,
Straightened her clothes and rose, composing her features.
She said: "Once I was a woman of the capital city,
My home lay near Shrimp Mound Ridge.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa;
My name belonged to the First Division of the Imperial Troupe.
When I finished a piece, even skilled masters admired me;
When dressed up, beautiful courtesans envied my grace.
Young men of the Five Tombs competed to toss me red silk scarves;
For a single song, I received countless bolts of fine fabric.
Jeweled hairpins broke keeping time to the beat;
Blood-red skirts spilled with stains of wine.
Year after year passed in laughter and revelry;
Autumn moons and spring winds were spent idly away.
Then my brother went off to join the army, and my aunt died;
Day by day, youth faded from my face.
The door before me grew cold; horses and carriages became scarce;
Aging, I married a merchant for a wife’s status.
He values profit above all else, indifferent to separation;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
Gone and gone, I guard an empty boat at the river mouth;
Around the vessel, bright moonlight reflects on chilling waters.
Deep in the night, I suddenly dreamt of youthful days;
Crying in my dreams, tears stained my makeup red."

Hearing the pipa, I had already sighed deeply;
Listening to these words, I moaned again in grief.
We are both down-and-out wanderers under heaven’s wide sky;
Meeting now, why bother wondering if we knew each other before?
Since last year, having left the Emperor’s capital,
I have been exiled, lying ill in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, devoid of music;
All year long, I hear not the sound of丝竹 (strings and flutes).
Living near the Pen River, where land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my dwelling.
What do I hear here, morning and evening?
Dusky cuckoos crying blood, apes wailing mournfully.
On spring river mornings, flower-filled dawns, autumn moonlit nights,
Often I take wine and pour it down alone.
Are there no mountain songs and village whistles?
Their harsh, grating sounds are painful to the ear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa melodies,
It is like listening to celestial music; my ears are temporarily cleared.
Please do not refuse to sit again and play one more tune;
For your sake, I shall compose the Song of the Pipa.
Moved by my words, she stood for a long time;
Then sat down, tightened the strings, which grew urgent once more.
Sorrowful tones unlike those heard before;
Everyone in the room listened again, weeping behind their hands.
Who among us shed the most tears?
The Blue-Robed official of Jiangzhou, whose robe was wet."}

By Bai Juyi

On the banks of Xunyang River, I bid a guest farewell by night,
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in autumn's chill.
The host dismounted; the guest stayed aboard his boat;
We raised our cups to drink, but had no pipes or strings.
Though drunk, we found no joy; grief hung heavy at parting,
Just as we left, the vast river lay drowned in moonlight.
Suddenly, from over the water, came the sound of a pipa!
The host forgot to return, the guest delayed his departure.
Following the notes, we quietly asked: "Who plays there?"
The pipa paused; the player seemed hesitant to speak.
We moved our boat closer and invited her to join us,
Refilled our wine, brightened the lamps, and resumed the feast.
After countless calls, she finally emerged,
Still holding her pipa, half-covering her face.
She tuned the pegs and plucked a few tentative strings,
Before the melody began, emotion already flowed.
Each string murmured with suppressed sighs,
As if telling of a life spent in frustration.
With lowered brows, she played on without pause,
Expressing all the boundless sorrows of her heart.
Her fingers gathered lightly, twisted slowly, stroked then picked—
First the 'Rainbow Robe,' then the 'Six Melodies' followed.
The thick strings roared like sudden rainstorms,
The thin strings whispered like private confidences.
Roaring and whispering intermingled their notes,
Like pearls large and small falling into a jade plate.
Smoothly gliding, like orioles singing beneath blossoms,
Choked and sobbing, like springs trapped under ice.
When the icy spring grows cold and sluggish, the strings seem to stop,
And when they cease entirely, silence falls briefly.
Yet hidden within that silence lie new melancholy and silent resentment,
For in this moment, silence speaks louder than sound.
Then suddenly bursting forth, like a silver vase shattering and water erupting,
Or iron cavalry charging out, swords and spears clashing.
At the song's end, she drew the pick across the center strings,
All four strings rang once together, tearing silk-like sharpness.
Boats to the east and west fell completely silent,
Only seeing the white autumn moon reflected in the river's heart.
Lost in thought, she inserted the pick between the strings,
Straightened her clothes, rose, and composed her expression.
She said she was originally a girl from the capital city,
Living near the Xiama Ling district. By thirteen,
she had mastered the pipa, ranked first among the imperial entertainers.
After finishing a tune, even master players would admire her skill;
Once made up, court beauties themselves grew envious of her charm.
Young men from noble families vied to gift her red silk,
For one performance alone, they gave piles beyond counting.
Jeweled hairpins snapped when keeping time;
Scarlet skirts were stained by spilled wine.
Year after year passed in laughter and revelry,
Autumn moons and spring breezes wasted idly away.
Then her brother enlisted in the army, her aunt died,
And as twilight faded into dawn, her beauty faded too.
Visitors dwindled before her door, horses became rare;
Now aging, she married a merchant's wife.
But merchants value profit over love of companionship;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea, leaving her behind.
Alone she guards an empty boat at the river mouth,
Wrapped in moonlight while the river water turns cold.
Deep in the night, dreams of youth return unbidden,
Waking with sobs, tears staining her makeup red.
Hearing the pipa, I sighed deeply;
Hearing her story, my sorrow deepened further.
We are both souls cast adrift at heaven's edge—
Meeting now, why must we have known each other before?
Since last year I departed the imperial capital,
Banished here, ill and bedridden in Xunyang Town.
This remote place knows no music;
All year long, not a single piped tune is heard.
My home lies near Pen River, low-lying and damp,
Surrounded by yellow reeds and bitter bamboo shoots.
What do I hear morning and evening? Cuckoos crying blood,
Monkeys wailing mournfully through the mountains.
On spring rivers under blooming flowers, or autumn nights beneath the moon,
Often I take wine alone and pour myself into solitude.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
Yes—but crude and discordant, painful to listen to.
Tonight hearing your pipa melodies,
It feels like listening to celestial music, clearing my ears anew.
Do not refuse; stay seated and play one more piece for me—I'll write
'The Ballad of the Pipa' just for you."}

At night by the Xunyang River, I saw off a friend;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn wind.
I dismounted from my horse while he waited on his boat,
We raised our cups to drink, but found no music to delight.
Drunk yet joyless, grief hung heavy at our parting hour;
The moon shimmered pale upon the vast, mist-covered river.
Suddenly, drifting over water, came the pipa's song;
My guest forgot to sail, and I forgot to go home.
Following the sound, I whispered: "Who plays so well?"
The music paused; she hesitated, loath to speak her tale.
I moved our boats close by, inviting her to join us here,
Adding fresh wine, lighting lamps, resuming the feast anew.
Though called ten thousand times, she shyly came at last,
Still hiding half her face behind the pipa as she passed.
She twisted pegs and plucked the strings a few tentative notes,
Before the melody began, emotion filled the throats.
Each string sighed low with deep suppressed sorrow and thought,
As if telling tales of ambitions forever thwart.
Head bowed, she played with ease, letting fingers roam,
Pouring out endless stories hidden in her soul's home.
Light touches, slow twists, sweeps, and plucks intertwined,
First 'Rainbow Feather', then 'Six Strings' melodies refined.
Thick strings crashed like sudden rain pouring fast and loud,
Thin strings whispered soft secrets, tender, gentle, proud.
Loud and soft intertwining, mixed in complex play—
Large and small pearls dropping into a jade tray.
Smooth as orioles singing under blossoms bright,
Then choked like spring water struggling through ice at night.
Cold and stiff, the strings seemed frozen, sound grew faint and still,
Silence held more meaning than any note could fill.
A hidden grief awakened, bitter resentment stirred,
In this quiet moment, silence spoke louder than heard.
Like silver vases bursting, water spraying high and clear,
Or iron cavalry charging, swords clashing near.
The tune ended; she drew the plectrum across the center,
Four strings snapped once, like tearing silk, sharp and tender.
East and west ships lay silent, hushed in wonderment,
Only the white autumn moon watched on the river bent.
Lost in thought, she put down her pick amid the strings,
Adjusted clothes, composed herself with quiet things.
"I was once a girl from the capital's grand halls," she said,
"My home stood beneath Xiama Ling's shaded beds."
"At thirteen, I mastered the pipa, skilled and fine,
Among the first in the Imperial Music Academy's line."
"Famous musicians envied me after every performance;
Even beauty queens felt jealousy at my adornments."
"Young nobles fought for favor, tossing bundles of silk red,
For one song, countless lengths of scarlet cloth were spread."
"Gold-inlaid combs broke rhythm’s beat in joyful dance;
Blood-red skirts stained with spilled wine in wild romance."
"Year after year of laughter, careless and free-flowing;
Autumn moons and spring winds passed, life brightly glowing."
"But brothers joined the army, aunties died away;
Days and nights turned, youth faded, colors lost their sway."
"The front gate fell silent, horses rare, visitors gone;
In old age, I married a merchant, cold and alone."
"Merchants value profit over love, care little for goodbyes;
Last month he left to Liang to buy tea, no more ties."
"He's gone, and I stay guarding an empty ship by the port;
Moonlight wraps around it, river water cold support."
"Deep in night, dreams of youthful days come flooding back;
Tears stain makeup red as pillowcases soak.""
Hearing the pipa made me sigh deeply in sympathy,
And her words brought renewed tears, drowning dignity.
"We are both drifters far from home, fallen alike;
Why must we have known each other before tonight?"
"Since last year, leaving the Emperor's city behind,
Exiled to Xunyang, sick and weary-minded."

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。

大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。

门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。

座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "By the banks of the Xun River, I bade a friend farewell at night;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn chill.
The host dismounted while his guest remained upon the boat;
We raised our cups to drink, but lacked the sound of pipes and strings.
Though drunk, no joy we found, as sorrow marked our parting;
At the moment of farewell, only the moon floated on the vast river’s face.

Suddenly, from over the water, came the notes of a pipa;
The host forgot to return home, the guest forbore to depart.
Following the sound, I quietly asked who played;
The pipa ceased, yet she hesitated, loath to speak.
I moved my boat close by to invite her sight;
I added wine, relit the lamps, and reopened the feast.

After a thousand calls, ten thousand summons, she finally emerged,
Still holding her pipa before her face, half-veiled.
She turned the pegs and plucked a few initial strings;
Before a melody formed, emotion was already there.
Each string veiled low, each note heavy with thought,
As if telling of a life unfulfilled and thwarted.
With downcast brows, her fingers moved freely onward,
Expressing all the boundless matters in her heart.

She lightly gathered, slowly twisted, swept and then picked;
First playing "Rainbow Skirt," then "Six Strings."
The great strings thundered like sudden rainstorm's rush;
The small strings whispered like intimate confessions’ hush.
Thundering and whispering mixed in complex play,
Like large pearls falling into a jade dish, scattering away.

Now clear like orioles singing beneath flowers, swift and smooth;
Now choked like spring water blocked beneath ice, slow and tough.
When cold as ice, the flow became stiff, strings grew silent;
Silence halted when the passage found no way to pass.
Then arose hidden sorrows and buried resentments—
In this stillness, silence surpassed even sound’s expression.

Suddenly, as if a silver vase burst open, water spraying;
Like armored cavalry charging forth, swords clashing, spears ringing.
When the tune ended, she swept her pick across the center;
One sharp cry from four strings, like tearing silk that splits.

East boats and west barges stood in quiet speechlessness;
Only the autumn moon shone white in the river’s heart.
She paused, deep in thought, inserted the pick among the strings,
Straightened her clothes and rose, composing her countenance.

She spoke: "Once I was a girl of the imperial capital,
My home lay near the Shama Ling, where tombs reside.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa; my skill was renowned,
And ranked first among those trained within the Imperial Music Bureau.
After finishing a piece, even skilled masters admired;
Once dressed up, other beauties envied my grace.

Young men of Five Tombs vied to offer me gifts of cloth;
For one song alone, countless bolts of red gauze were mine.
Gold-inlaid combs shattered keeping time with the beat;
Blood-red silk skirts stained by overturned wine.
Year after year passed amidst laughter and merriment,
Idly spending autumn moons and spring breezes’ fleeting time.

My brother joined the army; my auntie died;
Days fled, nights came, my beauty faded with age.
Few horses remained before my door, visitors scarce;
Aged beyond marriageable years, I wed a merchant’s wife.

He valued profit, slighted separation’s pain;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea, far away.
Since then, I’ve waited here at the river mouth, guarding an empty boat,
Surrounded by bright moonlight, the river waters cold.

Deep in the night, I suddenly dreamed of my youth’s affairs;
In dreams I wept, my makeup tears staining red upon my face."

Hearing the pipa, I had already sighed in sympathy;
Hearing these words, my sighs grew heavier still.
We are both castaways wandering under heaven’s span—
What need is there to have known each other before?

"Since last year I left the imperial capital behind,
Demoted, ill, I lie sick in Xunyang City’s confines.
Xunyang’s land is remote, devoid of music’s charm;
All year round, I hear not silk nor bamboo’s sound.
Near the Pen River lies my dwelling, low and damp;
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo encircle my house.

What do I hear between dawn and dusk in this place?
Cuckoos crying blood, apes wailing mournfully.
On spring rivers’ flower mornings or autumn nights’ moonlit hours,
I often take my wine and pour it out alone.

Are there no mountain songs? No village flutes’ simple tune?
Their harsh, grating sounds are difficult to bear to hear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa’s language, pure and sweet,
It is like listening to immortal music; my ears are cleared anew.

Do not refuse to sit again and play another tune;
For you, I shall compose the 'Song of the Pipa.'"

Moved by my words, she stood for a long while in thought;
Then sat back down, pressing strings that played more urgently now.
Melancholy tones unlike the previous ones sounded;
Everyone present, hearing again, wiped their eyes with tears.

Who wept most heavily among those seated there?
The Sima of Jiangzhou, his blue robe soaked through."}

Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn chill.
The host dismounted while his guest remained upon the boat;
We raised our cups to drink, but lacked the sound of pipes and strings.
Though drunk, no joy we found, as sorrow marked our parting;
At the moment of farewell, only the moon floated on the vast river’s face.

Suddenly, from over the water, came the notes of a pipa;
The host forgot to return home, the guest forbore to depart.
Following the sound, I quietly asked who played;
The pipa ceased, yet she hesitated, loath to speak.
I moved my boat close by to invite her sight;
I added wine, relit the lamps, and reopened the feast.

After a thousand calls, ten thousand summons, she finally emerged,
Still holding her pipa before her face, half-veiled.
She turned the pegs and plucked a few initial strings;
Before a melody formed, emotion was already there.
Each string veiled low, each note heavy with thought,
As if telling of a life unfulfilled and thwarted.
With downcast brows, her fingers moved freely onward,
Expressing all the boundless matters in her heart.

She lightly gathered, slowly twisted, swept and then picked;
First playing "Rainbow Skirt," then "Six Strings."
The great strings thundered like sudden rainstorm's rush;
The small strings whispered like intimate confessions’ hush.
Thundering and whispering mixed in complex play,
Like large pearls falling into a jade dish, scattering away.
