Maple leaves and reed flowers rustle in the autumn chill.
The host dismounts; the guest is already on his boat,
We raise our cups to drink, but lack the music’s note.
Though drunk, no joy remains before our parting tears,
When we must leave, the moonlight drowns in misty spheres.
Suddenly, from across the water, pipa sounds arise,
Forgetting home, I linger; guests delay their departure’s ties.
I follow the sound, asking softly who might play,
The strings fall silent, as if shy to speak or stay.
I move my vessel close, inviting her to show her face,
Refill the wine, trim lamps anew, resume the banquet’s grace.
After a thousand calls, she finally emerges slow,
Still holding near her pipa, half her beauty’s glow.
She turns the pegs, then plucks two, three tentative sounds,
Before the melody begins, emotion floods the grounds.
Each string suppresses sighs, each note conveys deep thought,
As if recounting all the dreams that life has not brought forth.
Her brows lowered low, she plays with fingers free and light,
Expressing boundless sorrows hidden in her heart’s retreat.
With gentle sweeps, slow twists, and flicks both up and down,
First playing Rainbow Robes, then Six Melodies’ profound.
The thick strings boom like sudden rain in torrents fierce,
The thin ones whisper secrets soft, as lovers rehearse.
Thick, thin intertwined, they crash and mingle in the air,
Like large pearls falling, small pearls skipping, on jade trays rare.
Clear birdsong glides through floral shadows, smooth and sweet,
Then muffled sobbing flows beneath the ice-bound street.
The cold spring freezes stiff, the strings seem severed tight,
In silence choked, the song pauses, losing its flight.
But deeper grief and hidden hate begin to stir within,
This void of sound speaks louder than any noise can win.
Then suddenly, silver vases break, water bursts apart,
Iron cavalry charge forward, blades clash, spears impart shock.
The tune concludes; she draws her pick across the center line,
Four strings snap once—like silk tearing—to make them mine.
East boats and west barges fall into hushed repose,
Only the white autumn moon reflects upon the river’s flow.
She pauses, inserts the pick among the strings with care,
Adjusts her garments, rises, composing countenance fair.
She states she was a girl from the Imperial Capital’s core,
Her home resided below Shama Ling’s ancient door.
At thirteen, mastering the pipa, skill attained its peak,
Named first among the teaching guilds, where talents seek.
After songs ended, even master musicians bowed in awe,
When dressed, her beauty caused rival courtesans’ envy’s flaw.
Young nobles of Five Tombs contended for her favor’s prize,
For one song played, countless red silks were given as dues.
Gold-inlaid combs broken keeping time’s rhythmic beat,
Blood-colored skirts stained by spilled wine’s crimson heat.
Year after year passed laughter, spring winds and autumn moons spent idly,
Until her brother joined the army, aunt departed silently.
Day fading into dawn, her youth’s vibrant hue grew pale,
The doorstep lonely now, few horses pass along the trail.
Aged beyond her prime, she wed a merchant man,
Who values profit high, disregards love’s tender span.
Last month to Fuliang Town he went, tea trading far away,
She guards this empty boat alone where waters cold display.
At night’s deep hour, old memories flood back in dreams,
Crying awake, makeup tears stream, leaving red streaks gleams.
Hearing her pipa sighs had stirred my soul with pain,
But hearing these words now makes my grief return again.
Both are exiled souls drifting at world’s vast edge, meeting true!
Why need we have known each other when hearts resonate so?
Since last year I left the imperial city’s grandeur bright,
Demoted here to Xunyang, sick, enduring endless night.

No strings or bamboo flutes reach my ear’s hollow sphere.

Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn chill.
The host dismounted, the guest remained aboard his boat;
We raised our cups to drink, but there were no pipes or strings.
Though drunk, we found no joy, as sorrow marked our parting;
In that moment, vast mists hung low, with moonlight sinking into the river.

Suddenly, from over the water, came the sound of a pipa.
The host forgot to return home; the guest delayed setting sail.
Following the music, I asked quietly who was playing;
The pipa’s song paused, hesitant, before words began.
I moved my boat closer, inviting her to appear,
Refilling the wine jars, trimming the lamps, restarting the feast.
After a thousand calls and ten thousand entreaties, she finally emerged,
Still holding her pipa, half-covering her face in modesty.

She turned the pegs and plucked the strings two or three times,
And before any melody was formed, emotion already stirred.
Each string suppressed deep sighs, each note carried thought,
Seeming to recount a life of unfulfilled ambition.
With lowered brows, she played continuously, letting her fingers roam freely,
Pouring out the endless tales hidden within her heart.

Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, sweeping then picking again,
First she played the "Rainbow Garment," then followed by the "Six Melodies."
The thick strings rumbled like a sudden downpour;
The thin strings whispered like lovers talking in private.
Loud and soft notes intertwined in complex harmony,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.

Now fluid and sweet, like warblers singing among flowers;
Now choked and difficult, like springs struggling beneath ice.
When cold brooks stagnate and strings cease to vibrate,
The silence breaks off, leaving only a temporary halt.
Then another sorrow arises, a buried resentment born—
At this moment, silence surpasses even the loudest sound.

Abruptly, like a silver vase shattering, water bursts forth;
Like iron cavalry charging, clashing swords and spears ring out.
As the song ended, she drew her plectrum across the center of the strings,
And all four chords sounded at once, like tearing silk.
Eastward boats and westward barges fell silent, listening intently;
Only the autumn moon on the river middle glowed white.

Hesitating, she placed her plectrum between the strings,
Straightened her dress, stood up, and composed her expression.
She said: "I was originally a girl from the capital city,
Living near Xiama Ling, where luxury thrived.
By thirteen, I had mastered the pipa;
My name belonged to the first section of the Imperial Music Bureau.
After finishing a tune, I could make great masters admire me;
Once dressed, I often provoked jealousy from famous courtesans.

Young men from the Five Tombs competed to offer gifts on heads,
For one song, they gave red silk beyond counting.
Gold-ornamented combs and hairpins broke while beating time,
Blood-red skirts spilled with wine stains.
Year after year passed in laughter and joy,
Wasting splendid nights under autumn moons and spring breezes.

But then, my brother joined the army, and my aunt died;
Beauty faded as days turned into years.
My door became desolate, horses rare;
Growing older, I married a merchant’s wife.
Merchants value profit above all else, caring little for separation;
Last month, he went to Fuliang to buy tea.

He left, and I stayed at the river mouth guarding an empty boat,
Surrounded by bright moonlight and cold river waters.
Late at night, I suddenly dreamed of my youth’s affairs,
Weeping in dreams, tears blurring my rouge-stained cheeks.

I heard the pipa and sighed deeply already,
And hearing these words, I lamented twice as much.
We are both fallen souls drifting to the end of the earth—
Why must we have known each other before meeting?

Since last year, I left the imperial capital,

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。

醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "On the banks of Xunyang River, I bid my guest farewell at night,
While maple leaves and reed flowers rustle in autumn's chill.
The host dismounts, the guest boards his boat;
We raise our cups to drink, but find no music there.
Though drunk, joy is lost as we prepare to part;
At the moment of leaving, vast mists soak the river moon.
Suddenly, from across the water, pipa notes arise;
The host forgets to return, the guest delays his departure.
Following the sound, I ask softly who plays;
The pipa stops, as if she wishes to speak but hesitates.
I move my boat close, inviting her to show herself;
More wine is poured, lamps trimmed, the feast renewed.
After countless calls she finally emerges,
Still holding the pipa, half her face concealed.
She turns the pegs and plucks two or three strings;
Before the melody forms, emotion already flows.
Every string suppresses deep sighs, every note carries thought,
As if telling of a lifetime unfulfilled by ambition.
With lowered brows, she plays continuously and freely,
Expressing all the boundless matters within her heart.
Light strumming, slow twisting, sweeping and flicking;
First 'Rainbow Garment', then 'Six Strings' follow.
The thick strings boom like sudden heavy rain;
The thin strings whisper like private conversation.
Loud and soft, mixed together they are played;
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Charming like birdsong sliding through flowers below;
Muffled like spring water flowing under ice, difficult.
The cold, stiff spring freezes; the strings seem to stop;
Stopped and blocked, the sound briefly ceases.
But another hidden sorrow and dark resentment emerge;
This silence surpasses any sound.
Then suddenly, silver jars break, water bursts forth;
Iron cavalry charge out, swords and spears clash.
When the song ends, she draws the pick across the center;
One final sound from four strings, like tearing silk.
East ships and west boats fall silent;
Only the white autumn moon shines upon the river's heart.
She meditates, inserts the pick among the strings;
Adjusts her clothes, rises, composing her expression.
She says: 'I was originally a girl of the capital city,
Living below Shama Ling.'
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa;
My name belonged to the first rank of the Teachings Hall.
After playing songs, even skilled masters admired me;
When dressed, I was often envied by Qiuniang.
Young men of the Five Tombs vied to offer gifts;
For one song, red silks beyond counting were given.
Gold-inlaid hairpins broke keeping time;
Blood-colored skirts stained with spilled wine.
This year laughter, next year still laughter;
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed idly.
My brother joined the army, my aunt died;
Evenings go, mornings come, my beauty fades.
Before my door, lonely now, horses rare;
Too old, I married a merchant's wife.
Merchants value profit lightly dismiss parting;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He left, I stay guarding the empty boat at the river mouth;
The bright moon surrounds the boat, the river water cold.
Late at night, suddenly dreaming of my youth;
Crying in dreams, tears ruin makeup, red streaks down.
Hearing the pipa, I have already sighed;
Hearing these words again, I deeply lament.
Both are drifting souls at world's edge;
Meeting here need not require prior acquaintance!
Since last year I left the Imperial Capital,
Banished to lie ill in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, without music;
All year round, no strings or bamboo sounds heard.
Living near Penjiang, land low and damp;
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboos grow around my home.
What do I hear morning or evening here?
Cuckoos bleeding cries, apes wailing mournfully.
Spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moon nights;
Often take wine and pour it alone.
Are there no mountain songs and village flutes?
Grating and harsh, hard to listen to.
Tonight hearing your pipa words;
Like listening to celestial music, ears temporarily clear.
Do not refuse to sit again and play one more piece;
For you, I will compose this 'Ballad of the Pipa'.
Moved by my words, she stands for a long while;
Returns to seat, tightens strings, tempo accelerates.
Melancholy unlike previous sounds;
Full assembly hears again, all cover faces weeping.
Who among the guests sheds most tears?
The Sima of Jiangzhou's blue robe is wet."}

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "On the banks of the Xun River, I bid my guest farewell by night;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn chill.
The host dismounted, the guest remained aboard his boat;
We raised our cups to drink, but there were no pipes or strings.
Though drunk, we found no joy, as sorrow marked our parting;
In that moment, vast mists hung low, with moonlight sinking into the river.

Suddenly, from over the water, came the sound of a pipa.
The host forgot to return home; the guest delayed setting sail.
Following the music, I asked quietly who was playing;
The pipa’s song paused, hesitant, before words began.
I moved my boat closer, inviting her to appear,
Refilling the wine jars, trimming the lamps, restarting the feast.
After a thousand calls and ten thousand entreaties, she finally emerged,
Still holding her pipa, half-covering her face in modesty.

She turned the pegs and plucked the strings two or three times,
And before any melody was formed, emotion already stirred.
Each string suppressed deep sighs, each note carried thought,
Seeming to recount a life of unfulfilled ambition.
With lowered brows, she played continuously, letting her fingers roam freely,
Pouring out the endless tales hidden within her heart.

Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, sweeping then picking again,
First she played the "Rainbow Garment," then followed by the "Six Melodies."
The thick strings rumbled like a sudden downpour;
The thin strings whispered like lovers talking in private.
Loud and soft notes intertwined in complex harmony,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.

Now fluid and sweet, like warblers singing among flowers;
Now choked and difficult, like springs struggling beneath ice.
When cold brooks stagnate and strings cease to vibrate,
The silence breaks off, leaving only a temporary halt.
Then another sorrow arises, a buried resentment born—
At this moment, silence surpasses even the loudest sound.

Abruptly, like a silver vase shattering, water bursts forth;
Like iron cavalry charging, clashing swords and spears ring out.
As the song ended, she drew her plectrum across the center of the strings,
And all four chords sounded at once, like tearing silk.
Eastward boats and westward barges fell silent, listening intently;
Only the autumn moon on the river middle glowed white.

Hesitating, she placed her plectrum between the strings,
Straightened her dress, stood up, and composed her expression.
She said: "I was originally a girl from the capital city,
Living near Xia Ma Ling [Frog Mound].
By thirteen, I had mastered the pipa;
My name ranked first in the Imperial Music Bureau's top division.
After finishing a tune, I could make great masters admire me;
Once dressed, I often provoked jealousy from famous courtesans.

Noble youths from the Five Hills vied to throw silk scarves at her head,
For one song, they gave red silk beyond counting.
Gold-ornamented combs and hairpins broke while beating time,
Blood-red skirts spilled with wine stains.
Year after year passed in laughter and joy,
Wasting splendid nights under autumn moons and spring breezes.

But then, my brother joined the army, and my aunt died;
Beauty faded as days turned into years.
My door became desolate, horses rare;
Growing older, I married a merchant’s wife.
Merchants value profit above all else, caring little for separation;
Last month, he went to Fuliang to buy tea.

He left, and I stayed at the river mouth guarding an empty boat,
Surrounded by bright moonlight and cold river waters.
Late at night, I suddenly dreamed of my youth’s affairs,
Weeping in dreams, tears staining my makeup red.

I heard the pipa and sighed deeply already,
And hearing these words, I lamented twice as much.
We are both fallen souls drifting to the end of the earth—
Why must we have known each other before meeting?

Since last year, I left the imperial capital,
Banished here to Jiujiang [Xunyang], bedridden with illness.
Jiujiang is remote, devoid of music;
All year long, I hear not the slightest sound of silk or bamboo.
Living near the Pen River, where land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.

What do I hear morning or evening in this place?
Cuckoos crying blood and apes wailing in grief.
On spring river mornings or autumn moonlit nights,
Often, I take wine and pour it alone.

Surely there are mountain songs and village flutes?
But they are harsh and discordant, unbearable to hear.
Tonight, upon hearing your pipa’s language,
It is like listening to celestial music; my ears are suddenly clear.

Please do not refuse to sit again and play one more piece;
For you, I shall compose the 'Song of the Pipa.'"

Moved by my words, she stood silently for a long time,
Then sat back down, tightening the strings, playing faster.
Her sounds were sad, unlike those before;
Everyone in the audience covered their faces, weeping anew.

Who among us wept the most?
The blue robe of the Jiangzhou Prefect was soaked through."}

As the song ended, she drew her plectrum across the center of the strings,
And all four chords sounded at once, like tearing silk.
Eastward boats and westward barges fell silent, listening intently;
Only the autumn moon on the river middle glowed white.

Hesitating, she placed her plectrum between the strings,
Straightened her dress, stood up, and composed her expression.
She said: "I was originally a girl from the capital city,
Living near Xiamaling.
By thirteen, I had mastered the pipa;
My name belonged to the first section of the Imperial Music Bureau.
After finishing a tune, I could make great masters admire me;
Once dressed, I often provoked jealousy from famous courtesans.

Young men from the Five Tombs competed to bestow silken rewards,
For one song, they gave red silk beyond counting.
Gold-ornamented combs and hairpins broke while beating time,
Blood-red skirts spilled with wine stains.
Year after year passed in laughter and joy,
Wasting splendid nights under autumn moons and spring breezes.

But then, my brother joined the army, and my aunt died;
Beauty faded as days turned into years.
My door became desolate, horses rare;
Growing older, I married a merchant’s wife.
Merchants value profit above all else, caring little for separation;
Last month, he went to Fuliang to buy tea.

He left, and I stayed at the river mouth guarding an empty boat,
Surrounded by bright moonlight and cold river waters.
Late at night, I suddenly dreamed of my youth’s affairs,
Weeping in dreams, tears staining my makeup red.

I heard the pipa and sighed deeply already,
And hearing these words, I lamented twice as much.
We are both fallen souls drifting to the end of the earth—
Why must we have known each other before meeting?

Since last year, I left the imperial capital,
Banished here to Xunyang, bedridden with illness.
Xunyang is remote, devoid of music;
All year long, I hear not the slightest sound of silk or bamboo.
Living near the Pen River, where land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.

What do I hear morning or evening in this place?
Cuckoos crying blood and apes wailing in grief.
On spring river mornings or autumn moonlit nights,
Often, I take wine and pour it alone.

Surely there are mountain songs and village flutes?
A cacophony, rough and jarring, painful to endure.
Tonight, upon hearing your pipa’s language,
It is like listening to celestial music; my ears are suddenly clear.

Do not refuse to return and play another tune;
For you, I shall compose the 'Song of the Pipa.'"

Moved by my words, she stood silently for a long time,
Then sat back down, tightening the strings, playing faster.
Her sounds were sad, unlike those before;
Everyone in the audience covered their faces, weeping anew.

Maple leaves and reed flowers rustle in the autumn chill.
The host dismounts; the guest is on the boat;
We raise our cups to drink, but there are no pipes or strings.
Drunk yet unable to find joy, we face a sorrowful parting,
At this moment of farewell, the vast river bathes the moon.
Suddenly, from over the water, comes the sound of a pipa,

Lowering her brow, she plays casually, again and again,
Pouring out the infinite affairs within her heart.

First the 'Rainbow Robe', then the 'Six Strings'.

Thin strings whisper like private conversation.
Rumbling and whispering intermingled together,
Big pearls and small pearls falling onto jade plates.
Sweetly sliding, like orioles singing beneath flowers,
Choking sobs, like springs flowing under ice.

Suddenly, a silver vase breaks, water bursts forth,
Like cavalry charging, swords and spears clashing.

Four strings sound once, like tearing silk.
Boats east and west fall silent, listening intently,
Only seeing the white moon in the center of the river.
Pondering, she places the plectrum into the strings,
Straightens her clothes, rises, composing herself.
She says she was originally a girl from the capital,
Her home lived near the Shrimp Mound Hill.
At thirteen, she mastered the pipa,
Renowned among the first rank of the imperial musicians.
After finishing a tune, masters would admire her skill,
When made up, other beauties felt envy.
Young men of the five tombs vied to give gifts,
For one song, red silk piles knew no count.
Hairpins and silver combs shattered keeping time,
Red skirts stained with spilled wine.
This year laughing, next year also happy,
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed idly away.
Brother went to join the army, aunt died,
Evenings pass, mornings come, beauty fades.
Before the door, cold and desolate, few carriages remain,
Aging, she married a merchant.
The merchant values profit above separation,
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
Leaving and returning, she guards an empty boat at the river mouth,
Around the boat, bright moonlight, cold river water.
Late at night, suddenly dreaming of youthful days,
In tears upon waking, makeup runs down her cheeks.
Hearing the pipa, I sigh deeply,
Hearing these words, I groan anew.
We are both people lost in the corner of heaven,
Meeting here, why need we have known each other before?
Since last year I left the imperial capital,
Banished to Jiujiang, sick and bedridden.
Jiujiang is remote, devoid of music,
All year long, never hearing strings or flutes.
Living near the Pen River, low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my home.
What do I hear there, morning and evening?
Dusky cuckoos crying blood, gibbons howling in grief.
Spring rivers, flower dawns, autumn nights—
Often taking wine, pouring alone.
Are there no mountain songs and village flutes?
Their hoarse, jarring sounds are hard to bear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa speech,
It's like heavenly music, my ears suddenly clear.
Please do not refuse; sit again and play one more tune,
To interpret for you, I shall compose this 'Song of the Pipa'.
Touched by my words, she stands for a long while,
Then sits back down, quickening strings, notes growing urgent.
Melancholy, unlike the earlier sound,
The whole room hears it again, everyone covering faces in tears.
Who sheds the most tears in the room?
The blue robe of the Sima of Jiangzhou is wet."}

座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "On the banks of the Xun River, I bid my guest farewell by night;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn chill.
The host dismounted, the guest remained aboard his boat;
We raised our cups to drink, but there were no pipes or strings.
Though drunk, we found no joy, as sorrow marked our parting;
In that moment, vast mists hung low, with moonlight sinking into the river.

Suddenly, from over the water, came the sound of a pipa.
The host forgot to return home; the guest delayed setting sail.
Following the music, I asked quietly who was playing;
The pipa’s song paused, hesitant, before words began.
I moved my boat closer, inviting her to appear,
Refilling the wine jars, trimming the lamps, restarting the feast.
After a thousand calls and ten thousand entreaties, she finally emerged,
Still holding her pipa, half-covering her face in modesty.

She turned the pegs and plucked the strings two or three times,
And before any melody was formed, emotion already stirred.
Each string suppressed deep sighs, each note carried thought,
Seeming to recount a life of unfulfilled ambition.
With lowered brows, she played continuously, letting her fingers roam freely,
Pouring out the endless tales hidden within her heart.

Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, sweeping then picking again,
First she played the "Rainbow Garment," then followed by the "Six Melodies."
The thick strings rumbled like a sudden downpour;
The thin strings whispered like lovers talking in private.
Loud and soft notes intertwined in complex harmony,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.

Now fluid and sweet, like warblers singing among flowers;
Now choked and difficult, like springs struggling beneath ice.
When cold brooks stagnate and strings cease to vibrate,
The silence breaks off, leaving only a temporary halt.
Then another sorrow arises, a buried resentment born—
At this moment, silence surpasses even the loudest sound.

Abruptly, like a silver vase shattering, water bursts forth;
Like iron cavalry charging, clashing swords and spears ring out.
As the song ended, she drew her plectrum across the center of the strings,
And all four chords sounded at once, like tearing silk.
Eastward boats and westward barges fell silent, listening intently;
Only the autumn moon on the river middle glowed white.

Hesitating, she placed her plectrum between the strings,
Straightened her dress, stood up, and composed her expression.
She said: "I was originally a girl from the capital city,
Living near Xiamaling.
By thirteen, I had mastered the pipa;
My name belonged to the first section of the Imperial Music Bureau.
After finishing a tune, I could make great masters admire me;
Once dressed, I often provoked jealousy from famous courtesans.

Young men from the Five Tombs competed to bestow silken rewards,
For one song, they gave red silk beyond counting.
Gold-ornamented combs and hairpins broke while beating time,
Blood-red skirts spilled with wine stains.
Year after year passed in laughter and joy,
Wasting splendid nights under autumn moons and spring breezes.

But then, my brother joined the army, and my aunt died;
Beauty faded as days turned into years.
My door became desolate, horses rare;
Growing older, I married a merchant’s wife.
Merchants value profit above all else, caring little for separation;
Last month, he went to Fuliang to buy tea.

He left, and I stayed at the river mouth guarding an empty boat,
Surrounded by bright moonlight and cold river waters.
Late at night, I suddenly dreamed of my youth’s affairs,
Weeping in dreams, tears staining my makeup red.

I heard the pipa and sighed deeply already,
And hearing these words, I lamented twice as much.
We are both fallen souls drifting to the end of the earth—
Why must we have known each other before meeting?

Since last year, I left the imperial capital,
Banished here to Xunyang, bedridden with illness.
Xunyang is remote, devoid of music;
All year long, I hear not the slightest sound of silk or bamboo.
Living near the Pen River, where land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.

What do I hear morning or evening in this place?
Cuckoos crying blood and apes wailing in grief.
On spring river mornings or autumn moonlit nights,
Often, I take wine and pour it alone.

Surely there are mountain songs and village flutes?
A cacophony, rough and jarring, painful to endure.
Tonight, upon hearing your pipa’s language,
It is like listening to celestial music; my ears are suddenly clear.

Do not refuse to return and play another tune;
For you, I shall compose the 'Song of the Pipa.'"

Moved by my words, she stood silently for a long time,
Then sat back down, tightening the strings, playing faster.
Her sounds were sad, unlike those before;
Everyone in the audience covered their faces, weeping anew.

Who among us wept the most?
I, the Sima of Jiangzhou, with my blue robe soaked through."}

Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn chill.
I dismounted from my horse while he remained on his boat;

At the moment of goodbye, vast was the river, steeped in moonlight.
Suddenly, from across the water, came the sound of a pipa;
The host forgot to return home, and the guest did not depart.
Following the sound, I asked softly who was playing;
The pipa stopped, and the player seemed hesitant to speak.
We moved our boat closer and invited her to come out;
Wine was added, lamps were turned up, and the banquet resumed.
After many calls and entreaties she finally emerged,
Still holding the pipa to half-hide her face.
She tuned the pegs and plucked two or three strings;
Before a melody formed, emotion had already been conveyed.
Each string murmured with suppressed feeling, each note full of thought,

Expressing all the endless matters within her heart.

The thin strings whispered like private secrets.

Autumn moons and spring breezes slipped by unnoticed.

Days and nights passed, and her beauty faded.

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "On the banks of the Xunyang River, I bid a guest farewell at night;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn chill.
The host dismounted from his horse, while the guest sat on the ship;
We raised our wine to drink, yet lacked pipes and strings for music.
Though drunk, joy was absent, and grief filled the parting moment;
Looking out, only moonlight shimmered on the vast, misty river.

Suddenly, the sound of a pipa drifted over the water;
The host forgot to return, and the guest delayed his departure.
Following the sound, I asked softly who played it;
The pipa stopped, as if the player wished to speak but hesitated.
I moved my boat closer and invited her to meet us;
We added more wine, lit the lamps anew, and resumed the feast.
After countless calls and entreaties, she finally appeared,
Still holding the pipa, half-hiding her face behind it.

She twisted the pegs and plucked the strings a few times;
Before the melody formed, emotion was already present.
Each string suppressed a sigh, each note carried deep thought,
As if lamenting a lifetime of frustrated ambitions.
With lowered brows, she played casually, note after note,
Expressing all the endless sorrows within her heart.
Lightly sweeping, slowly pinching, stroking then picking—
First playing "Rainbow Garments," then later "Six Strings" (Liuyao).

The thick strings thundered like a sudden shower;
The thin strings whispered like private murmurs.
Rapid and soft notes intertwined in complex harmony,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Smooth and clear, like orioles singing beneath flowers;
Choked and muffled, like springs trapped under ice.
The cold, stagnant water froze the strings' resonance;
The flow ceased, and the sound briefly paused.

Then arose a hidden sorrow, a dark resentment;
At this moment, silence surpassed any sound.
Abruptly, like a silver vase breaking with water bursting forth,
Or iron cavalry charging with swords clashing loudly.
When the tune ended, she drew the plectrum across the center;
The four strings sounded together like tearing silk.

East and west boats fell silent, no words were spoken;
Only the white autumn moon shone upon the river's heart.
Lost in thought, she inserted the plectrum among the strings,
Straightened her robes, stood up, and composed her expression.
She said: "I was originally a girl from the capital city;
My home lay below Shama Ling (Frog Hill).
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa;
My name belonged to the first division of the Imperial Conservatory.
After performing, even great masters admired my skill;
When made up, courtesans like Qiuniang envied me.
Young nobles from Five Tombs competed to give me gifts;
For one song, I received countless bolts of red damask.
Jeweled hairpins and silver combs broke keeping time;
Blood-colored silk skirts stained by spilled wine.
Year after year, laughter continued;
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed idly.
My brother joined the army, my aunt died;
Days turned into nights, and my beauty faded.
Before my door, visitors grew scarce, horses rare;
Getting older, I married a merchant’s wife.
Merchants value profit, disregarding separation;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He left, and I waited alone by the river mouth on an empty boat;
Surrounding me, bright moonlight reflected on the cold river water.
Deep in the night, I dreamed of youthful affairs;
Waking weeping, makeup tears streaked down my red cheeks."

Hearing the pipa, I had already sighed deeply;
Hearing these words, my sorrow weighed even heavier.
Both of us are wanderers fallen from grace at heaven's edge;
In this meeting, why must we have known each other before?

Since last year, I left the imperial capital,
Demoted and ill, residing in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, devoid of music;
All year round, no sound of strings or flutes is heard.
Living near the Peng River, the land is low and damp;
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear here at dawn and dusk?
Cuckoos crying blood, and apes wailing mournfully.
In spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn nights, and moonlit skies,
Often I take wine and pour it out alone.
Is there not mountain songs and village flute tunes?
But their harsh, discordant sounds are painful to hear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa speech,
It seems like celestial music; my ears are suddenly cleared.
Do not refuse to sit again and play another tune;
For you, I shall compose the Ballad of the Pipa.

Moved by my words, she stood for a long moment;
Returning to her seat, she tightened the strings, playing faster.
The melancholy tone differed from earlier melodies;
Everyone in the room listened again, covering faces to weep.
Among those seated, whose tears flowed most profusely?
The Jiangzhou Prefect, his blue robe soaked through."}

Young men from the Five Tombs vied to give me red silk;
One song earned more bolts than could be counted.
Jeweled hairpins and silver combs broke keeping time;
Blood-red skirts were stained with spilled wine.
Year after year of laughter and merriment,
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed idly away.
But my brother joined the army, and my aunt died;
Evenings come, mornings pass, and my beauty faded.
Before my door it became cold; horses and carriages rare;
In my old age, I married a merchant's wife.
The merchant values profit over parting;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He left, and I guarded the empty boat at the river mouth;
Around the boat, bright moonlight, cold river water.
Deep in the night, I suddenly dreamt of youthful days;
Waking crying, my tear-streaked makeup ran down.
Hearing the pipa, I sighed;
Hearing these words, again I murmured sympathetically.
We are both lost souls adrift at the edge of the world;
Since we meet now, why need we have known each other before?
Since last year I left the imperial capital,
Demoted and ill, I lie low in Xunyang City.

All year round, no sound of silk and bamboo.

Are there no mountain songs and village flutes?
Clashing noise, hard to listen to.
Tonight hearing your pipa speech,

Do not refuse to sit again and play one more tune,
For you, I shall compose the 'Song of the Pipa'.
Moved by my words, she stood for a long while;
Then sat back, tightened the strings, which played faster.

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "On the banks of the Xun River, I bid farewell to my guest at night;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn chill.
The host dismounted, while the guest remained aboard his boat;
We raised our cups to drink, but there were no pipes or strings.
Though drunk, we found no joy, as sorrow marked our parting;
At that moment, vast mists hung low, with moonlight sinking into the river.

Suddenly, from over the water, came the sound of a pipa.
The host forgot to return; the guest delayed setting sail.
Following the music, I asked quietly who was playing;
The pipa’s song paused, hesitant, before words began.
I moved my boat closer, inviting her to appear,
Refilling the wine jars, trimming the lamps, restarting the feast.
After a thousand calls and ten thousand entreaties, she finally emerged,
Still holding her pipa, half-covering her face in modesty.

She turned the pegs and plucked the strings two or three times,
And before any melody was formed, emotion already stirred.
Each string suppressed deep sighs, each note carried thought,
Seeming to recount a life of unfulfilled ambition.
With lowered brows, she played continuously, letting her fingers roam freely,
Pouring out the endless tales hidden within her heart.

Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, sweeping then picking again,
First she played the "Rainbow Garment," then followed by the "Six Melodies."
The thick strings rumbled like a sudden downpour;
The thin strings whispered like lovers talking in private.
Loud and soft notes intertwined in complex harmony,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.

Now fluid and sweet, like warblers singing among flowers;
Now choked and difficult, like springs struggling beneath ice.
When cold brooks stagnate and strings cease to vibrate,
The silence breaks off, leaving only a temporary halt.
Then another sorrow arises, a buried resentment born—
At this moment, silence surpasses even the loudest sound.

Abruptly, like a silver vase shattering, water bursts forth;
Like iron cavalry charging, clashing swords and spears ring out.
As the song ended, she drew her plectrum across the center of the strings,
And all four chords sounded at once, like tearing silk.
Eastward boats and westward barges fell silent, listening intently;
Only the autumn moon on the river middle glowed white.

Hesitating, she placed her plectrum between the strings,
Straightened her dress, stood up, and composed her expression.
She said: "I was originally a girl from the capital city,
Living near Xia Ma Ling [Frog Mound].
By thirteen, I had mastered the pipa;
My name belonged to the first section of the Imperial Music Bureau.
After finishing a tune, I could make great masters admire me;
Once dressed, I often provoked jealousy from famous courtesans.

Young men from the Five Tombs competed to offer gifts on heads,
For one song, they gave red silk beyond counting.
Gold-ornamented combs and hairpins broke while beating time,
Blood-red skirts spilled with wine stains.
Year after year passed in laughter and joy,
Wasting splendid nights under autumn moons and spring breezes.

But then, my brother joined the army, and my aunt died;
Beauty faded as days turned into years.
My door became desolate, horses rare;
Growing older, I married a merchant’s wife.
Merchants value profit above all else, caring little for separation;
Last month, he went to Fuliang to buy tea.

He left, and I stayed at the river mouth guarding an empty boat,
Surrounded by bright moonlight and cold river waters.
Late at night, I suddenly dreamed of my youth’s affairs,
Weeping in dreams, tears staining my makeup red.

I heard the pipa and sighed deeply already,
And hearing these words, I lamented twice as much.
We are both fallen souls drifting to the end of the earth—
Why must we have known each other before meeting?

Since last year, I left the imperial capital,
Banished here to Jiujiang [Xunyang], bedridden with illness.
Jiujiang is remote, devoid of music;
All year long, I hear not the slightest sound of silk or bamboo.
Living near the Pen River, where land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.

What do I hear morning or evening in this place?
Cuckoos crying blood and apes wailing in grief.
On spring river mornings or autumn moonlit nights,
Often, I take wine and pour it alone.

Surely there are mountain songs and village flutes?
But they are harsh and discordant, unbearable to hear.
Tonight, upon hearing your pipa’s language,
It is like listening to celestial music; my ears are suddenly clear.

Please do not refuse to sit again and play one more piece;
For you, I shall compose the 'Song of the Pipa.'"

Moved by my words, she stood silently for a long time,
Then sat back down, tightening the strings, playing faster.
Her sounds were sad, unlike those before;
Everyone in the audience covered their faces, weeping anew.

Who among us wept the most?
The blue robe of the Jiangzhou Prefect was soaked through."}

Maple leaves and reed flowers rustle in the autumn breeze.
The host dismounts his horse while my guest is already on board,
We raise our cups to drink but have no strings or pipes.
Drunk yet joyless, we face a sorrowful parting;
At departure, the vast river gleams with moonlight.
Suddenly, pipa music drifts over the water;
The host forgets to return, and the guest delays his start.
I follow the sound and quietly ask who plays;
The pipa pauses, as if hesitant to speak.
I move my boat closer to invite her out,
Add wine, trim the lamp, and restart the feast.
After many calls and entreaties she finally appears,
Still holding her pipa half-covering her face.
She tunes the pegs and plucks a few tentative notes;
Before a melody forms, emotion already fills the air.
Every string sighs, every note carries longing,
As if telling a lifetime of thwarted ambition.
Eyes lowered, fingers moving freely one after another,
She pours out all the infinite matters in her heart.
Light presses, slow twists, sweeps, then picks;
First 'Rainbow Garments,' then 'Six Strings' dance.
The thick strings rumble like sudden rain,
The thin strings whisper like secret talks.
Rumbling and whispering tangle together:
Large beads and small pearls fall on jade plates.
Birds chirp smoothly beneath blossoms,
A spring chokes under ice, struggling to flow.
Ice-cold and sluggish, the strings tighten to silence;
Frozen and blocked, the sound temporarily ceases.
Hidden sorrows and dark resentments arise anew;
In this stillness, silence speaks louder than sound.
Then silver bottles burst, water splashing forth;
Iron cavalry charges, swords and spears clashing.
The song ends; she strikes all four strings with a sweep—
One sharp tear, like silk ripped apart.
Boats east and west fall silent;
Only the white autumn moon reflects on the river's heart.
Lost in thought, she inserts her plectrum among the strings,
Straightens her clothes, rises, composing her face.
She says: 'I was originally a girl from the capital,
My home near the Frog Hill district.
By thirteen I mastered the pipa,
Named first in the Imperial Music Bureau.
After performances, great masters would admire me;
Once made up, even famous beauties grew jealous.
Young men of the Five Mausoleums competed for my favors,
One song earned countless rolls of red silk.
Gold-inlaid hairpins broke keeping time,
Blood-red skirts stained with spilled wine.
Year after year of laughter and mirth,
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed idly by.
Then my brother joined the army, my aunt died;
Days turned to nights, and beauty faded away.
Before my gate, carriages grew sparse and cold;
Getting old, I married a merchant as his wife.
The merchant values profit above all, light on partings;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
Since then, guarding an empty boat at the river mouth,
Surrounded by bright moon and chilling waters.
Late at night I suddenly dream of youthful days,
Waking in tears, red makeup streaking down my cheeks.'

Hearing the pipa, I already sighed deeply;
Hearing these words, my grief intensifies.
We are both lost souls wandering the earth;
Meeting now, why must we have known each other before?
Ever since leaving the imperial capital last year,
Exiled and ill, I've lived in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, without any music;
All year round I hear not a single string or pipe.
Living near the Pen River where land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboos surround my home.
What do I hear here morning and evening?
Dusko cuckoos bleeding cries, apes wailing mournfully.
Spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moonlit nights—
Often I take wine and pour it alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
Their rough, grating sounds are unbearable to hear.

Like celestial music, they clear my ears and mind.

For you, I'll compose this 'Ballad of the Pipa.'

Moved by my words, she stands long in silence,
Then sits back, tightening strings that turn urgent.

Beauty faded as days turned into years.
My door became desolate, horses rare;
Growing older, I married a merchant’s wife.

Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn chill.
The host dismounted, the guest remained on his boat;
We raised wine cups but lacked pipes and strings.
Drunk yet without joy, we parted in sorrow;
At parting, vast mists hung low, moonlight submerged in the river.
Suddenly, from over the water, came the sound of a pipa.
The host forgot to return; the guest delayed setting sail.
Following the music, I asked quietly who was playing;
The pipa paused, hesitant, before words began.
I moved my boat closer to invite her out,
Refilled the wine, trimmed the lamps, restarted the feast.
After thousand calls and ten thousand entreaties, she finally emerged,
Still holding her pipa, half-covering her face.
She turned the pegs and plucked two or three times,
And before any tune was formed, emotion already stirred.
Each string suppressed deep sighs, each note carried thought,
Seeming to recount a life of unfulfilled ambition.
With lowered brows, she played continuously, fingers roaming freely,
Poured out the endless tales hidden within her heart.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, sweeping then picking again,
First she played the "Rainbow Garment," then the "Six Melodies."
The thick strings rumbled like a sudden downpour;
The thin strings whispered like intimate talk.
Loud and soft notes intertwined in complex harmony,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Now fluid and sweet, like warblers singing among flowers;
Now choked and difficult, like springs struggling beneath ice.
When cold brooks stagnate and strings cease to vibrate,
The silence breaks off, leaving only a temporary halt.
Then another sorrow arises, a buried resentment born—
At this moment, silence surpasses even the loudest sound.
Abruptly, like a silver vase shattering, water bursts forth;
Like iron cavalry charging, clashing swords and spears ring out.
As the song ended, she drew her plectrum across the center of the strings,
And all four chords sounded at once, like tearing silk.
Eastward boats and westward barges fell silent, listening intently;
Only the autumn moon on the middle river glowed white.
Hesitating, she placed her plectrum between the strings,
Straightened her dress, stood up, and composed her expression.

Living near Frog Mound (Xiama Ling).
By thirteen, I had mastered the pipa;
My name belonged to the first section of the Imperial Music Bureau.
After finishing a tune, I could make great masters admire me;
Once dressed, I often provoked jealousy from courtesans.
Young men from the Five Tombs competed to offer gifts,
For one song, they gave red silk beyond counting.
Gold-ornamented combs broke while beating time,
Blood-red skirts spilled with wine stains.
Year after year passed in laughter and joy,
Wasting splendid nights under autumn moons and spring breezes.
But then, my brother joined the army, and my aunt died;
Beauty faded as days turned into years.
My door became desolate, horses rare;
Growing older, I married a merchant’s wife.
Merchants value profit above all else, caring little for separation;
Last month, he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He left, and I stayed at the river mouth guarding an empty boat,
Surrounded by bright moonlight and cold river waters.
Late at night, I suddenly dreamed of my youth’s affairs,
Weeping in dreams, tears staining my makeup red.
Upon hearing the pipa, I had already sighed;
Hearing her tale, my sighs grew deeper still.
We are both fallen souls drifting to the end of the earth—
Why must we have known each other before meeting?
Since last year, I left the imperial capital,
Banished to Xunyang, bedridden with illness.
Xunyang is remote, devoid of music;
All year long, I hear not the slightest sound of silk or bamboo.

Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.

Blood-weeping cuckoos and mournful gibbon cries.

Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn chill.
The host dismounted, the guest remained on board;
We raised our wine cups, yet lacked the music of pipes and strings.
Drunkenness brought no joy as we faced parting’s sorrow,
Only the vast river immersed in moonlight greeted our farewell.

Suddenly, over the water came the sound of a pipa;
The host forgot to return home, the guest delayed his departure.
Following the melody, I asked softly who was playing,
But the pipa paused, hesitant before answering.
I moved my boat closer, inviting her to meet me,
Refilled the wine, lit the lamps, and resumed the feast.
After many calls and entreaties, she finally emerged,
Still holding the pipa, half-concealing her face.

She turned the pegs and plucked the strings a few times;
Though no tune had formed, emotion was already there.
Each string was muffled with sighs, every note laden with thought,
As if telling the story of a life unfulfilled.
With downcast eyes, fingers moving naturally, she played on,
Expressing all the boundless secrets of her heart.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, sweeping then picking,
First she played “Rainbow Robes,” then followed by “Six Strings.”

The thick strings thundered like a sudden heavy rain,
The thin strings murmured hurriedly, like private whispers.
Thundering and whispering intertwined in complex play,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Birdlike songs flowed smoothly beneath blossoms,
Then choked sounds struggled through springs under ice.
Like cold ice blocking the flow, the strings seemed to freeze and stop;
In this frozen silence, the sound paused briefly.
A new hidden sorrow and dark resentment arose—
At this point, silence surpassed any sound.

Suddenly, a silver jar bursts, water erupting forth,
Like iron cavalry charging, swords and spears clangored.
The piece ended; she gathered the plectrum and struck the center string,
The four strings sounded once, sharp as tearing silk.
East and west boats lay quiet, speechless alike,
Seeing only the pale autumn moon reflected in the river’s heart.

She pondered deeply, inserted the plectrum among the strings,
Straightened her clothes, rose, and composed her expression.
She said: “I was originally a girl from the capital city,
Living near Shrimp Hill. By thirteen, I had mastered the pipa,
My name inscribed in the First Hall of the Music Academy.
After finishing a song, even great masters would admire,
And after makeup, peers often envied my beauty.
Young nobles from Five Mausoleums vied to gift me brocade,
For one performance, countless bolts of red silk were presented.
Gold-inlaid combs snapped keeping time,
Crimson skirts stained with spilled wine.
Year after year, laughter repeated itself,
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed casually by.
My brother joined the army, my aunt died,
Days turned to nights, and my youth faded away.
Before my gate, visitors grew scarce, horses rare,
So when old, I married a merchant man.
Merchants prize profit over affection, leaving easily,
Last month he went to Fuliang to trade tea.
He left, and I waited alone by the river mouth,
Surrounded by bright moonlight, the river water cold.
Deep in the night, I suddenly dreamed of my younger days,
Waking with tears staining my makeup red.”

Hearing the pipa, I had already sighed,
Now hearing these words, my grief deepened further.
“Both of us are wanderers fallen from grace,
Meeting here, why should previous acquaintance matter?
Since last year I left the Imperial Capital,
Banished to lie ill in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, devoid of music,
All year long, I hear not a single string or pipe.
Near the Pen River, where land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my home.
What do I hear there, morning and evening?
Cuckoos crying blood, monkeys wailing in sorrow.
Spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moonlit nights—
Often I pour wine, drinking alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
Their harsh, discordant tones are hard to bear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa’s language,
It is like listening to celestial music, clearing my ears.
Do not refuse to sit and play another tune,
For you, I will compose ‘The Ballad of the Pipa.’”

Moved by my words, she stood for a long while,
Then returned to sit, tightening the strings, playing faster.
Her mournful notes differed from those before,
To the full audience, each covered their faces and wept.
Who shed the most tears in the room?
The Green-robed Sima of Jiangzhou, his shirt wet."}

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "On the banks of the Xunyang River, I saw off a friend at night;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn chill.
The host dismounted, the guest remained on board;
We raised our wine cups, yet lacked the music of pipes and strings.
Drunkenness brought no joy as we faced parting’s sorrow,
Only the vast river immersed in moonlight greeted our farewell.

Suddenly, from over the water, came the sound of a pipa;
The host forgot to return home, the guest delayed his departure.
Following the melody, I asked softly who was playing,
But the pipa paused, hesitant before answering.
I moved my boat closer, inviting her to meet me,
Refilled the wine, lit the lamps, and resumed the feast.
After many calls and entreaties, she finally emerged,
Still holding the pipa, half-concealing her face.

She turned the pegs and plucked the strings a few times;
Before the tune took form, emotion already spoke.
Each string was muffled with sighs, every note laden with thought,
As if telling the story of a life unfulfilled.
With downcast eyes, fingers moving naturally, she played on,
Expressing all the boundless secrets of her heart.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, sweeping then picking,
First she played “Rainbow Robes,” then followed by “Liu Yao.”

The thick strings thundered like a sudden heavy rain,
The thin strings whispered like private conversations.
Thundering and whispering intertwined in complex play,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Birdlike songs flowed smoothly beneath blossoms,
Then choked sounds struggled through springs under ice.
Ice-cold springs slowed the strings to stillness,
When silence fell and the voice ceased for a moment.
A new hidden sorrow and dark resentment arose—
At this point, silence surpassed any sound.

Then, like a silver vase bursting open, water splashed forth,
Like iron cavalry charging, swords and spears clangored.
The piece ended; she gathered the plectrum and struck the center string,
One final cry from the four strings, like silk tearing apart.
East and west boats lay quiet, speechless alike,
Seeing only the pale autumn moon reflected in the river’s heart.

She pondered deeply, inserted the plectrum among the strings,
Straightened her clothes, rose, and composed her expression.
She said: “I was originally a girl from the capital city,
Living near Shrimp Hill, in the old quarter.
By thirteen, I had mastered the pipa,
My name inscribed in the First Division of the Imperial Music Bureau.
After finishing a song, even great masters would admire,
And after makeup, peers often envied my beauty.
Young nobles from Five Mausoleums vied to gift me brocade,
For one performance, countless bolts of red silk were presented.
Gold-inlaid combs snapped keeping time,
Crimson skirts stained with spilled wine.
Year after year, laughter repeated itself,
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed casually by.
My brother joined the army, my aunt died,
Days turned to nights, and my youth faded away.
Before my gate, visitors grew scarce, horses rare,
So when old, I married a merchant man.
Merchants prize profit over affection, leaving easily,
Last month he went to Fuliang to trade tea.
He left, and I waited alone by the river mouth,
Surrounded by bright moonlight, the river water cold.
Deep in the night, I suddenly dreamed of my younger days,
Waking with tears staining my makeup red.”

Hearing the pipa, I had already sighed,
Now hearing these words, my grief deepened further.
“Both of us are wanderers fallen from grace,
Meeting here, why should previous acquaintance matter?
Since last year I left the Imperial Capital,
Banished to lie ill in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, devoid of music,
All year long, I hear not a single string or pipe.
Near the Pen River, where land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my home.
What do I hear there, morning and evening?
Cuckoos crying blood, monkeys wailing in sorrow.
Spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moonlit nights—
Often I pour wine, drinking alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
Their harsh, discordant tones are hard to bear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa’s language,
It is like listening to celestial music, clearing my ears.
Do not refuse to sit and play another tune,
For you, I will compose ‘The Ballad of the Pipa.’”

Moved by my words, she stood for a long while,
Then returned to sit, tightening the strings, playing faster.
Her mournful notes differed from those before,
To the full audience, each covered their faces and wept.
Who shed the most tears in the room?
The Jiangzhou Sima, his blue robe soaked."}

Jeweled hairpins and silver combs broken keeping time,
Blood-red silk skirts stained by overturned wine.

At the moment of farewell, the vast river soaks the moon.

The pipa stops; she seems hesitant to speak. 
I move my boat closer and invite her out; 
More wine is poured, the lamp light turned up, the feast renewed. 
After many calls, at last she emerges,

She turns the pegs, plucks the strings a few times—
Before the tune takes shape, emotion already flows. 
Each string suppressed carries sigh upon sigh,

With downcast eyes, she plays freely without pause, 
Telling all the infinite matters within her heart. 
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, brushing and picking,

The thick strings thunder like sudden rain; 
The thin strings whisper like private conversation. 
Thundering and whispering, mingled together,

Smooth as orioles singing through flowers beneath them; 
Choked as springs trickling under ice, struggling. 
Ice-cold streams congeal, the strings seem frozen; 
Frozen, blocked—the sound halts for an instant. 
Then hidden sorrows and silent resentments arise; 
At this moment, silence surpasses sound. 
As if silver bottles burst, splashing their contents; 
As if armored cavalry charge, swords clashing. 
The song ends; she draws the plectrum with a final sweep; 
All four strings sound once, like tearing silk. 
East-side boats and west-side barges fall silent; 
Only the white autumn moon remains in the river's heart. 
Deep in thought, she puts the plectrum away among the strings; 
She straightens her clothes, rising with composed dignity. 
She says she was originally a girl from the capital, 
Living near Shrimp Mound Lane. 
By age thirteen she mastered the pipa, 
Named first in the Imperial Music Bureau's troupe. 
Once her songs made master performers admire; 
Her makeup always stirred envy in beauties. 
Young nobles from Five Mausoleums vied to give headbands; 
One song earned countless bolts of red silk. 
Gold-inlaid combs broken beating time; 
Blood-red skirts stained by spilled wine. 
Joy and laughter year after year repeated, 
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed idly. 
Her brother joined the army, her aunt died; 
Evenings came, mornings went—her beauty faded. 
Her door became desolate, few horses arrived; 
Aging, she married a merchant's wife. 
The merchant values profit over separation; 
Last month he left for Fuliang to buy tea. 
He goes and comes, leaving her alone guarding the boat at the river mouth; 
Surrounding the ship, bright moonlight; the river water cold. 
In deep night suddenly she dreams of youthful days; 
Waking crying, tears wash the rouge from her cheeks. 
Hearing the pipa, I had already sighed; 
Hearing these words, I sigh again deeply. 
Both are wanderers fallen from heaven's path; 
Meeting here, why have we needed to know each other before? 
Since last year I parted from the imperial city, 
Demoted and ill, dwelling in Xunyang town. 
Xunyang is remote, devoid of music; 
Year-round no strings nor flutes are heard. 
Living near the Pen River on low, damp ground, 
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house. 
From dawn to dusk, what do I hear there? 
Bleeding cuckoos cry, apes wail mournfully. 
Spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moon nights— 
Often I take wine and pour it alone. 
Are there no mountain songs or village pipes? 
They are harsh and rough, hard on the ear. 
Tonight I hear your pipa language; 
It is celestial music; my ears are momentarily clear. 
Do not refuse to sit and play another piece; 
For you I shall compose the Song of the Pipa. 
Moved by my words, she stands long in silence; 
Then sits again, quickening the tempo, strings urgent. 
Melancholy sounds unlike those before; 
The whole audience hears again and covers faces in tears. 
Who among us shed the most tears?

By the Xunyang River at night I bid farewell to a guest;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn chill.

We raised our cups to drink, but no pipes or strings were near.
Though drunk, we could not be joyful as parting drew close;
When we parted, the river was vast and moon-drenched.
Suddenly, over the water came the sound of a pipa;
The host forgot to return, the guest did not set sail.
Following the sound, I asked softly who was playing;
The pipa paused, the player hesitated to speak.
I moved my boat closer and invited her to come out;
We added wine, lit the lamps anew, and resumed the feast.
After countless calls, she finally appeared,
Still holding the pipa before her face, partly hid.
She turned the pegs and plucked the strings a few times;
Before the melody formed, emotion already flowed.
Each string was suppressed, each note carried sorrow,
As if telling of a life spent in frustration.
Her head bowed, fingers moving freely, she played on,
Expressing all the endless things within her heart.
Light presses, slow twists, wipes then plucks again—
First 'Rainbow Skirt', then 'Six Strings' melodies.
The thick strings rumbled like sudden rain;
The thin strings whispered like private talk.
Rumbling and whispering intertwined in playing—
Large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Flowing like orioles singing beneath the flowers;
Choking like spring water flowing under ice.
Cold springs froze stiff, the strings seemed to stop;
Stopped and blocked, the sound briefly ceased.
Then arose hidden grief and secret resentment—
At this moment, silence spoke louder than sound.
A silver vase burst suddenly, water splashing out;
Iron cavalry charged forth, blades clashing loud.
The tune ended; the plectrum swept across the center—
Four strings rang once, like silk tearing apart.
Boats to east and west fell silent without a word;
Only the white autumn moon shone upon the river's heart.
She pondered, put down the plectrum, tucked it in the strings;
Straightened her clothes, stood up, composed her face.
She said: 'Originally I was a girl from the capital,
My home near Shama Ridge.'
By age thirteen I mastered the pipa;
My name belonged to the first troupe of the imperial academy.
After finishing a piece, skilled masters would marvel;
Done with makeup, Song girls often envied me.
Young men from the Five Tombs vied to give gifts;
For one song, red silk rolls counted beyond number.
Silver combs with jeweled heads broke keeping time;
Blood-red skirts stained by spilled wine.
Years of laughter followed years of joy,
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed casually away.
Her brother joined the army, her aunt died;
Day turned to night, beauty faded.
Before her door grew desolate, few horses came;
Past youth, she married a merchant's wife.
The merchant valued profit more than love;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
Leaving her alone at the river mouth guarding an empty boat,
Around the boat bright moonlight, cold river water.
Late at night she dreamed of youthful days;
Waking, tears streamed down her painted face.
Hearing the pipa, I sighed long;
Hearing her words, I lamented again.
Both of us wanderers lost at heaven's edge—
Since meeting here, what need for prior acquaintance?
Since last year I left the imperial city,

Maple leaves and reed flowers rustle in the autumn chill.
The host dismounts, the guest remains on his boat,
We raise our wine cups, yet there are no pipes or strings to play.
Drunk, we find no joy; the parting is bitter and sad,
As we leave, the vast river is steeped in moonlight.
Suddenly, from over the water, comes the sound of a pipa,
The host forgets to return home, and the guest delays departure.
Seeking the source of the sound, I quietly ask who plays it;
The pipa stops, hesitant as if about to speak.
I move my boat closer and invite her to meet me,
Add more wine, trim the lamp, and resume the feast.
After countless calls and entreaties, she finally emerges,
Still holding the pipa, half-hiding her face.
She tunes the pegs and plucks a few strings,
Before the melody forms, emotion already stirs.
Every string muffled, every note laden with thought,
As if telling of a lifetime’s thwarted ambitions.
Head lowered, fingers moving steadily, she plays on,
Expressing all the boundless matters within her heart.
Gently pressing, slowly twisting, sweeping then picking,
First playing "Rainbow Garments," then "The Six Melodies."
The thick strings rumble like a sudden downpour,
The thin strings whisper like private conversations.
Rumbling and whispering intermingled in the performance,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Clear and sweet as orioles singing beneath flowers,
Muffled and choked as spring water flowing under ice.
Ice-cold, sluggish, the strings seem to freeze and cease,
Blocked and still, the sound briefly halts.
Then arises a hidden sorrow and silent resentment,
At this moment, silence speaks louder than sound.
As if a silver vase suddenly bursts, spraying water and broth,
Like armored cavalry charging out, swords and spears clashing.
When the song ends, she draws the plectrum across the center,
A single stroke from the four strings sounds like tearing silk.
The boats to the east and west fall silent,
Only the white autumn moon shines on the heart of the river.

Straightens her clothes, rises, and composes her expression.

My home lay below Xiama Ling.
By thirteen I had mastered the pipa,
And my name was listed first among the teaching workshops.

When fully made up, even beauty Qiu Niang would envy me.
The young nobles of Wuling scrambled to offer gifts,
For one song, red silk was given without count.
Jeweled hairpins and silver combs snapped to keep time,
Blood-red skirts were stained by spilled wine.
Year after year of laughter and joy,
Passing autumn moons and spring breezes casually.
When my brother went off to war and my aunt died,
The years passed, morning turned to evening, and my looks faded.
My door grew cold, horses and carriages sparse,
So I married an older man, becoming a merchant’s wife.

Only the vast river immersed in moonlight greeted our farewell.

Suddenly, from over the water, came the sound of a pipa;
The host forgot to return home, the guest delayed his departure.
Following the melody, I asked softly who was playing,
But the pipa paused, hesitant before answering.
I moved my boat closer, inviting her to meet me,
Refilled the wine, lit the lamps, and resumed the feast.
After many calls and entreaties, she finally emerged,
Still holding the pipa, half-concealing her face.

She turned the pegs and plucked the strings a few times;
Before the tune took form, emotion already spoke.
Each string was muffled with sighs, every note laden with thought,
As if telling the story of a life unfulfilled.

Expressing all the boundless secrets of her heart.

And after makeup, peers often envied my beauty.

For one performance, countless bolts of red silk were presented.

Crimson skirts stained with spilled wine.

Autumn moons and spring breezes passed casually by.

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "On the banks of the Xunyang River, I bid farewell to a guest at night; 
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn chill. 
The host dismounted while the guest remained on his boat, 
We raised our wine cups, longing to drink, but lacked music. 
Drunkenness failed to bring joy as we faced a sorrowful parting, 
In that moment, only the vast river reflected the moon. 
Suddenly, from over the water, came the sound of a pipa (Chinese lute), 
The host forgot to return home, and the guest refused to depart. 
Following the sound, I quietly asked who was playing; 
The pipa stopped, and she seemed hesitant to speak. 
I moved my ship closer to invite her out, 
Refilled the wine, relit the lamps, and resumed the banquet. 
After countless calls and invitations, she finally emerged, 
Still holding the pipa, half-covering her face. 
She turned the tuning pegs and plucked two or three strings, 
Before forming a melody, emotion already filled the air. 
Each string suppressed, each note laden with thought, 
As if recounting a lifetime of unfulfilled ambition. 
With head bowed, fingers moving with practiced ease, 
She poured out all the endless matters of her heart. 
Lightly pressing, slowly twisting, sweeping then picking, 
First playing 'Rainbow Feather,' then 'Sixth Melody.' 
The thick strings rumbled like sudden rain, 
The thin strings whispered like private talk. 
Rumbles and whispers intertwined in complex play, 
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate. 
Smooth and fluid, like orioles singing beneath flowers, 
Choked and low, like spring water struggling under ice. 
The cold spring slowed, the strings froze, cutting off the flow, 
When sound ceases and cannot pass through, silence takes hold. 
A hidden sorrow and secret resentment arose, 
At this moment, silence surpassed any sound. 
Then, like a silver bottle bursting open, water splashing forth, 
Or iron cavalry charging, the clash of swords ringing out. 
The piece ended; she drew the plectrum across the center, 
All four strings struck together, ripping like silk tearing. 
Boats to the east and west fell silent, no one spoke, 
Only the white autumn moon shone upon the river's heart. 
She pondered deeply, placed the plectrum among the strings, 
Straightened her clothes, rose, and composed her expression. 
She said she had originally been a girl of the capital city, 
Her home near Xiama Ling. 
By thirteen, she had mastered the pipa, 
Listed among the first troupe of the imperial music academy. 
After performing, even master musicians admired her skill, 
Once made up, women of renown often envied her beauty. 
Young men of the Five Mausoleums competed to give her gifts, 
For each song, she received countless bolts of red silk. 
Jeweled hairpins and silver combs broke keeping time, 
Crimson skirts stained by spilled wine. 
Years of laughter followed years of merriment, 
Autumn moons and spring winds passed casually by. 
Her brother went to war, her aunt died, 
Days and nights wore on, her beauty faded. 
Few horses and carriages stopped at her door now, 
Past her prime, she married a merchant’s wife. 
Merchants value profit more than separation, 
Last month, he left for Fuliang to buy tea. 
Since leaving, she has guarded an empty boat at the river mouth, 
Surrounded by bright moonlight and cold river waters. 
Deep into the night, she suddenly dreamed of her youth, 
Waking, tears streaming down her painted cheeks. 
Hearing her pipa, I already sighed, 
And hearing these words, my sighs deepened further. 
Both of us are wanderers lost in the world, 
Meeting thus, why need we have known each other before? 
Since last year, I left the Imperial Capital, 
Demoted and bedridden in Xunyang City. 
Xunyang is remote, devoid of music, 
All year long, no stringed instruments are heard. 
Living near the Pen River, the land is low and damp, 
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo surround the house. 
What do I hear there, morning and evening? 
Cuckoos crying blood, apes wailing mournfully. 
On spring nights with blooming flowers, or autumn nights beneath the moon, 
Often I take wine and pour it alone. 
Are there truly no mountain songs or village flutes? 
Their harsh, discordant notes are hard to bear. 
Tonight, hearing your pipa’s voice, 
It is like celestial music, clearing my ears at once. 
Do not refuse to sit again and play another piece, 
For you, I will compose a ballad of the Pipa. 
Moved by my words, she stood for a long time, 
Then sat back down, tightened the strings, and played faster. 
The melancholy tone differed from before, 
Upon hearing it anew, everyone present wiped away tears. 
Who among them shed the most tears? 
The Blue-robed Prefect of Jiangzhou, his shirt soaked."}

轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。

门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
