座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "Song of the Pipa

By the Yangtze at Xunyang, I bid a guest farewell by night,
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn chill.
The host dismounted; the guest was already on his boat.
We raised our cups to drink, but there were no pipes or strings.
Though drunk, we found no joy; sorrow loomed as parting drew near,
And when we parted, the vast river seemed steeped in moonlight.
Suddenly, from over the water, came the sound of a pipa.
I forgot my return home; my guest did not set forth.
Following the sound, we asked softly who was playing.
The pipa’s notes paused, hesitant, as if about to speak.
We moved our boats close together and invited her out.
More wine was poured, lamps trimmed, and the banquet reopened.
After many calls and entreaties, she finally emerged,
Still holding her pipa, half-covering her face.
She adjusted the pegs and plucked two or three chords;
Before any melody formed, emotion was already there.
Each string sounded with suppressed melancholy, every note filled with longing,
As if telling of a life thwarted in its ambitions.
With downcast eyes, she played casually yet continuously,
Expressing all the boundless matters within her heart.
Lightly pressing, slowly twisting, brushing then picking—
First the 'Rainbow Robe,' then the 'Six Strings' followed.
The thick strings rumbled like sudden rain;
The thin strings whispered like private talk.
Rumbling and whispering intermingled in her play,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Clear and sweet, like orioles singing beneath the flowers;
Muffled and choked, like springs flowing under ice.
Ice-cold and sluggish, the strings froze and ceased;
Ceasing, blocked, the sounds rested for a while.
Then arose hidden sorrow and secret resentment—
At such moments, silence surpasses sound.
Like a silver vase shattering, water bursting forth;
Like iron cavalry charging out, the clash of swords and spears.
The tune ended; she gathered the plectrum and swept across the center;
All four strings rang out once, like tearing silk.
The boats to east and west fell silent, speechless,
Only seeing the white autumn moon in the middle of the river.
She pondered for a moment, tucked the plectrum into the strings,
Straightened her clothes, rose, and composed her expression.
She said: "Originally a girl from the capital city,
My home was below Xiama Ridge.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa;
My name belonged to the first division of the Imperial Music Bureau.
After finishing a piece, even great masters would admire;
When fully dressed, even courtesans would envy me.
The young men of the Five Tombs vied to give me gifts;
For one song, I received countless bolts of red silk.
Jeweled hairpins and silver combs broke keeping time;
Blood-red skirts stained by spilling wine."
"Year after year of laughter and joy,
Taking spring winds and autumn moons lightly for granted."
"But then my brother joined the army, and my aunt died;
Days turned to nights, and my beauty faded."
"The door grew desolate, few horses remained;
Getting old, I married a merchant’s wife."
"Merchants value profit above all, indifferent to parting;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea."
"Gone and come, I guard an empty boat at the river mouth;
Around the boat shines the bright moon, the river waters are cold."
"Deep in the night, I suddenly dream of youthful days;
Waking, I cry, makeup tears streaming red down my cheeks."
Hearing the pipa, I had already sighed;
Hearing these words, I sighed again deeply.
We are both exiles at the end of the earth;
Why must we have known each other before meeting?
Since last year, leaving the Imperial Capital,
Demoted, I lay ill in the city of Xunyang.
Xunyang is remote, lacking music;
All year round, I hear not the sound of strings or flutes.
Living near the Pen River, the land is low and damp;
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo surround my house.
What do I hear morning and evening here?
Cuckoos crying blood, monkeys wailing in grief.
On spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn nights under the moon,
Often I take wine, pouring it alone.
Are there no mountain songs and village flutes?
They are harsh, discordant, difficult to bear hearing.
Tonight, hearing your pipa melodies,
It is like listening to fairy music; my ears are suddenly clear.
Do not refuse to sit again and play one more tune;
For you, I will compose 'The Song of the Pipa.'
Moved by my words, she stood for a long time,
Then sat back, tightened the strings—the tempo quickened.
Sorrowful, unlike the earlier tunes,
The whole company heard it again and wiped away tears.
Who among us shed the most tears?
The Magistrate of Jiangzhou, his blue robe wet."}

Suddenly, from over the water, came the sound of a pipa;
The host forgot to return home, the guest did not depart.
Following the sound, I quietly asked who was playing,
But the pipa paused, hesitant before answering.
I moved my boat closer to invite her out,
Refilled the wine, brought back the lamp, and reopened the feast.
After thousands of calls and ten thousand entreaties she finally emerged,
Still clutching the pipa, half-concealing her face.

She turned the pegs and plucked the strings two or three times;
Before the melody formed, emotion was already there.
Each string was muffled with sighs, every note heavy with longing,
As if telling of a life that found no fulfillment.
With downcast eyes, fingers moving casually, she played on,
Expressing all the boundless matters of her heart.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, sweeping then picking,
First she played "Rainbow Robes," then followed by "Green Waist."

The thick strings thundered like sudden heavy rain,
The thin strings whispered like private conversation.
Thundering and whispering intertwined in complex play,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Birdlike songs flowed smoothly beneath blossoms,
Then choked sounds struggled through springs under ice.
The notes froze like ice-bound springs, until silence came.
A new hidden sorrow and dark resentment arose—
At this point, silence surpassed any sound.

Then, like a silver vase bursting open, water splashed forth,
Like iron cavalry charging, swords and spears clangored.
The piece ended; she gathered the plectrum and struck the center,
One final cry from the four strings, sharp as rending silk.
East and west boats lay quiet, speechless alike,
Seeing only the pale autumn moon reflected in the river’s heart.

She pondered deeply, inserted the plectrum among the strings,
Straightened her clothes, rose, and composed her expression.

Living near Toad Mound, in the old quarter.

After finishing a song, even master players would admire,
And after makeup, peers often envied my beauty.
Young dandies from the Five Tombs competed to shower me with brocade,
For one performance, countless bolts of red silk were presented.
Gold-inlaid combs snapped keeping time,
Crimson skirts stained with spilled wine.
Year after year, laughter repeated itself,
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed casually by.
My brother joined the army, my aunt died,
Days turned to nights, and my youth faded away.
Before my gate, visitors grew scarce, horses rare,

Merchants prize profit over affection, leaving easily,
Last month he went to Fuliang to trade tea.
He left, and I waited alone by the river mouth,
Surrounded by bright moonlight, the river water cold.
Deep in the night, I suddenly dreamed of my younger days,

By the Xunyang River, at night I bid a guest farewell,
As autumn winds rustled maple leaves and reed flowers.
The host dismounted; the guest was aboard his ship,
We raised our cups to drink, but no music played.
Drunk yet joyless, we faced the sorrow of parting,
While the vast river soaked the moon in its depths.
Suddenly, pipa strings sounded over the water;
The host forgot to return, the guest delayed his departure.
We followed the sound, asking softly who could play,
But the pipa ceased, and she hesitated to speak.
We moved our ships closer, inviting her to appear,
Refilled the wine, relit the lamps, and resumed the feast.
Called upon a thousand times, ten thousand times, she finally emerged,
Still holding the pipa half-covering her face.
She turned the pegs and plucked two or three strings,
Before the melody formed, emotion already flowed.
Each string muffled, each note heavy with thought,
Seeming to tell of a lifetime's thwarted ambitions.
Head bowed, fingers moving casually again and again,
Expressing all the boundless matters of her heart.
Lightly pressing, slowly twisting, sweeping then picking,
First playing 'Rainbow Garment,' then 'Six Strings.'
The thick strings rumbled like sudden rain,
The thin strings whispered like private talk.
Rumbling and whispering interwoven in play,
Like large and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Sweet as orioles singing under blossoms, flowing smooth,
Low and choked as spring water struggling beneath ice.
Ice-cold springs grew sluggish, strings froze, sound died,
Frozen, blocked, for a moment silence held sway.
Then arose hidden sorrows and unspoken resentments—
At this moment, silence surpassed sound.
Silver vases suddenly burst,浆 spurting forth,
Iron cavalry charged out, swords and spears clanging.
The tune ended; she drew the plectrum across the center,
The four strings rang once, like tearing silk.
Ships east and west fell silent, speechless,
Only the white autumn moon was seen in the river's heart.
Hesitant, she put down the plectrum among the strings,
Straightened her clothes, rose, and composed her features.
She said she was originally a girl from the capital,
Living near Shama Hill by old habit.
At thirteen she mastered the pipa,
Her name listed among the finest in the Imperial Academy.
After playing, even skilled masters were impressed,
When made up, rivals like Qiuniang envied her beauty.
Young men of Five Tombs vied to give her gifts,
For one song, countless bolts of red silk.
Gold-headed combs broke beating time,
Blood-red skirts stained with spilled wine.
Year after year laughter returned, and next year came,
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed idly away.
Her brother went to war, her aunt died,
Evenings passed, mornings came, fading her youth.
The door became desolate, horse carts rare,
Aging, she married a merchant as wife.
Merchants value profit, care little for parting,
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He left; here at the river mouth she guards an empty ship,
Around the ship, bright moonlight, cold river waters.
Late at night she dreamed of youthful days,
Waking, tears ran down her painted cheeks.
I heard the pipa and sighed,
And hearing these words, my sighs deepened.
Both are drifters at the end of the world,
Why must we have known each other before?
Since last year I left the imperial city,
Banished to Xunyang, sick and bedridden.
Xunyang is remote, lacking music,
All year long, no string or flute sounds.
Living near the Pen River, low and damp land,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo surround my home.
What do I hear morning and evening there?
Cuckoos bleeding cries, monkeys wailing mournfully.
Spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moon nights,
Often I take wine and pour it alone.

For you, I will compose this 'Song of the Pipa.'

Then sat, quickened the strings, which grew urgent.

Maple leaves and reed flowers tremble in the autumn chill.
I, the host, dismount my horse while my guest stands by his boat;
We raise our cups to drink, but there is no music here.

Drunk yet joyless on the brink of parting,
Gazing at the moon floating in the vast, misty river.
Suddenly, from across the water, comes the sound of a pipa;
The host forgets to return home, the guest delays departure.

Following the sound, I ask softly who plays;
The pipa stops, as if the player hesitates to speak.
I move my boat closer to invite her out,
Add more wine, trim the lamps, and resume the feast.

After many calls and entreaties she finally appears,
Still holding her pipa half-covering her face.
She turns the pegs and plucks the strings two or three times;
Before the melody forms, emotion already speaks.

Each string murmurs deeply, each note full of thought,
Seeming to tell of a lifetime’s unfulfilled ambitions.
Head lowered, fingers moving freely and continuously,
Pouring out infinite matters within her heart.

At first playing the "Rainbow Skirt," then later the "Six Strings."
The thick strings rumble loudly like sudden rain;
The thin strings whisper intimately like private talk.

Loud and soft notes interweave in mixed play,
Like large and small pearls falling into a jade plate.
Clear and sweet, orioles singing amidst blossoms glide smoothly;
Muffled and choked, spring water flowing under ice struggles hard.

The cold, sluggish spring freezes the strings in silence;
In this stillness, blocked sounds cease for a moment.
But new hidden sorrows and secret resentments arise—
At such moments, silence surpasses any sound.

Then suddenly, a silver vase shatters, water bursts forth;
Iron cavalry charge out with swords clashing and spears ringing.
As the song ends, she gathers the plectrum for a final stroke,
And all four strings sound together like tearing silk.

Eastward boats and westward barges fall silently quiet;
Only the white autumn moon on the river center is seen.

Straightens her clothes, rises, and composes her countenance.

Living near Xiama Hill where my family resided.
At thirteen, I mastered the art of the pipa,
My name listed in the top rank of the Imperial Music Bureau.
When a piece was finished, even great masters would admire;
When makeup was done, other beauties often felt envy.
Young men from the Five Mausoleums competed to give gifts;
For one song, red silks were received beyond counting.
Gold-inlaid hairpins broke keeping time;
Blood-red brocade skirts stained by spilled wine.
This year laughter again next year,
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed casually away.
Brother went off to the army, aunt died of illness;
Evenings came, mornings went, beauty faded with age.
The door grew cold, riders and horses became scarce;
Getting old, I married a merchant who cares only for profit.
He neglects separation, last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea;
Leaving me alone guarding an empty boat at the river mouth.
Around the boat, bright moonlight shines on cold river waters;
Late at night, dreaming suddenly of youthful days,

Hearing these words, I sigh again deeply.
Both we are people adrift to the ends of the earth;
Meeting now, why should it matter if we knew each other before?

By Bai Juyi

At night I bid farewell to a guest by the Xunyang River,
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in autumn's chill.
The host dismounted, his guest was aboard the boat;
We raised our cups to drink, but there were no pipes or strings.
Tipsy yet joyless, we faced our sad parting;
In that moment of leaving, vast was the river, bathed in moonlight.
Suddenly, from over the water, came the sound of pipa playing;
The host forgot to return, and the guest did not depart.
Following the sound, I quietly asked who played it;
The pipa music stopped, as if about to speak, then hesitated.
I moved my boat closer and invited her to appear;
More wine was added, lamps turned up, and the feast resumed.
After countless calls and pleas, she finally emerged,
Still holding her pipa, half-covering her face.
She tuned the pegs and plucked a few strings;
Before the melody took shape, emotion had already arisen.
Each string suppressed, each note filled with longing,
As if telling of unfulfilled ambitions in life.
With lowered brow, she casually played on and on,
Expressing all the boundless thoughts within her heart.
Lightly pressing, slowly twisting, sliding then plucking,
First playing 'Rainbow Feather,' then 'Sixth String.'
The thick strings rumbled like sudden heavy rain,
The thin strings whispered like secret confessions.
Rumbling and whispering intertwined in complex play,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Chirping like an oriole gliding through flowers below,
Sobbing like spring water struggling under ice.
Ice-cold springs grew sluggish, strings froze tight;
Frozen and impassable, the sound momentarily ceased.
Hidden sorrows and secret resentments arose;
At this moment, silence surpassed sound.
Like a silver vase suddenly bursting, water spraying forth,
Like iron cavalry charging out, blades and spears clashing.
When the tune ended, she drew the pick across the center strings,
All four strings rang out once, like tearing silk.
Boats to the east and west fell silent without a word;
Only the white autumn moon remained visible in the river’s heart.
Lost in thought, she placed the pick among the strings,
Smoothed her clothes, rose, and composed her expression.
She said: "Originally I was a girl from the capital city,
Living near Shrimp Mound Hill.
By thirteen I had mastered the pipa,
My name recorded in the first division of the Imperial Music Bureau.
After performing a piece, even master musicians admired me;
Once made up, often envied by courtesans like Qiuniang.
Young nobles from Five Tombs fought over gifts of silk;
For one song, red silks arrived beyond counting.
Jeweled hairpins and silver combs broke keeping time,
Blood-red skirts stained by spilled wine.
This year laughter, next year again,
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed idly away.
My brother went off to war, my aunt died;
Evenings came, mornings followed, and beauty faded.
The door was cold and deserted, horses rare;
Growing old, I married a merchant wife.
The merchant values profit above separation;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He left me guarding an empty boat at the river mouth,
Around the ship, bright moon and cold river waters.
Deep in night, I suddenly dreamt of youthful days;
Waking tears streaked down my painted cheeks.
Hearing the pipa, I already sighed longingly;
Hearing these words, I groaned again deeply.
Both are wanderers fallen low beneath heaven;
Meeting now, why must we have known each other before?
Since last year I left the imperial capital,
Demoted to lie ill in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, devoid of music;
Throughout the year, I hear no wind or string instruments.
Living near the Pen River, land low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my home.
What do I hear here morning and evening?
Cuckoos crying blood and apes wailing mournfully.
On spring rivers amid flowering mornings, on autumn nights under full moons,
Often I take wine and pour alone.
Are there none mountain songs or village flutes?
Unharmonious and harsh, difficult for ears to bear.
Tonight hearing your pipa speech,
It is like listening to celestial music; my ears suddenly clear.
Do not refuse to sit again and play another piece;
For you, I will compose 'The Ballad of the Pipa.'
Moved by my words, she stood for a long while;
Then sat back down, tightening strings which played faster.
Mournful sounds unlike those from before;
The entire audience, hearing again, covered their faces and wept.
Who shed the most tears among them?
The Blue-robed Sima of Jiangzhou."}

座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "On the banks of the Xunyang River, I bid farewell to a guest at night;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustle in the autumn chill.
The host dismounts; the guest is on his boat;
We raise our cups to drink, but there are no pipes or strings.
Drunk yet unable to find joy, we sorrow over parting;
At the moment of departure, vast waters soak the moon.
Suddenly, the sound of a pipa drifts across the water;
The host forgets to return, the guest delays his journey.
Seeking the source, I whisper to ask who plays;
The pipa pauses, hesitating to speak.
I move my boat closer, inviting her to meet us;
More wine is poured, lamps turned up, the banquet reopened.
After countless calls, she finally emerges,
Still holding her pipa, half-covering her face.
She turns the pegs, plucks two or three strings;
Before the melody forms, emotion already flows.
Each string suppressed, each note laden with thought,
As if telling of a life’s unfulfilled ambitions.
Head lowered, fingers play lightly and continuously,
Voicing all the boundless matters of her heart.
Light pressings, slow rubs, slurs and picks;
First the 'Rainbow Garment,' then the 'Six Strings' piece.
The thick strings rumble like sudden rain;
The thin strings whisper like private talk.
Rumbling and whispering intermingle in play;
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Cooing like orioles sliding through blossoms;
Choking like springs trapped beneath ice.
The cold spring seizes, the strings halt utterly;
Utterly halted, blocked, the sound briefly ceases.
Another hidden sorrow, dark resentment arises;
In this moment, silence surpasses sound.
Then, as if a silver vase suddenly bursts, water spraying;
Or armored cavalry charging out, swords clashing.
When the tune ends, she places the plectrum centrally;
One strum from the four strings, like tearing silk.
Boats east and west fall silent;
Only the white autumn moon remains in the river’s center.
Lost in thought, she sets down the plectrum among the strings,
Adjusts her clothes, rises with composed dignity.
She says: ‘I was originally a girl from the capital,
Living near the Xiama Hill.'
At thirteen years old, I mastered the pipa;
My name belonged to the first rank of the imperial music school.
After playing, even master performers would admire me;
Dressed up, beautiful women like Qiuniang would envy me.
Young men from the Five Tombs competed to give gifts;
For one song, they gave an unknown number of red silks.
Gold-inlaid combs snapped keeping time;
Blood-red skirts spilled with wine stains.
This year laughing, next year again;
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed casually.
My brother went off to war, my aunt died;
Evening comes and morning goes, fading my beauty.
Before my door, it grew lonely, horses rare;
Getting older, I married a merchant's wife.
The merchant values profit above all, lightly dismissing separation;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
Away and back, guarding an empty boat at the river mouth;
Around the boat, bright moonlight, the river water cold.
Deep in the night, I suddenly dream of youthful days;
Waking with tears staining my makeup, running down my cheek.
Hearing the pipa, I sighed deeply;
Hearing these words, I lament anew.
Both of us are wanderers fallen low at the edge of the world;
Since we meet now, why must we have known each other before?
I left the Imperial Capital last year,
Demoted to sickbed in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, lacking music;
All year long, no sound of silk and bamboo is heard.
Living near the Pen River, the land is low and damp;
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboos grow around my home.
What do I hear here, day and night?
Cuckoos bleeding cries, apes wailing mournfully.
In spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moon nights,
Often I take wine and pour it alone for myself.
Are there not folk songs and village flutes?
But their harsh, noisy sounds are hard to listen to.
Tonight hearing your pipa speech,
It’s like hearing celestial music; ears suddenly clear.
Do not refuse to sit again and play one more tune;
For you, I will compose this Ballad of the Pipa.
Moved by these words, she stood for a long while;
Then sat down, tightening the strings, playing faster.
The melancholy did not resemble the earlier sound;
Everyone present listened again, covering faces to weep.
Who shed the most tears in the room?
The blue robe of the Sima of Jiangzhou was wet."}

By Bai Juyi

At night by the Xunyang River I saw off a guest;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn chill.
The host dismounted; the guest was on his boat.
We raised our cups, wishing to drink, but there was no music.
Drunk yet joyless, sorrowful at parting,
As we bid farewell, the vast river held the moon in its depths.
Suddenly, from the water, came the sound of a pipa;
The host forgot to return, and the guest did not depart.
Following the sound, I quietly asked who was playing;
The pipa stopped, as if about to speak, then hesitated.
I moved my boat closer to invite her out for tea,
Refilled the wine, trimmed the lamp, and renewed the feast.
Called a thousand times, urged ten thousand, she finally came out,
Still holding the pipa, half covering her face.
She tuned the pegs and plucked the strings two or three times;
Before the melody formed, emotion was already present.
Each string suppressed, each note filled with thoughts,
As if telling of a lifetime's unfulfilled ambitions.
With lowered brows, she played casually on,
Expressing all the boundless matters of her heart.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, strumming and picking,
First playing "Rainbow Skirt," then "Six One."
The bass strings boomed like heavy rain,
The treble strings whispered like private talk.
Booming and whispering, mixed together they rang,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Clear and sweet, like orioles singing under flowers,
Muffled and choked, like springs flowing beneath ice.
Ice-cold and sluggish, the strings seemed to freeze and stop;
Blocked and silent, the sound momentarily ceased.
Then arose hidden sorrows and dark grudges;
At this moment, silence surpassed speech.
Suddenly, like a silver vase bursting open, water gushed forth;
Like iron cavalry charging out, swords and spears clashed.
When the song ended, she swept the plectrum across the center;
All four strings sounded once, like silk tearing.
East boats and west ships were quiet, no one spoke;
Only the white autumn moon in the river's center was seen.

Silver combs adorned with jewelry shattered keeping time;
Red-dyed skirts stained by overturned wine.

The autumn moon and spring breeze passed idly by.
My brother went off to join the army; my aunt died;
Evenings came and mornings went, and my beauty faded.
The door became desolate; carriages and horses grew rare;
Getting old, I married the wife of a merchant.

Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.

Around the boat, bright moonlight, cold river water.

Hearing these words added further lamentation.

低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。

座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "On the banks of the Xunyang River, I saw off a friend at night;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn chill.
The host dismounted, the guest remained on board;
We raised our wine cups, yet lacked the music of pipes and strings.
Drunkenness brought no joy as we faced parting’s sorrow,
Only the vast river immersed in moonlight greeted our farewell.

Suddenly, from over the water, came the sound of a pipa;
The host forgot to return home, the guest delayed his departure.
Following the melody, I asked softly who was playing,
But the pipa paused, hesitant before answering.
I moved my boat closer, inviting her to meet me,
Refilled the wine, lit the lamps, and resumed the feast.
After many calls and entreaties, she finally emerged,
Still holding the pipa, half-concealing her face.

She turned the pegs and plucked the strings a few times;
Before the tune took form, emotion already spoke.
Each string was muffled with sighs, every note laden with thought,
As if telling the story of a life unfulfilled.
With downcast eyes, fingers moving naturally, she played on,
Expressing all the boundless secrets of her heart.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, sweeping then picking,
First she played “Rainbow Robes,” then followed by “Six Strings.”

The thick strings thundered like a sudden heavy rain,
The thin strings whispered like private conversations.
Thundering and whispering intertwined in complex play,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Birdlike songs flowed smoothly beneath blossoms,
Then choked sounds struggled through springs under ice.
Ice-cold springs slowed the strings to stillness,
When silence fell and the voice ceased for a moment.
A new hidden sorrow and dark resentment arose—
At this point, silence surpassed any sound.

Then, like a silver vase bursting open, water splashed forth,
Like iron cavalry charging, swords and spears clangored.
The piece ended; she gathered the plectrum and struck the center string,
One final cry from the four strings, like silk tearing apart.
East and west boats lay quiet, speechless alike,
Seeing only the pale autumn moon reflected in the river’s heart.

She pondered deeply, inserted the plectrum among the strings,
Straightened her clothes, rose, and composed her expression.
She said: “I was originally a girl from the capital city,
Living near Shrimp Hill, in the old quarter.
By thirteen, I had mastered the pipa,
My name inscribed in the First Hall of the Music Academy.
After finishing a song, even great masters would admire,
And after makeup, peers often envied my beauty.
Young nobles from Five Mausoleums vied to gift me brocade,
For one performance, countless bolts of red silk were presented.
Gold-inlaid combs snapped keeping time,
Crimson skirts stained with spilled wine.
Year after year, laughter repeated itself,
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed casually by.
My brother joined the army, my aunt died,
Days turned to nights, and my youth faded away.
Before my gate, visitors grew scarce, horses rare,
So when old, I married a merchant man.
Merchants prize profit over affection, leaving easily,
Last month he went to Fuliang to trade tea.
He left, and I waited alone by the river mouth,
Surrounded by bright moonlight, the river water cold.
Deep in the night, I suddenly dreamed of my younger days,
Waking with tears staining my makeup red.”

Hearing the pipa, I had already sighed,
Now hearing these words, my grief deepened further.
“Both of us are wanderers fallen from grace,
Meeting here, why should previous acquaintance matter?
Since last year I left the Imperial Capital,
Banished to lie ill in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, devoid of music,
All year long, I hear not a single string or pipe.
Near the Pen River, where land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my home.
What do I hear there, morning and evening?
Cuckoos crying blood, monkeys wailing in sorrow.
Spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moonlit nights—
Often I pour wine, drinking alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
Their harsh, discordant tones are hard to bear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa’s language,
It is like listening to celestial music, clearing my ears.
Do not refuse to sit and play another tune,
For you, I will compose ‘The Ballad of the Pipa.’”

Moved by my words, she stood for a long while,
Then returned to sit, tightening the strings, playing faster.
Her mournful notes differed from those before,
To the full audience, each covered their faces and wept.
Who shed the most tears in the room?
The Green-robed Sima of Jiangzhou, his sleeves soaked."}

On the banks of Xunyang River, I bid a guest farewell at night;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustle in the autumn chill.
I dismount from my horse to where my guest waits on the boat;
We raise our cups to drink, yet no music plays in sight.
Drunkenness brings no joy; sorrow looms as we must part;
At the moment of leaving, the vast river is bathed in moonlight.
Suddenly, over the water, we hear the sound of a pipa;
The host forgets his return, the guest delays his departure.
Following the sound, I ask in hush who might be playing;
The pipa stops, but she hesitates before speaking her name.
We move our boat closer, inviting her to appear;
We add wine, relight the lamps, and restart the banquet.
After many calls, she finally emerges,
Still holding her pipa, half-hiding her face.
She turns the pegs and plucks the strings a few times,
Before the tune begins, emotion already fills the air.
Each string suppresses deep thought within each note,
As if recounting a lifetime of unfulfilled ambitions.
With lowered brows, she plays with casual ease,
Telling all the boundless stories of her heart.
Lightly pressing, slowly twisting, sweeping and picking again,
First she plays "Rainbow Robe," then "Six Strings."
The thick strings roar like sudden heavy rain;
The thin strings whisper like private murmurs.
Roaring and whispering intermingle in complex play,
Like large and small pearls falling into a jade plate.
Smooth and clear, like orioles singing beneath flowers;
Low and choked, like spring water flowing under ice.

When blocked and unable to flow, the sound temporarily ceases.
Then arises a hidden sorrow, a dark resentment,
And silence at this moment surpasses speech.

Like iron cavalry charging forth, swords and spears clash and ring.

One final chord sounds like tearing silk.
Boats to the east and west fall silent without words;
Only the white autumn moon shines upon the river's heart.

Straightens her clothes, rises, composing her expression.

My home was located near Xiama Ridge.
At thirteen, I completed my training on the pipa,
My name listed in the first division of the Imperial Music Bureau.
After performing a piece, even masters would admire me;
When made up, every beauty felt envious of my grace.
The young nobles of Five Tombs competed to give gifts;
For one performance, countless bolts of red silk were given.
Hairpins studded with gems broke keeping time;
Crimson skirts stained by spilled wine during revelry.
Year after year passed in laughter and merriment;
Autumn moons and spring breezes were viewed casually.
My brother went off to join the army; my auntie died;
Evenings pass, mornings come, and my beauty fades away.
Before my door, desolation reigns; horses and saddles are scarce;
In old age, I married a merchant as his wife.
The merchant values profit highly and takes parting lightly;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
Gone and gone, I guard an empty boat at the river mouth;
Surrounding the boat, the bright moon casts a cold light on the river.

Dreaming, I cry tears that stain my rouge-streaked face.

Hearing these words further, I sigh with renewed grief.

Having met now, why should it matter if we knew each other before?

All year long I hear no sound of strings or pipes.

Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.

Dusky cuckoos bleeding cries, apes howling in anguish.

Often I take wine and pour myself alone.

Then returned to sit and tightened the strings, making them sound quicker.

Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn chill.
The host dismounted; the guest stood on his boat.
We raised our cups to drink, yet had no strings or pipes for music.
Drunk but not joyful, gloomy as parting drew near—
At the moment of farewell, vast was the river, soaked in moonlight.
Suddenly, from over the water, the sound of a pipa drifted up;
The host forgot to return home, the guest delayed setting sail.
Following the sound, we asked softly who was playing;
The pipa stopped, and the player hesitated to speak.
We moved our boats close to invite her out,
Refilled the wine, trimmed the wicks, and reopened the feast.
Called a thousand times, urged ten thousand, she finally emerged,
Still holding her pipa, half-covering her face.
She turned the pegs and plucked two or three strings;
Before forming a melody, emotion already flowed.
Each string suppressed, each note laden with thought,
As if telling of a lifetime’s unfulfilled ambitions.
Brows lowered, fingers moving freely, she played on continuously,
Expressing all the boundless matters in her heart.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, sweeping then flicking,
First playing “Rainbow Skirt,” then “Six Strings.”
The thick strings rumbled like sudden heavy rain,
The thin ones whispered closely like private murmurs.
Rumbling and whispering intertwined in complex play,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Chattering like an oriole sliding through flowers below,
Muffled sobs like a spring flowing under ice.
Then the icy spring grew cold and sluggish, strings frozen tight;
Frozen and blocked, the sound paused briefly.
Another sorrow took root in darkness and hidden resentment—
Now silence spoke louder than any sound could.

Iron cavalry charged forth, swords and spears clashing.

All four strings rang together, tearing like silk.

Living my home beneath Shrimp Mound Hill.

My name was listed among the finest in the Imperial Music Academy.

Once made up, courtesans often envied me.
Young men of Five Tombs competed to gift me silks;
For one song, countless lengths of red gauze were bestowed.
Jeweled hairpins and silver combs broke keeping time;
Blood-red skirts stained by spilled wine during revels.

Autumn moons and spring breezes enjoyed carelessly.

Evenings came, mornings went, beauty faded away.

In dreams, crying, tears washed rouge down my face.

Hearing these words, I felt fresh waves of grief once more.

On a night by the Xunyang River, I saw off my guest;
Maple leaves and reed flowers shivered in autumn's breath.
The host dismounted; the guest was already aboard,
We raised our cups for wine, but had no pipes or strings.
Drunk yet joyless, we faced the sorrow of parting;
At farewell, the vast river drowned the moon in its glow.
Suddenly, from across the water, pipa music rose;
The host forgot to return, the guest delayed his start.
Following the sound, I whispered: who plays? The music ceased,
Someone wished to speak, but hesitated.
I moved my boat close to invite them out,
Refilled the wine, adjusted the lamps, resumed the feast.
Amid countless calls and pleas, she finally emerged,
Still holding her pipa, half-covering her face.
She turned the pegs and plucked two or three strings;
Before the melody formed, emotion was already there.
Each string suppressed a sigh, each note carried longing,
As if telling of a lifetime’s unfulfilled ambition.
With downcast eyes, casually playing on and on,
She poured out infinite matters from her heart.
Lightly pressing, slowly twisting, sweeping then picking,
First 'Rainbow Garment,' then 'Six Strings.'
Thick strings thrummed like sudden rain;
Thin strings whispered like private talk.
Loud and soft notes intertwined in varied play,
Like large and small pearls falling into a jade plate.
Clear as orioles singing under blossoms, flowing smoothly;
Muffled as springs choking beneath ice, struggling hard.
Cold ice, sluggish flow, strings froze in silence;
Frozen still, blocked up, sound temporarily ceased.
There arose a different hidden sorrow, secret resentment;
In this moment, silence surpassed all sound.
Then, like a silver vase bursting with splashing water,
Or iron cavalry charging with clashing swords and spears.
When the tune ended, she swept the plectrum across the center;
Four strings rang once, like tearing silk.
Boats east and west fell silent, speechless;
Only the white autumn moon reflected in the river's heart.
Pondering deeply, she put the plectrum among the strings,
Straightened her clothes, rose, gathering her composure.
She said herself: "Originally a girl from the capital city,
My home lay below the Xiama Ling district.
By thirteen, I mastered the pipa;
My name ranked first in the Imperial Music Bureau.
After performing a piece, even skilled masters were impressed;
Once made up, courtesans often envied me.
Young nobles from the Five Mausoleums competed in gifts,
For one song, I received countless bolts of red silk.
Gold-ornamented hairpins broke keeping time,
Blood-red skirts stained with spilled wine.
Year after year, laughter continued;
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed idly away.
Then my brother joined the army, my aunt died;
Days went by, mornings came, and beauty faded.
The door grew cold, horses and carriages rare;
Growing old, I married a merchant's wife.
The merchant values profit high, cherishes separation little;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He left me here at the river mouth to guard an empty boat;
Surrounding the boat, moonlight bright, river water cold.
Late at night, suddenly dreaming of youthful days;
Waking with tears streaming through makeup, red stains streaking.
Hearing the pipa, I had already sighed;
Hearing these words, I lamented again deeply.
We are both fallen people wandering far from home;
Meeting now, why should it matter that we haven't known each other before?
Since last year, I left the Imperial Capital,
Demoted, sick, lying low in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, without music;
All year long, I hear no stringed instruments.
Living near the Pen River, land low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear here, morning and evening?
Cuckoos crying blood, apes wailing mournfully.
Spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moon nights,
Often take wine alone, pouring it down myself.
Are there not mountain songs and village flutes?
They are harsh and discordant, hard to bear listening.
Tonight, hearing your pipa language,
It's as if hearing celestial music, ears momentarily cleared.
Do not refuse to sit and play one more piece;
For you, I will re-compose the 'Song of the Pipa.'
Moved by my words, she stood long;
Then sat back down, tightened strings, tempo quickening.
Sorrowful sounds unlike those played before;
The entire company, hearing again, covered faces and wept.
Who shed the most tears among the seated guests?
The Prefect of Jiangzhou, whose blue robe became wet."}

At night, by the Xunyang River, I saw off a guest;
Maple leaves and reed flowers shivered in autumn's chill.
The host dismounted; the guest was aboard his boat,
We raised our cups to drink, but lacked music’s sweet sound.
Drunk yet joyless, we faced a sad parting;
When we said farewell, vast was the river, moonlight submerged.
Suddenly, from the water, came the sound of pipa strings;
The host forgot to return home, the guest did not set sail.
Following the sound, I asked quietly who was playing,
But the pipa paused, the player hesitating to speak.
I moved my boat close to invite her out,
Added wine, turned up the lamps, and resumed the feast.
After countless calls, she finally emerged,
Still holding the pipa, half-covering her face.
She tuned the pegs and plucked three or four notes,
Before a melody formed, emotion already poured forth.
Each string suppressed, each note full of longing,
As if telling of a life unfulfilled.
Head lowered, fingers moving freely one after another,
Singing out all the boundless troubles of her heart.
Lightly pressing, slowly twisting, sweeping then picking,
First she played “Rainbow Garments,” then the “Six Strings.”
The thick strings rumbled like sudden rain,
The thin strings whispered like private murmurs.
Rumbling and whispering intertwined in play,
Like large and small pearls falling into a jade plate.
Smooth as orioles singing beneath flowers,
Choked and sobbing as spring water froze underground.
Ice-cold water, stiffened strings, sound cut off abruptly,
Blocked and silent, the music paused for a moment.
Yet hidden sorrows and secret resentments arose,
In that silence, more than any voice could say.
Then suddenly, like a silver vase breaking, water bursting forth,
Or armored cavalry charging, swords clashing loudly.
The song ended; she drew the plectrum across the center,
A sharp snap of the four strings, like tearing silk.
To the east boats and west ships stood silent, no word spoken,
Only seeing the autumn moon bright on the river’s heart.
She pondered a while, tucked the plectrum among the strings,
Straightened her clothes, rose with a composed dignity.
She said: "I was originally a girl from the capital city,
My home near Shrimp Hill, under its foot."
"At thirteen, I mastered the pipa,
My name belonged to the top tier of the Imperial Music Bureau."
"After finishing a piece, even great masters would admire me,
When dressed up, often envied by beautiful courtesans."
"Young men of the Five Tombs vied to give gifts,
One song earned bolts of red silk beyond counting."
"Jeweled hairpins broken keeping time,
Blood-red skirts stained with spilled wine."
"This year laughing, next year still joking,
Casually passing through autumn moons and spring breezes."
"My brother went to war, my aunt died,
Evenings passed, mornings came, my beauty faded."
"Cold and deserted before my door, few carriages remained,
So when older, I married a merchant’s wife."

Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea."

Surrounded by bright moonlight, cold river waters."
"Late at night, suddenly dreaming of youthful days,
Waking, tears flowing down my painted face, staining it crimson."

And hearing these words, I sighed deeply again.

Meeting now—what need is there for having known each other before?"

It is like listening to immortal music; my ears clear for a moment."

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "On the banks of the Xunyang River, I saw off a guest at night;
Maple leaves and reed flowers shivered in the autumn chill.
The host dismounted, the guest remained on board;
We raised our wine cups to drink, yet lacked pipes and strings.
Drunkenness brought no joy as parting loomed with despair,
Just the vast river steeped in moonlight when we said goodbye.

Suddenly, from over the water, came the sound of a pipa;
The host forgot to return home, the guest did not depart.
Following the sound, I quietly asked who was playing,
But the pipa paused, hesitant before answering.
I moved my boat closer to invite her out,
Refilled the wine, brought back the lamp, and reopened the feast.
After thousands of calls and ten thousand entreaties she finally emerged,
Still clutching the pipa, half-concealing her face.

She turned the pegs and plucked the strings two or three times;
Before the melody formed, emotion was already there.
Each string was muffled with sighs, every note heavy with longing,
As if telling of a life that found no fulfillment.
With downcast eyes, fingers moving casually, she played on,
Expressing all the boundless matters of her heart.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, sweeping then picking,
First she played "Rainbow Robes," then followed by "Green Waist."

The thick strings thundered like sudden heavy rain,
The thin strings whispered like private conversation.
Thundering and whispering intertwined in complex play,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Birdlike songs flowed smoothly beneath blossoms,
Then choked sounds struggled through springs under ice.
Ice-cold, sluggish notes ceased like frozen streams,
When silence fell and the voice stopped entirely.
A new hidden sorrow and dark resentment arose—
At this point, silence surpassed any sound.

Then, like a silver vase bursting open, water splashed forth,
Like iron cavalry charging, swords and spears clangored.
The piece ended; she gathered the plectrum and struck the center,
One final cry from the four strings, sharp as rending silk.
East and west boats lay quiet, speechless alike,
Seeing only the pale autumn moon reflected in the river’s heart.

She pondered deeply, inserted the plectrum among the strings,
Straightened her clothes, rose, and composed her expression.
She told us: “I was originally a girl from the capital city,
Living near Shrimp Hill, in the old quarter.
By thirteen, I had mastered the pipa,
My name listed in the first division of the Imperial Music Bureau.
After finishing a song, even master players would admire,
And after makeup, peers often envied my beauty.
Young nobles from Five Mausoleums competed to present me with silk bundles,
For one performance, countless bolts of red silk were received.
Gold-inlaid combs snapped keeping time,
Crimson skirts stained with spilled wine.
Year after year, laughter repeated itself,
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed casually by.
My brother joined the army, my aunt died,
Days turned to nights, and my youth faded away.
Before my gate, visitors grew scarce, horses rare,
So when old, I married a merchant man.
Merchants prize profit over affection, leaving easily,
Last month he went to Fuliang to trade tea.
He left, and I waited alone by the river mouth,
Surrounded by bright moonlight, the river water cold.
Deep in the night, I suddenly dreamed of my younger days,
Waking with tears staining my makeup red.”

Hearing the pipa, I had already sighed,
Now hearing these words, my grief deepened further.
“Both of us are wanderers fallen from grace,
Meeting here, why should previous acquaintance matter?
Since last year I left the Imperial Capital,
Banished to lie ill in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, devoid of music,
All year long, I hear not a single string or pipe.
Near the Pen River, where land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my home.
What do I hear there, morning and evening?
Cuckoos crying blood, monkeys wailing in sorrow.
Spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moonlit nights—
Often I pour wine, drinking alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
Their harsh, discordant tones are hard to bear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa’s language,
It is like listening to celestial music, clearing my ears.
Do not refuse to sit and play another tune,
For you, I will compose ‘The Ballad of the Pipa.’”

Moved by my words, she stood for a long while,
Then returned to sit, tightening the strings, playing faster.
Her mournful notes differed from those before,
To the full audience, each covered their faces and wept.
Who shed the most tears in the room?
The Green-robed Sima of Jiangzhou, his sleeves soaked."}

On the banks of the Xunyang River, I bid my guest farewell at night,
Where maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in the autumn breeze.
I dismounted from my horse while he stayed aboard his boat;
We raised our cups to drink, yet lacked the sound of strings and pipes.
Drunk but joyless, sorrow filled the parting hour,
As moonlight drowned in the vast, misty expanse of the river.

Suddenly, above the water, a pipa’s music rose,
Forgetting home, I lingered; my guest held back his sails.
Seeking the source, I asked softly who played thus,
The music paused as if the player wished to speak, then hesitated.
We moved our boats closer, inviting her to meet us,
Refilled the wine, relit the lamps, and resumed the feast.

After countless calls and pleas, she finally emerged,
Still holding the pipa to half-conceal her face.
She turned the pegs and plucked a few preliminary notes,
Before any melody formed, emotion already stirred.
Each string suppressed a sigh, each note conveyed longing,
Seeming to tell the tale of ambitions thwarted in life.
Eyes lowered, fingers moving casually, she continued playing,
Pouring out all the endless sorrows within her heart.

Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, sweeping and picking again,
First she played the *Rainbow Feather*, then followed with the *Six Strings*.
The thick strings thundered like a sudden rainstorm,
The thin ones whispered soft secrets between lovers.
Thunders and whispers intertwined in complex harmony,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.

Melodious warbling slid like orioles singing among blossoms,
Muffled sobs choked like spring water trapped beneath ice.
Ice-cold springs slowed, then froze the strings into silence,
When motion ceased, the music too came briefly to rest.
A hidden grief, a silent resentment now arose,
At this moment, no sound was louder than any sound.

Then suddenly, like a silver vase bursting open, water sprayed,
Like iron cavalry charging forth, swords and spears clashed loudly.
The song ended; with a single stroke across the center,
Four strings snapped together, tearing silk in one sharp cry.

East and west, the boats fell into quietude,
Only the white autumn moon reflected on the river’s heart remained.
Lost in thought, she set down her plectrum among the strings,

Living near Shama Ling, by the old terraces.
By thirteen, I had mastered the pipa’s art,
My name listed first among the Imperial Music Bureau.
When songs ended, even great masters bowed in admiration;
With makeup done, I made Autumn Flower jealous of my grace.
Young nobles from Five Tombs vied to give me gifts,
For one performance, bolts of red silk piled high beyond count.
Gold-inlaid hairpins broke marking time for dance,
Blood-red skirts were stained with spilled wine during revelry.

Year after year passed in laughter and gaiety,
Autumn moons and spring breezes wasted away carelessly.

Days turned to nights, and beauty faded with age.

So when older, I married a merchant’s wife.

He values profit more than love, indifferent to separation,
Last month he went floating Liang to buy tea, leaving me alone.
Returning, I guard an empty boat at the river mouth,
Surrounded by bright moonlight, the river waters cold.
Deep in the night, I dream vividly of youthful days,
Waking weeping, tears streaming through red makeup.'"

And hearing her words, I lamented anew.

What need have we to know each other before today?

Demoted, sick, lying low in Xunyang City’s confines.
This place is remote, devoid of music’s charm,
All year long, never heard strings nor bamboo flutes.

On the banks of the Xunyang River, I bid my guest farewell at night,
Where maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in the autumn breeze.
I dismounted from my horse while he stayed aboard his boat;
We raised our cups to drink, yet lacked the sound of strings and pipes.
Drunk but joyless, sorrow filled the parting hour,
As moonlight drowned in the vast, misty expanse of the river.

Suddenly, above the water, a pipa’s music rose,
Forgetting home, I lingered; my guest held back his sails.
Seeking the source, I asked softly who played thus,
The music paused as if the player wished to speak, then hesitated.
We moved our boats closer, inviting her to meet us,
Refilled the wine, relit the lamps, and resumed the feast.

Still holding the pipa to half-conceal her face.

Before any melody formed, emotion already stirred.

Seeming to tell the tale of ambitions thwarted in life.
Eyes lowered, fingers moving casually, she continued playing,
Pouring out all the endless sorrows within her heart.

First she played the *Rainbow Feather*, then followed with the *Six Strings*.
The thick strings thundered like a sudden rainstorm,
The thin ones whispered soft secrets between lovers.
Thunders and whispers intertwined in complex harmony,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.

Melodious warbling slid like orioles singing among blossoms,
Muffled sobs choked like spring water trapped beneath ice.
Ice-cold springs slowed, then froze the strings into silence,
When motion ceased, the music too came briefly to rest.
A hidden grief, a silent resentment now arose,
At this moment, no sound was louder than any sound.

Then suddenly, like a silver vase bursting open, water sprayed,
Like iron cavalry charging forth, swords and spears clashed loudly.
The song ended; with a single stroke across the center,
Four strings snapped together, tearing silk in one sharp cry.

East and west, the boats fell into quietude,
Only the white autumn moon reflected on the river’s heart remained.
Lost in thought, she set down her plectrum among the strings,
Straightened her clothes, stood up, composing her expression.

By thirteen, I had mastered the pipa’s art,

With makeup done, I made Autumn Flower jealous of my grace.
Young nobles from Five Tombs vied to give me gifts,
For one performance, bolts of red silk piled high beyond count.
Gold-inlaid hairpins broke marking time for dance,
Blood-red skirts were stained with spilled wine during revelry.

Year after year passed in laughter and gaiety,
Autumn moons and spring breezes wasted away carelessly.
Then my brother joined the army, my aunt died,
Days turned to nights, and beauty faded with age.
Deserted front gate saw few horses or carriages,
So when older, I married a merchant’s wife.

He values profit more than love, indifferent to separation,
Last month he went floating Liang to buy tea, leaving me alone.
Returning, I guard an empty boat at the river mouth,
Surrounded by bright moonlight, the river waters cold.
Deep in the night, I dream vividly of youthful days,
Waking weeping, tears streaming through red makeup.'"

And hearing her words, I lamented anew.

What need have we to know each other before today?

Since last year, I left the Imperial Capital behind,
Demoted, sick, lying low in Xunyang City’s confines.
This place is remote, devoid of music’s charm,
All year long, never heard strings nor bamboo flutes.
Near the Peng River, where land lies low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo ring my dwelling.

What do I hear here, morning and evening?
Cuckoos crying blood, gibbons wailing mournfully.
On spring river mornings, flower-filled dawns, autumn moonlit nights,
Often I take wine, pouring it alone.

Moved by my words, she stood long in silence,
Then sat again, tightening strings that played faster still.
Mournful tones unlike those played before,
Filled the room once more; all listeners covered their faces, weeping.

Who shed the most tears among them?
The Magistrate of Jiangzhou—his blue robe soaked through."}

Silence blocked all flow, sound temporarily ceased.
Secret sorrows and hidden hatreds arose,
At this moment, silence surpassed any sound.
Then, like a silver bottle suddenly bursting with splashing water,
Or iron cavalry charging with clashing blades.
The song ended; she drew her plectrum across the center,
All four strings sounded once, like tearing silk.
Boats east and west stood silently in awe,
Seeing only white autumn moon in the river's heart.
She pondered, placed the plectrum between the strings,
Straightened her clothes, rose, and composed her expression.
She spoke: "Originally from the capital city,
My home lived near Xiama Tomb.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa,
My name listed first among the Imperial Music Bureau.
After performances, even great masters admired me;
When dressed up, other courtesans were envious.
Young nobles of Five Tombs competed to offer gifts,
For one song, they gave countless red silks.
Gold-inlaid hairpins and silver combs broke keeping time,
Blood-red skirts stained by spilled wine.
Year after year passed in laughter and joy,
Autumn moons and spring breezes spent casually.
My brother went off to war; my aunt died;
Evenings came, mornings passed, my beauty faded.
My gate grew desolate, horses rarely came,
Getting older, I married a merchant's wife.
Merchants value profit over partings;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
Since he left, I've guarded this empty boat at the river mouth,
Surrounded by bright moon and cold river waters.
Deep in the night I dreamt of youth's events,
Crying in dreams, makeup tears streaked red.
I sighed hearing the pipa,
And again, listening to these words, deeply grieved.
We are both lost souls drifting far from home,
Why should meeting require prior acquaintance?
Since last year I left the imperial capital,
Demoted and ill, living in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, lacking music;
All year long, no strings or pipes are heard.
Living near the Pen River, land low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear here day and night?
Blood-crying cuckoos and mourning apes' cries.
Spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moon nights,
Often I take wine and pour it alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
They are rough, harsh, and hard to listen to.
Tonight hearing your pipa language,
It is like celestial music; ears momentarily clear.
Do not refuse to sit and play another tune;
For you, I will write this 'Ballad of the Pipa.'
Moved by my words, she stood for a long while,

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。

移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。

曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。

门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。

我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。

莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。

座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "On the banks of the Xun River, I bid my guest farewell by night;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn chill.
The host dismounted, the guest remained aboard his boat;
We raised our cups to drink, but there were no pipes or strings.
Though drunk, we found no joy, as sorrow marked our parting;
In that moment, vast mists hung low, with moonlight sinking into the river.

Suddenly, from over the water, came the sound of a pipa.
The host forgot to return home; the guest delayed setting sail.
Following the music, I asked quietly who was playing;
The pipa’s song paused, hesitant, before words began.
I moved my boat closer, inviting her to appear,
Refilling the wine jars, trimming the lamps, restarting the feast.
After a thousand calls and ten thousand entreaties, she finally emerged,
Still holding her pipa, half-covering her face in modesty.

She turned the pegs and plucked the strings two or three times,
And before any melody was formed, emotion already stirred.
Each string suppressed deep sighs, each note carried thought,
Seeming to recount a life of unfulfilled ambition.
With lowered brows, she played continuously, letting her fingers roam freely,
Pouring out the endless tales hidden within her heart.

Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, sweeping then picking again,
First she played the "Rainbow Garment," then followed by the "Six Melodies."
The thick strings rumbled like a sudden downpour;
The thin strings whispered like lovers talking in private.
Loud and soft notes intertwined in complex harmony,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.

Now fluid and sweet, like warblers singing among flowers;
Now choked and difficult, like springs struggling beneath ice.
When cold brooks stagnate and strings cease to vibrate,
The silence breaks off, leaving only a temporary halt.
Then another sorrow arises, a buried resentment born—
At this moment, silence surpasses even the loudest sound.

Abruptly, like a silver vase shattering, water bursts forth;
Like iron cavalry charging, clashing swords and spears ring out.
As the song ended, she drew her plectrum across the center of the strings,
And the four strings rang out in one sudden crash, like tearing silk.
Eastward boats and westward barges fell silent, listening intently;
Only the autumn moon on the river middle glowed white.

Hesitating, she placed her plectrum between the strings,
Straightened her dress, stood up, and composed her expression.
She said: "I was originally a girl from the capital city,
Living near Xia Ma Ling.
By thirteen, I had mastered the pipa;
My name belonged to the first tier of the Imperial Music Bureau.
After finishing a tune, I could make great masters admire me;
Once dressed, I often provoked jealousy from famous courtesans.

Young men from the Five Tombs competed to offer gifts on heads,
For one song, they gave red silk beyond counting.
Gold-ornamented combs and hairpins broke while beating time,
Blood-red skirts spilled with wine stains.
Year after year passed in laughter and joy,
Wasting splendid nights under autumn moons and spring breezes.

But then, my brother joined the army, and my aunt died;
Beauty faded as days turned into years.
My door became desolate, horses rare;
Growing older, I married a merchant’s wife.
Merchants value profit above all else, caring little for separation;
Last month, he went to Fuliang to buy tea.

He left, and I stayed at the river mouth guarding an empty boat,
Surrounded by bright moonlight and cold river waters.
Late at night, I suddenly dreamed of my youth’s affairs,
Weeping in dreams, tears staining my makeup red.

I heard the pipa and sighed deeply already,
And hearing these words, I lamented twice as much.
We are both fallen souls drifting to the end of the earth—
Why must we have known each other before meeting?

Since last year, I left the imperial capital,
Banished here to Jiujiang [Xunyang], bedridden with illness.
Jiujiang is remote, devoid of music;
All year long, I hear not the slightest sound of silk or bamboo.
Living near the Pen River, where land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.

What do I hear morning or evening in this place?
Cuckoos crying blood and apes wailing in grief.
On spring river mornings or autumn moonlit nights,
Often, I take wine and pour it alone.

Surely there are mountain songs and village flutes?
But they are harsh and discordant, unbearable to hear.
Tonight, upon hearing your pipa’s language,
It is like listening to celestial music; my ears are suddenly clear.

Please do not refuse to sit again and play one more piece;
For you, I shall compose the 'Song of the Pipa.'"

Moved by my words, she stood silently for a long time,
Then sat back down, tightening the strings, playing faster.
Her sounds were sad, unlike those before;
Everyone in the audience covered their faces, weeping anew.

Who among us wept the most?
The blue robe of the Sima of Jiangzhou was soaked through."}

By the Yangtze at Xunyang, in the night I bid a guest farewell;
Maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in the autumn chill.
The host dismounts as the guest boards his boat,
We raise our cups to drink, yet lack music's note.
Drunk but not joyful, sorrowful we part,
At leaving, vast is the river where moonlight lies.
Suddenly from the water comes a pipa's song,
The host forgets to return, the guest delays departure.
Following the sound, I quietly ask who plays,
The pipa ceases, she hesitates to speak.
I move my boat closer, invite her to meet us,
Pour more wine, trim the lamp, resume the banquet.
After thousand calls and ten thousand summons she emerges,
Still holding her pipa, half-covering her face.
She turns the tuning pegs, plucks two or three strings,
Before the melody forms, emotion already stirs.
Each string suppressed, every tone full of longing,
As if telling a life spent unfulfilled.
Eyes downcast, fingers casually strum on,
Expressing all infinite matters of the heart.
Lightly pressing, slowly twisting, sweeping, then picking,
First playing "Rainbow Garments," then "Six Strings."
The thick strings rumble like sudden rain,
The thin strings whisper like private talk.
Rumbling and whispering intermingle,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Sweet as orioles singing beneath blossoms,
Labored as springs flowing under ice.
When icy springs turn cold and sluggish, the strings seem frozen;
Frozen and halted, the sound briefly stops.
Hidden sorrows and secret resentments arise—
This silence surpasses any sounding voice.
Then silver vases burst, water spurts out,
Iron cavalry charges, swords clash loud.
The piece ends; she draws the pick across the center,
Four strings strike once, like silk tearing apart.
Boats east and west fall silent, no one speaks,
Only seeing white autumn moon upon the river's heart.
Lost in thought, she puts the pick among the strings,
Straightens her clothes, stands with composed demeanor.
She says: "I was originally a girl of the capital city,
My home lay near the Shrimp Mound Hill.
At thirteen I mastered playing the pipa,
My name ranked first among the Imperial Music Bureau.
After finishing songs, great masters admired me,
Once dressed up, beauties like Qiu Niang envied me.
Young dukes and nobles competed to give gifts,
For one song, red silk bolts knew no count.
Gold-inlaid hairpins snapped keeping time,
Blood-red skirts stained by spilled wine.
Joy this year, joy next year again,
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed idly by.
Brother went off to war, aunt died,
Days and nights wear on, fading beauty remains.
Front gate deserted, horse carriages rare,
Getting older, I married a merchant’s wife.
The merchant values profit over separation,
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He leaves and returns; I guard an empty boat,
Around the ship bright moon, river waters cold.
Deep in the night I suddenly dream of youthful days,
In dreams I weep, makeup tears streak red across my face.
Hearing the pipa, I sighed deeply,
Hearing these words, I sigh even more heavily.
Both are drifters fallen far from home—
To meet here, why must we have known each other before?
Since last year I left the imperial capital,
Banished, ill, resting in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, devoid of music,
All year long, no strings or flutes heard.

Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear morning and evening there?
Dusky cuckoos crying blood, apes wailing mournfully.
Spring rivers, flower morns, autumn moonlit nights,
Often take wine, pour alone.

Like celestial music, ears suddenly clear.
Don’t refuse to sit and play another tune,
For you I shall compose this Ballad of the Pipa.

Sat back down, tightened strings, tempo sped up.

Full audience hears again, all cover faces weeping.

By the Xun River, at night, I saw off a guest;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn chill.
The host dismounted; his guest remained on the boat.
He raised his cup to drink, but there was no music—no strings, no flutes.

Drunk, yet unable to find joy, sad we were about to part;
At the moment of leaving, boundless was the river, steeped in moonlight.
Suddenly, from over the water, came the sound of a pipa.
The host forgot to return home; the guest did not set sail.

We followed the sound, quietly asking who played;
The pipa stopped, hesitating before speaking.
We moved our boats closer, inviting her to meet us,
Refilled the wine, trimmed the lamps, and resumed the feast.

Called out a thousand times, a myriad calls, she finally emerged,
Still holding the pipa, half-covering her face.
She turned the tuning pegs, plucked two or three strings,
Before the melody formed, emotion was already present.

Each string suppressed, each note full of thought,
As if telling a lifetime of unfulfilled ambitions.
With lowered brows, she casually continued to play,
Expressing all the infinite matters within her heart.

First *Nishang*, then *Liuyao*.
The thick strings rumbled like sudden rain,
The thin strings whispered like private talk.
Rumbling and whispering mixed together,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.

Soft and sweet as an oriole singing under blossoms,
Muffled and choked as a spring flowing beneath ice.
Ice-cold, sluggish, the strings seemed to stop,
Stopped and blocked, the sound briefly ceased.

Yet another kind of hidden sorrow, dark resentment arose—
At this moment, silence surpassed sound.
Then—as if a silver bottle burst, water spraying forth,
As if iron cavalry charged, swords and spears clashing.

When the tune ended, she drew the pick across the center,
Four strings snapped once, like tearing silk.
Boats to the east and ships to the west fell silent,
Only seeing the white autumn moon in the middle of the river.

She paused, put away the pick among the strings,
Straightened her clothes, stood up with composed dignity.

My family lived below Xia Ma Ling (Toad Mausoleum).
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa,
My name belonged to the first troupe of the Imperial Conservatory.

After finishing a song, even great masters would admire me;
When I completed my makeup, every beauty envied me.
Young nobles from five mausoleums competed to offer gifts,
For one song, countless rolls of red silk were given.

Jeweled hairpins and silver combs shattered keeping time,
Blood-red silk skirts stained by spilled wine.
Joy and laughter this year, and next year again,
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed casually by.

My brother went to join the army, my aunt died,
Evenings passed, mornings came, and my beauty faded.
Before my door grew cold, horsemen became scarce,
Aged now, I married to become a merchant’s wife.

Merchants value profit above all else, lightly esteeming separation;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
Now he is gone, and I guard this empty boat at the river mouth,
Surrounded by bright moonlight, the river water cold.

Deep in the night, I suddenly dreamt of events from my youth,
Crying in my dream, tears staining my rouge red along the rails."

Hearing these words, I sobbed anew.
We are both people fallen from grace in distant lands—
What need is there for us to have known each other before?

Since last year, I left the Imperial Capital,
Demoted and bedridden due to illness here in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, lacking music;
All year round, I hear no sound of silk strings or bamboo flutes.

Living near the Pen River, the land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboos grow around my house.
What do I hear here, morning and evening?
Cuckoos crying blood, monkeys wailing in despair.

On spring rivers when flowers bloom, on autumn nights under the moon,
Often I take wine and pour it alone.

Their cacophony and clatter are difficult to bear listening to.

Tonight, hearing your pipa speech,
It is as if I hear celestial music; my ears are suddenly cleared.
Do not refuse; sit down again and play one more piece—
For you, I shall compose the *Ballad of the Pipa*.

Moved by my words, she stood for a long while,
Then sat back down, tightening her strings; the tempo grew urgent.

Sorrowful sounds, unlike those from before,
Filled the room; everyone heard them anew and covered their faces to weep.
Who in the audience shed the most tears?
The Sima of Jiangzhou’s blue robe was wet through."}

By Bai Juyi

At night I bid a guest farewell beside the Xunyang River;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustle in the autumn chill.
The host dismounts; the guest is on his boat;
We raise our cups to drink, but there is no music.
The wine brings no joy; we part in sorrow;
As we leave, the vast river holds the moon.
Suddenly, over the water, comes the sound of a pipa;
The host forgets to return; the guest delays his departure.
Following the sound, I ask who plays;
The pipa stops, as if hesitating to speak.
We move our boats closer to invite her out;
We add more wine, relight the lamps, and resume the feast.
After many calls she finally appears,
Still holding the pipa, half hiding her face.
She turns the pegs and plucks a few strings;
Before the tune begins, feeling is already present.
Each string is suppressed, each note full of thought,
Seeming to tell of a life unfulfilled.
She lowers her brow and plays on freely,
Expressing all the boundless events of her heart.
With light presses, slow twists, sweeps, and picks,
First playing "Rainbow Feather," then "Six Strings."
The thick strings rumble like sudden rain;
The thin strings whisper like private talk.
Rumbling and whispering intermingle,
Like large and small pearls falling into a jade plate.
Smooth as orioles singing beneath the flowers;
Choked like spring water flowing under ice.
The cold, sticky spring makes the strings freeze;
When they cannot connect, the sound pauses briefly.
Then a hidden sorrow and secret hate arise;
At this moment, silence surpasses sound.
Like a silver bottle suddenly bursting with splashing water;
Like iron cavalry charging with clashing swords and spears.
When the tune ends, she draws the pick across the center;
All four strings snap once, like tearing silk.
Boats to the east and west fall silent;
Only the white autumn moon is seen in the middle of the river.
She pauses, puts the pick between the strings;
Adjusts her clothes, rises with a composed demeanor.
She herself says: "I was originally a girl from the capital,
My home was near Xiama Ling.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa;
My name belonged to the first rank of the music academy.
After each song, master musicians admired me;
After each makeup, beautiful women envied me.
The young men of the Five Tombs vied to give gifts;
One song would earn countless pieces of red silk.
Silver combs with jeweled heads were broken keeping time;
Blood-red skirts were stained by spilled wine.
This year of laughter led to next year's laughter;
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed casually away.
My brother went off to war; my aunt died;
Evenings came and mornings went, until my beauty faded.
The door before me became desolate; horses and carriages grew rare;
In old age I married a merchant's wife.
The merchant values profit and轻视 partings;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
Since then, I guard an empty boat at the river mouth;
Around the boat, the moonlight is bright, the river water cold.
Deep in the night, I suddenly dream of youthful days;
I wake crying, my tear-stained makeup running down in red streaks."

Hearing the pipa, I had already sighed;
Hearing these words, I sigh even deeper.
We are both people adrift at the edge of the world;
Meeting here, why do we need to have known each other before!
Since last year, leaving the Imperial Capital,
I was banished to lie ill in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote and has no music;
All year round, I hear no sounds of silk and bamboo.
Living near the Pen River, where the land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboos grow around my home.
What do I hear here morning and evening?
Cuckoos bleeding their cries, apes wailing mournfully.
On spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn nights,
I often take wine and pour it alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
They are harsh and jarring, difficult to listen to.
Tonight, hearing your pipa melodies,
It is like hearing celestial music; my ears suddenly clear.
Do not refuse to sit again and play one more song;
For you, I will compose the "Ballad of the Pipa."
Moved by my words, she stood for a long time;
Then sat back down, tightening the strings, which played faster.
Her mournful notes were different from the previous ones;
The whole audience, hearing them again, covered their faces and wept.
Who among those seated shed the most tears?
The Magistrate of Jiangzhou, his blue robe wet."}
