By Bai Juyi

On the banks of the Xunyang River at night, I saw off a guest;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn breeze.
The host dismounted, while the guest remained on the boat;
We raised our cups to drink, but had no music.
Though drunk, there was no joy, sorrowing over our parting;
At the moment of farewell, the vast river reflected the moon.
Suddenly, over the water, we heard the sound of a pipa;
The host forgot to return, and the guest did not set sail.
Following the sound, I asked quietly who was playing;
The pipa music stopped, as if the player wished to speak but hesitated.
I moved my boat closer to invite her out;
Refilled the wine, relit the lanterns, and reopened the feast.
After many calls and pleas, she finally emerged,
Still holding the pipa before her face, half hiding it.
She turned the pegs and plucked the strings a few times;
Before the melody took form, emotion was already present.
Each string suppressed, each note filled with longing,
As if telling of a life of frustration.
Head lowered, fingers moving freely, she played on,
Expressing all the boundless affairs within her heart.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, sweeping and plucking,
First playing "Rainbow Skirts," then "Six Strings."
The thick strings roared like a sudden downpour,
The thin strings whispered like private conversation.
Roaring and whispering intertwined in complex play,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Smooth as orioles singing beneath flowers, clear and flowing,
Choked and sobbing like springs trapped under ice.
As the cold spring froze and the strings stalled,
The silence lingered, unable to break through.
A hidden melancholy and silent resentment arose;
In that moment, silence surpassed sound.
Then suddenly, a silver vase burst, water splashing forth,
Iron cavalry charged, swords and spears clanging.
The song ended; she drew the plectric across the center of the strings;
All four strings sounded once, like tearing silk.
Boats to the east and west fell silent;
Only the white autumn moon shone on the heart of the river.
She pondered, placed the plectrum between the strings,
Straightened her clothes, rose, and composed her expression.
She said she was originally a girl from the capital,
Living near Shama Ling.
At thirteen, she mastered the pipa,
Her name belonging to the first department of the Imperial Music Bureau.
After finishing a piece, even skilled musicians admired her;
When dressed, every beauty felt envy.
The young men of Wuling vied to give her gifts,
For one song, red silk went uncounted.
Jeweled hairpins and silver combs broke keeping time,
Blood-red satin skirts stained by spilled wine.
Year after year, laughter continued,
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed casually.
Her brother joined the army, her aunt died,
Day by day, her youth faded.
Her door grew cold, visitors rare;
Growing older, she married a merchant's wife.
The merchant valued profit over separation,
Last month he left for Fuliang to buy tea.
He came and went, leaving me alone on the boat at the river mouth,
Surrounded by bright moonlight and cold river water.
Deep in the night, I suddenly dreamed of my youthful days,
Waking crying, makeup tears staining my face red.
Hearing the pipa, I sighed deeply;
Hearing her words, I lamented again.
Both of us are wanderers fallen in the world;
Meeting now, why does it matter if we knew each other before?
I too, since last year, left the imperial capital,
Banished to live ill in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, without music;
All year long, no stringed instruments are heard.
Living near the Pen River, the land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around the house.
What do I hear there morning and evening?
Cuckoos crying blood, gibbons wailing sadly.
On spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moon nights,
Often I take wine and pour it alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
Their harsh cacophony is painful to listen to.
Tonight hearing your pipa song,
It is like hearing celestial music; my ears are momentarily clear.
Do not refuse to sit down and play another tune;
I will compose a poem, "Song of the Pipa," for you.
Moved by my words, she stood for a long time,
Then sat back, plucking faster and more urgently.
The mournful sound unlike the previous performance;
Everyone in the room, hearing it again, covered their faces weeping.
Who among us shed the most tears?
The Prefect of Jiangzhou, whose blue robe became wet."}

By Bai Juyi

At night I bid farewell to a friend on the banks of the Xunyang River,
Where maple leaves and rush flowers rustle in the autumn chill.
I dismount, my guest remains aboard the boat;
We raise our cups, but there is no music to accompany us.
Inebriated yet joyless, we face a sorrowful parting;
As we leave, the vast river soaks the moonlight in its depths.
Suddenly, over the water, I hear the sound of a pipa.
The host forgets his return; the guest does not set sail.
Following the notes, I whisper-ask who plays;
The pipa pauses, hesitant to speak.
I move our boats closer, inviting her to appear;
Refill the wine, relight the lamps, resume the feast.
After countless calls and entreaties, she finally emerges,
Still holding the pipa, half-covering her face.
She turns the pegs, plucks a few strings;
Before the melody takes form, emotion already flows.
Each string sighs with suppressed longing,
As if telling of a lifetime unfulfilled.
Her head bowed low, she plays with ease,
Expressing all the boundless sorrows within.
Light strums, slow twists, sweeps, then picks;
First 'Rainbow Skirt,' then 'Six Melodies' follow.
The thick strings thunder like sudden rain,
The thin strings whisper like private talk.
Thunders and whispers mingle in complex play,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Warbled like orioles singing beneath flowers,
Then choked like springs struggling under ice.
Ice-cold springs turn sluggish; strings seem to freeze,
Frozen silence halts the sound for a moment.
But hidden grief and dark resentment arise anew—
This silence speaks louder than any note could.
Then suddenly, a silver vase breaks, water bursts forth;
Iron cavalry charges out, swords and spears clash.
The song ends; she draws the plectrum across the center,
A single sweep makes four strings tear silk-like.
Boats east and west fall silent; only the white autumn moon
Shines upon the heart of the river.
She hesitates, places the plectrum among the strings,
Straightens her clothes, rises with composed dignity.
She says: 'I was once a girl from the capital city,
My home near Xiamaoling, where willows sway.'
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa's art,
My name ranked first among the imperial academy's finest.
When I finished playing, masters applauded me;
When made up, even the famous beauties envied me.
Young nobles from Wuling vied to offer gifts,
For one tune, bolts of red silk flowed endlessly.
Gold-inlaid combs snapped keeping rhythm,
Blood-red skirts stained by spilled wine.
One year of laughter followed another;
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed casually away.
Then my brother joined the army, my aunt died;
Days turned into years, my beauty faded.
Before my door, visitors dwindled, horses rare;
In old age, I married a merchant man.
Merchants care more for profit than for partings;
Last month he went to Liangling to buy tea.
He left; I wait at the river mouth on an empty boat,
Surrounded by moonlight and cold river waters.
Deep in the night, I dream of youthful days,
Waking with tears staining my rouge-covered cheeks.
Hearing her pipa, I sighed deeply;
Hearing her story, I felt renewed pity.
We are both exiles wandering the ends of earth,
Why must we have known each other before?
Since last year, I left the emperor's capital,
Banished to lie sick in this remote town.
Xunyang is secluded, devoid of music;
All year long, no sound of strings or flutes.
Living near the Pen River, on damp, low ground,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo surround my home.
What do I hear here, dawn to dusk?
Cuckoos bleeding cries, apes wailing mournfully.
On spring nights with flowers bright as the moon,
I often drink alone, pouring out my solitude.
Are there no folk songs or village pipes?
Their harsh, discordant sounds are unbearable.
Tonight, hearing your pipa melodies,
It is like listening to celestial music; my ears awaken.
Do not refuse to sit and play one more tune;
I shall write for you this 'Song of the Pipa.'
Moved by my words, she stood for a long while,
Then sat down quickly, tightening the strings. Their pace grew frantic.
Sorrowful tones unlike those before;
The entire audience listened again, covering their faces in tears.
Who among them wept the most? The Blue-robed Magistrate 
of Jiangzhou had his sleeves soaked through."}

By Bai Juyi

By the Xunyang River, I bid a guest farewell at night;
Maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in the autumn chill.
The host dismounts; his guest is on the boat below,
We raise our cups to drink, but no music plays.
Drunk yet unjoyful, grief awaits our parting;
When we go, vast waters drown the moon's reflection.
Suddenly, from the water, a pipa's sound arrives;
The host forgets to return, the guest delays departure.
Following the sound, I quietly ask who plays;
The pipa stops, its owner hesitates to speak.
I move my boat closer, inviting her to meet us;
More wine is poured, lamps turned up, the feast resumes.
Called a thousand times, she finally appears,
Still holding her pipa, half-covering her face.
She turns the pegs, tests the strings with two or three notes;
Before the tune begins, emotion already flows.
Each string sighs low, each note carries sorrow,
As if telling tales of ambitions never fulfilled.
With lowered brows, she plays continuously,
Confiding all the boundless things within her heart.
Her fingers sweep lightly, slowly twist and pluck;
First 'Rainbow Robes,' then 'The Sixth Order' follow.
The deep strings roar like sudden heavy rain,
The thin ones whisper like private conversations.
Deep and thin sounds interweave in complex play,
Like large and small pearls falling into a jade plate.
Smooth as birdsong beneath the flowers, winding clear;
Choked as spring water struggling under ice.
Ice-cold, sluggish, the strings seem frozen tight;
Stuck and silent, the sound temporarily ceases.
Another hidden sorrow, another secret hate arises;
At this moment, silence speaks louder than sound.
The silver vase suddenly bursts, water sprays out;
Iron cavalry charges forth, swords and spears clash loud.
The song ends; she sweeps the plectrum across the center;
All four strings ring once, tearing silk apart.
Boats to east and west fall silent, none can speak;
All that remains is white autumn moon on river's heart.
Lost in thought, she places her plectrum among the strings;
Adjusts her clothes, stands up, composes her expression.
She says: "I was originally a girl of the capital;
My home lay near Shrimp-Hill Mound, by the city wall.
I mastered the pipa when thirteen years old;
My name belonged to the First Section of the Music Bureau.
After finishing tunes, even skilled masters bowed in praise;
When made up, rivals like Qiuniang often grew envious.
Young men of the Five Mausoleums competed for my favors;
One song earned bolts of red silk beyond counting.
Jeweled hairpins and silver combs broke keeping time;
Blood-red skirts stained by spilled wine during revelry.
This year laughing, next year again, joy repeated;
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed casually away.
My brother joined the army; my aunt died young;
Days went, nights came, my beauty faded.
Coldness settled before my door; few horses visited;
Growing older, I became a merchant's wife.
The merchant values profit but thinks little of parting;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
Leaving me here at the river mouth guarding an empty boat;
Moonlight circles the hull, river waters cold.
Late at night, dreams of youth suddenly return;
In dream, I weep, makeup tears stain my red cheeks.
Hearing the pipa, I already sighed deeply;
Hearing these words, my sighs grow heavier still.
We are both people lost at heaven's edge;
Why must we have known each other first?
Since last year leaving the imperial capital,
Exiled, sickly, lying idle in Xunyang town.
Xunyang is remote, without any music;
All year long, not even the sound of silk and bamboo.
Living near Pen River, the land is low and wet;
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo surround my home.
What do I hear morning and evening amidst it all?
Cuckoos crying blood and monkeys wailing sadly.
Spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moonlit nights—
Often I take wine and pour it out alone.
Are there not mountain songs and village flutes?
Their harsh, discordant sounds are painful to hear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa language,
It is like celestial music; my ears become clear.
Do not refuse to sit and play one more piece;
For you, I shall compose this Song of the Pipa.
Moved by my words, she stood for a long while;
Then sat down, tightening strings, playing faster now.
The sorrowful notes differ from those played before;
The whole audience, hearing them again, covers their faces and weeps.
Who among the guests shed the most tears?
The Magistrate of Jiangzhou, whose blue robe is soaked through."}

By the Xunyang River, at night I bid a guest farewell;
Maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in autumn's chill.
The host dismounts; the guest is aboard his ship;
We raise our wine cups, but there are no flutes or strings to play.
Drunk yet joyless, we sadly part;
As we depart, the vast river reflects the moon.
Suddenly, over the water, comes the sound of a pipa.
The host forgets to return home; the guest delays his departure.
Following the sound, I quietly ask: "Who plays?"
The pipa music stops; she wishes to speak but hesitates.
I move my boat close and invite her to meet us;
We add more wine, light the lamps again, and reopen the feast.
After countless calls, she finally emerges,
Still holding the pipa, half-covering her face.
She turns the tuning pegs and plucks a few strings;
Before the melody forms, emotion already flows.
Each string sighs with suppressed feeling;
It seems to tell of a life unfulfilled.
With lowered brows, she casually continues to play,
Expressing all the boundless sorrows in her heart.
Lightly pressing, slowly twisting, sweeping then picking:
First she plays "Rainbow Robes," then "Six Strings."
The thick strings rumble like sudden rain;
The thin strings whisper like private conversation.
Rumbling and whispering mix together;
Like large and small pearls falling into a jade dish.
Sweet as orioles singing under blooming flowers;
Choked as spring water flowing under ice.
Ice-cold, the water stalls; the strings freeze;
Frozen and blocked, the sound temporarily ceases.
But hidden grief and secret resentment arise—
In this silence, sound says more than words ever could.
Then suddenly, like a silver vase bursting, water splashes forth;
Like iron cavalry charging, swords clash and spears ring out.
The tune ends; she draws the pick across the center;
One final strike on four strings sounds like tearing silk.
The boats to the east and west fall silent;
All that remains is the white autumn moon in the middle of the river.
She pauses thoughtfully, inserts the pick between the strings,
Straightens her clothes, rises, and assumes a composed demeanor.
She speaks: "My home was originally in the capital city,
Living near Xiama Ridge.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa;
My name belonged to the First Division of the Imperial Music Bureau.
When I finished playing, renowned masters were impressed;
When I made up, other beautiful women envied me.
Young nobles from Five Tombs vied to give me gifts;
For one song, I received countless bolts of red silk.
Jeweled hairpins and silver combs broke keeping time;
Blood-red silk dresses stained by spilled wine.
Year after year, laughter continued;
Moonlit autumns and breezy springs passed idly away.
Then my brother joined the army; my aunt died;
Days turned to nights, nights to days, and my beauty faded.
My door grew cold and lonely; horses rarely came;
Too old for suitors, I married a merchant.
Merchants value profit and disregard separation;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
While he is gone, I guard an empty boat at the river mouth,
Surrounded by bright moonlight and cold river water.
Late at night, I suddenly dream of youthful affairs;
I wake crying, tears staining my makeup red.
Hearing her pipa, I had already sighed;
Hearing these words, my sorrow deepens further.
We are both people fallen from grace, drifting at the edge of the world;
Why must we have known each other before meeting today?
Since last year, I left the imperial capital,
Exiled to Xunyang City, lying ill.
Xunyang is remote and has no music;
Throughout the year, I hear not a single string or flute.
Living near the Pen River, the land is low and damp;
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear here, morning and evening?
Cuckoos bleeding their cries, gibbons moaning in grief.
On spring rivers, flower-filled mornings, autumn moonlit nights,
Often I take wine and pour it alone.
Do hill songs and village flutes exist?
Their hoarse, discordant sounds are unbearable to hear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa language,
It is like listening to celestial music; my ears are suddenly clear.
Please do not refuse to sit and play one more tune;
For you, I will compose this 'Song of the Pipa.'
Moved by my words, she stands for a long while,
Then sits back down, tightening the strings, which now sound urgent.
The mournful tone differs from earlier notes;
The full audience hears it again, all covering their faces and weeping.
Who among them shed the most tears?
The Magistrate of Jiangzhou, his blue robe wet."}

At night by the Xunyang River I bid a guest farewell,
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustle in autumn's chill.
The host dismounts, the guest is on his boat,
We raise our cups but lack music to lift our throats.
Drunk yet joyless, grief hangs at parting,
The river vast, moonlight submerged in water.
Suddenly pipa sounds rise from the water,
The host forgets homecoming, the guest delays departure.
Following the sound, I ask in the dark who plays,
The pipa pauses; hesitation before speech.
I move my ship close to invite her out,
Add wine, return lantern light, reopen the feast.
After countless calls she finally appears,
Still holding the pipa half-covering her face.
Turning pegs, plucking strings, a few notes first,
Before melody forms, emotion already breathes.
Each string suppressed, each note a sigh,
As if telling a life of thwarted dreams.
Eyes lowered, fingers casually continue playing,
Telling all the boundless thoughts within.
Light pinches, slow twists, sweeps then picks,
First 'Rainbow Skirt', then 'Six Strings'.
The thick strings rumble like sudden rain,
The thin strings whisper like private talk.
Rumble and whisper intermingle,
Like large and small pearls falling into a jade plate.
Chirping like orioles sliding beneath blossoms,
Sobbing like springs blocked under ice.
Ice-cold streams stagnant, strings freeze to silence,
Silence where no sound passes, music briefly stops.
Yet hidden sorrow and secret regret arise;
This silence speaks louder than any sound.
A silver vase suddenly bursts, water spurts forth,
Iron cavalry charges, swords clash and ring.
The song ends; the plectrum strikes the center,
One final cry like tearing silk.
East ships and west boats fall silent,
Only seeing white moonlight on the river's heart.
She hesitates, puts the plectrum among strings,
Straightens her clothes, assumes a composed face.
She says: 'I was originally a girl from the capital,
My home near Shama Ridge below the city.'
At thirteen I mastered the pipa,
Named in the first section of the Imperial Music Bureau.
After each piece even master musicians admired me,
When dressed up, even famed beauties were envious.
Young nobles from Five Mausoleums vied to give gifts,
For one song, red silk received beyond counting.
Gold-ornamented combs broke keeping time,
Blood-red skirts stained with spilled wine.
Year after year laughter continued,
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed carelessly away.
Then brother went to army, aunt died,
Days fade, nights pass, beauty fades.
Before my door desolate, horses rare,
Old age forced marriage to a merchant wife.
The merchant values profit over separation,
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
Leaving me alone guarding an empty ship at the river mouth,
Moonlight circles the ship, river water cold.
Late at night I dream of youthful days,
Wake crying, makeup tears streaming down red cheeks.
Hearing the pipa I already sighed,
Hearing these words I sigh again deeply.
'Though strangers meeting now, we share fate:
Both are wanderers fallen from grace beyond the sky's edge!'
Since last year I left the imperial capital,
Banished, sick in bed in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, lacking music,
All year round no sound of strings or bamboo flutes.
Living near Pen River, low land damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear morning and evening here?
Cuckoos bleeding cries, apes wailing mournfully.
Spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moon nights,
Often take wine, drink it alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village pipes?
Crude, discordant sounds hard to bear listening to.
Tonight hearing your pipa language,
Like hearing celestial music, ears momentarily clear.
Do not refuse to sit again, play one more piece,
For you I shall write this 'Song of the Pipa'.

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。

嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。

Suddenly, from the water came the sound of a pipa; The host forgot to go home, the guest delayed departure. Following the sound, I asked quietly who was playing; The pipa music stopped, then hesitated before answering. I moved my boat closer and invited her to meet me; Wine was replenished, lamps turned up, the banquet resumed. Called out many times, she finally emerged, Still holding the pipa, her face half-hidden. Turning pegs, plucking strings two or three times, Before forming a tune, emotion already flowed. Each string suppressed and sighed with longing, Seeming to tell a life of unfulfilled ambition. Head bowed, fingers moving freely yet continuously, Pouring out infinite matters within her heart. Lightly pinching, slowly twisting, sweeping then plucking, First playing "Rainbow Garments," then "Sixth String." The heavy strings thundered like sudden rain; The light strings whispered like private conversation. Thunder and whisper intermingled in strumming— Large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate. Melodious as warbling birds sliding beneath flowers; Muffled as spring water trickling through ice below. Cold and sticky as frozen springs, the strings ceased; Silence fell, for no sound could pass through. Yet hidden grief and dark resentment stirred anew— At this moment, silence spoke louder than sound. Then silver bottles burst, water splashing forth; Iron cavalry charged, blades clashing loudly. To end the piece, the plectrum swept across the center; Four strings sounded once, like tearing silk. Boats east and west fell silent; Only the white autumn moon shone on the river’s heart. She paused, tucked the plectrum among the strings, Straightened her clothes, rose with composed dignity. She said: "I was originally a girl from the capital, Living near the Xiama Ling district. At thirteen, I mastered the pipa; My name ranked first in the Imperial Music Academy. After performing, even skilled players admired me; After makeup, courtesans envied my beauty. Young dukes from Five Tombs vied to shower me with gifts; For one song, bolts of red gauze were countless. Ornate hairpins snapped to keep time; Blood-red skirts stained by spilled wine. This year laughter returned next year; Autumn moons and spring breezes passed unnoticed. My brother joined the army, aunt died; Days went by, morning after morning, age faded my charm. Guests thinned at my door, horses sparse; Older now, I married a merchant. He valued profit over separation; Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea. Since his leaving, I guard an empty boat at the river mouth; Moonlight surrounds the vessel, river water cold. Late at night, suddenly dreaming of youth; Waking weeps stain my makeup, tears reddening the railing. Hearing the pipa, I sighed deeply; Hearing these words, I lamented again and again. Both are wanderers fallen from grace! Meeting here, why need prior acquaintance? Since last year, I left the imperial capital, Banished and bedridden in Xunyang City. Remote land without music; All year round, no piping sounds heard. Near Pen River living low and damp; Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo surround my house. What do I hear dawn and dusk there?杜鹃 crying blood, apes wailing mournfully. By spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn nights, Often take wine alone to pour. Are there no mountain songs or village flutes? Hoarse and harsh, difficult to listen to. Tonight hearing your pipa speech— Like celestial music, ears newly cleared. Do not refuse to sit and play another tune; For you, I compose this 'Song of the Pipa.' Moved by my words, she stood long; Returned to seat, tightened strings growing urgent. Sad notes unlike those before; Full audience covering faces, all weeping. Who shed most tears among them? Jiangzhou Sima, blue robe soaked."}

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。

五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。

门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "One autumn night by Xunyang River I saw a guest off,
the maple leaves and reed flowers shivered in the chill.
The host dismounted, the guest aboard his boat;
we raised our cups to drink, but there were no flutes or strings.
Drunk without joy, in sorrow we were about to part;
at parting the vast river swallowed the moon.
Suddenly from the water came the sound of a pipa;
the host forgot to go home, the guest delayed his departure.
Following the sound I quietly asked who was playing;
the pipa stopped and she hesitated to answer.
We drew our boats near and invited her to meet us;
more wine was brought, the lamps rekindled, the feast renewed.
After a thousand calls she finally emerged,
still holding her pipa, half hiding her face.
She turned the pegs and plucked a few strings—
before a tune was formed, feeling was already there.
Each string was muted, each note full of longing,
as if telling of a life of unfulfilled dreams.
She lowered her brows and played on without pause,
pouring out all the endless things within her heart.
She plucked, rolled, and flicked—
first the *Rainbow Skirt*, then the *Six Little Songs*.
The heavy strings roared like sudden rain,
the light strings whispered like private talk.
Roaring and whispering, entangled and crossed,
like big and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Like oriole song gliding smooth beneath the flowers,
like a hidden brook choking under ice.
The icy brook froze, the strings congealed and broke;
the sound halted, silent for a while.
Then a hidden sorrow and deep resentment rose—
in that silence, more than any sound.
Suddenly a silver bottle shattered, water gushed forth;
iron cavalry charged out, swords and spears clashing.
At the song's end she struck the strings at the heart,
four strings sounded as one, like tearing silk.
The boats east and west were hushed and still;
only the white autumn moon on the river's heart.
She pondered, then tucked the pick back among the strings,
straightened her clothes, rose with a solemn face.
She said she was a girl from the capital,
living beneath the Toad Mound.
At thirteen she mastered the pipa,
her name first in the ranks of the court troupe.
After each song even the finest players bowed,
and when she dressed, the beauties envied her.
The young lords of the five tombs competed for her favors,
one song earned her red silk without count.
Ornamented combs shattered in time to the music,
her crimson skirt stained with spilled wine.
Year after year of laughter and joy,
the autumn moon and spring breeze passed by in vain.
Her brother went to war, her aunt died;
dusk turned to dawn and her beauty faded.
Before her gate, carriages and horses grew sparse;
grown old, she married a merchant.
The merchant valued profit and cared little for parting—
last month he went to buy tea at Fuliang.
She waits alone by the river mouth in an empty boat;
moonlight surrounds the boat, the river water cold.
Deep in the night she dreams of her youth,
and in her dream she weeps, her rouge-stained tears streaming.
I had sighed already upon hearing her pipa,
and now hearing her words I sighed again.
We are both lost souls at the ends of the earth—
why must we have known each other before?
Since last year I left the imperial capital,
banished and ill to Xunyang town.
Xunyang is remote and has no music;
all year I hear no strings or flutes.
I live near the Pen River, low and damp,
yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear from morn to eve?
The cuckoo crying blood, the gibbon's mournful wail.
On flower mornings and moonlit autumn nights,
I often take my wine and drink alone.
Are there no hill songs or village flutes?
Their harsh squawks are hard to bear.
Tonight I hear your pipa's words,
like celestial music that clears my ears.
Do not refuse—sit and play once more,
and I will turn it into this *Song of the Pipa*.
Moved by my words, she stood long,
then sat back and quickened the strings.
Sorrowful it was, unlike the sound before;
the whole company wept as they listened.
Who wept the most among those present?
The Jiangzhou official, whose blue gown was wet."}

At night, I bid my guest farewell at Xunyang River's head,
As maple leaves and reed flowers rustle in the autumn chill.
The host dismounts; the guest is on his boat already there,
We raise our cups to drink, but lack the music’s air.
Though drunk, no joy remains before our parting tears,
When we must leave, the moon sinks in the vast river’s mist.
Suddenly, from across the water, pipa notes arise,
I forget to return home; my guest delays his departure.
I follow the sound, asking softly who might play,
The strings fall silent, as if shy to speak or stay.
I move my vessel close, inviting her to show her face,
Refill the wine, trim lamps anew, resume the banquet’s grace.
After a thousand calls, she finally emerges slow,
Still holding near her pipa, half her beauty’s glow.
She turns the pegs, then plucks two, three tentative sounds,
Before the melody begins, emotion floods the grounds.
Each string suppresses sighs, each note conveys deep thought,
As if recounting all the dreams that life has not brought forth.
Her brows lowered low, she plays with fingers free and light,
Expressing boundless sorrows hidden in her heart’s retreat.
With gentle sweeps, slow twists, and flicks both up and down,
First playing *Rainbow Garments*, then *Six Melodies’* mournful frown.
The thick strings boom like sudden rain in torrents fierce,
The thin ones whisper secrets soft, as lovers rehearse.
Thick, thin intertwined, they crash and mingle in the air,
Like large pearls falling, small pearls skipping, on jade trays rare.
Clear birdsong glides through floral shadows, smooth and sweet,
Then muffled sobbing flows beneath ice-bound streams, hard to meet.
The cold spring freezes stiff, the strings seem severed tight,
In silence choked, the song pauses, losing its flight.
But deeper grief and hidden resentment begin to stir within,
This void of sound speaks louder than any noise can win.
Then suddenly, silver vases break, water bursts apart,
Iron cavalry charge forward, blades clash, spears impart shock.
The tune concludes; she draws her pick across the center line,
Four strings snap once—like silk tearing—to make them mine.
East boats and west barges fall into hushed repose,
Only the white autumn moon reflects upon the river’s flow.
She pauses, inserts the pick among the strings with care,
Adjusts her garments, rises, composing countenance fair.
She states she was a girl from the Imperial Capital’s core,
Her home resided below Shama Tomb’s ancient door.
At thirteen, mastering the pipa, skill attained its peak,
Named first among the teaching guilds, where talents seek.
After songs ended, even master musicians bowed in awe,
When dressed, her beauty caused rival beauties’ envy’s flaw.
Young nobles of Five Tombs contended for her favor’s prize,
For one song played, countless red silks were given as dues.
Gold-inlaid combs broken keeping time’s rhythmic beat,
Blood-colored skirts stained by spilled wine’s crimson heat.
Year after year passed laughter, spring winds and autumn moons spent idly,
Until her brother joined the army, aunt departed silently.
Day fading into dawn, her youth’s vibrant hue grew pale,
The doorstep lonely now, few horses pass along the trail.
Aged beyond her prime, she wed a merchant man,
Who values profit high, disregards parting’s pain.
Last month to Fuliang Town he went, tea trading far away,
She guards this empty boat alone where bright moonlight displays.
At night’s deep hour, old memories flood back in dreams,
Crying awake, makeup tears stream, leaving red streaks gleams.
Hearing her pipa sighs had stirred my soul with pain,
But hearing these words now makes my grief return again.
Both are exiled souls drifting at world’s vast edge, meeting true!
Why need we have known each other when hearts resonate so?
Since last year I left the imperial city’s grandeur bright,
Demoted here to Xunyang, sick, enduring endless night.
This place remote lacks music entirely throughout the year,
No strings or pipes reach my ear’s hollow sphere.
Living near Pen River, land low and damp surrounds,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboos enclose my dwelling grounds.
What do I hear from dusk till dawn in this desolate place?
Cuckoos bleeding cries, apes wailing in mournful case.
On spring river banks under blooming flowers, autumn nights serene,

My ears awakened fresh, washed clean by heavenly beams.

Sat down again, tightened strings, letting tempo draw.

寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。

曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。

五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！

浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。

座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "Song of the Pipa

At Xunyang River's head, I bid farewell to a guest at night,
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustle in the autumn chill.
The host dismounts; the guest is on the boat.
We raise our cups to drink, but there are no strings or pipes.
Drunk yet not joyful, we mourn the coming parting;
When we part, the vast river soaks the moon.
Suddenly, from over the water, comes the sound of a pipa;
The host forgets to return home, the guest delays his departure.
Following the sound, I ask softly who plays;
The pipa stops, as if she wishes to speak but hesitates.
I move my boat close to invite her out;
More wine is added, lamps brought back, and the feast resumes.
After a thousand calls, ten thousand summons, she finally appears,
Still holding the pipa, half-covering her face.
She turns the pegs and plucks the strings a few times;
Before the tune begins, emotion already flows.
Each string sighs, each note carries thought,
As if telling of a life frustrated by fate.
Eyes lowered, fingers moving freely, she plays on,
Expressing all the endless sorrow within her heart.
Light chords, slow twists, sweeping strokes, then picks—
First "Rainbow Shirt," then "Six Melodies."
The thick strings rumble like a sudden downpour,
The thin strings whisper like private talk.
Rumbling and whispering intertwine,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Smooth as orioles singing beneath blossoms,
Then choking like springs trapped under ice.
Ice-cold and stagnant, the strings seem to freeze;
Frozen and blocked, the sound abruptly stops.
A new sadness and hidden resentment arise;
Here, silence surpasses all sound.
Then suddenly, like a silver vase breaking with water bursting forth,
Like iron cavalry charging with swords clashing loud.
When the song ends, she draws the pick across the center;
All four strings strike together, tearing silk with a sharp snap.
Boats to the east and west fall silent;
Only the white autumn moon reflects in the river’s heart.
Pondering deeply, she places the pick among the strings,
Straightens her clothes and stands up, composing her expression.
She says, "Once I was a girl from the capital city,
My home lay near Shama Ling.
By thirteen, I had mastered the pipa;
My name belonged to the first troupe of the Imperial Music Bureau.
When I finished a piece, even master virtuosos bowed in admiration;
When I dressed, every renowned beauty grew jealous.
Young men of the Five Tombs fought to wrap me in brocade,
For one song, countless bolts of red silk were given.
Gold-inlaid combs snapped in time to the beat,
Blood-red skirts stained by spilling wine.
Year after year passed in laughter and joy,
Autumn moons and spring breezes treated casually.
Then my brother went off to war, and my aunt died;
Days turned to nights, and my beauty faded away.
The front gate became cold, horsemen rare;
Too old now, I married a merchant as his wife.
Merchants value profit over love, indifferent to separation;
Last month he bought tea and left for Fuliang.
He comes and goes, leaving me alone guarding an empty boat,
Surrounded only by bright moonlight and chilling river waters.
Deep in the night, I dream suddenly of youthful days,
Crying in my sleep, tears streaming through makeup, staining it crimson.
Hearing the pipa, I sighed long ago;
Now hearing these words, again I lament deeply.
"Both of us are kindred souls cast down by fate across the world’s edge;
Since we meet here, why must we have known each other before?
"I left the imperial capital last year,
Banished to lie sick in the city of Xunyang.
This place is remote, without any music;
All year round, I never hear the sound of strings or flutes.
Living near the Pen River, where land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear there day and night?
Cuckoos bleeding from their cries, monkeys wailing in grief.
On spring rivers’ flowering mornings and autumn nights beneath the moon,
Often I take wine and pour it alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
They are harsh and jarring, painful to listen to.
Tonight, hearing your pipa speech,
It is like listening to celestial music; my ears are suddenly clear.
Please, sit again and play another tune;
For you, I will compose this 'Song of the Pipa.'"
Moved by my words, she stood for a long time,
Then sat down again, tightening the strings, playing faster.
Sorrowful sounds, unlike those heard before;
Everyone in the room, hearing them anew, covered faces and wept.
Who shed the most tears among those seated?
The Jiangzhou Scribe, whose azure robe is stained with tears.""}

By Bai Juyi

At night by the Xunyang River, I bid a guest farewell;
Maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in the autumn chill.
The host dismounts; the guest remains aboard the boat;
We raise our wine cups to drink, but find no music for it.
Drunk yet unjoyful, sorrow fills this parting scene;
When we depart, the vast river soaks the moon's pale sheen.
Suddenly, pipa strings sound upon the water’s flow,
The host forgets his home; the guest delays his row.
I seek the source, asking softly: "Who plays thus?"
The pipa stops, as if the player lingers over us.
I move my boat closer and invite her to appear;
We add more wine, relight lamps, resume the feast here.
After many calls and cries, she finally comes forth,
Still holding her pipa, half shielding her face from north.
She turns the tuning pegs, plucks strings a few times through,
Before the tune begins, emotion already breaks through.
Each string is muffled low, each note full of thought and sigh,
As if telling of a life where ambition had to die.
With downcast eyes, fingers glide on smoothly without haste,
Expressing all the endless sorrows time has wasted.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, then sliding and picking,
First 'Rainbow Skirt', then 'Six Strings'—the melodies are striking.
The thick strings rumble loud like sudden rainstorm’s roar;
The thin strings whisper soft like lovers’ secret lore.
Rumbling and whispering interweave in complex play,
Like large and small pearls falling onto jade trays.
Birdsong flows smooth beneath flowers, sweet and clear,
Then chokes like spring water trapped by ice severe.
Cold ice blocks the stream, the strings freeze tight and stop,
Silence reigns when notes can no longer hop.
A hidden grief and silent hate now start to grow,
This silence speaks louder than any sound could show.
Silver bottles burst, water splashes out in spray,
Iron cavalry charges, swords clash in battle fray.
The tune ends; she draws her pick across the heart-strings tight,
One final chord tears silk with sharp and startling might.
East and west, boats fall silent, no word is spoken there,
Only the white autumn moon sees the river bare.
She muses long, places her pick among the strings,
Straightens her clothes, rises up, composed and serious things.
"I was originally a girl from the capital city,
My home was near Xiama Ling, where memories linger."
"At thirteen, I mastered the pipa’s every art,
And belonged to the first troupe of the imperial court."
"Even great masters praised my tunes when they were done,
And beauty rivals envied me when makeup was won."
"Rich youths of Wuling fought to give me red silk scarves,
For one song alone, countless bolts filled their drawers."
"Gold hairpins broke keeping time, silver combs shattered too,
Blood-red skirts stained with spilled wine, revelry ran through."
"Year after year, laughter echoed, seasons passed away,
Moonlight and breeze consumed my youth in idle play."
"My brother joined the army; my aunt died young and frail,
Days turned to nights, and my youthful beauty grew pale."
"The door stood cold and empty; horses rarely came,
So in old age, I wed a merchant, lost in trade’s game."
"He values profit high, cares little for our parting,
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea, heart hardening."
"While he was gone, I guarded the empty boat at the mouth,
Moonlight encircled the ship; river waters flowed south."
"Late at night, I dreamed of events in my younger days,
Woke crying, tears mixed with rouge running in hazy ways."

I heard the pipa and sighed deeply at its pain,
Then heard her words, and lamented twice again.
Both of us are wanderers stranded far from home,
Meeting need not require that we have known before.
Since last year I left the imperial capital behind,
Demoted to Xunyang, lying ill, confined and blind.
This place is remote, devoid of music’s charm,
All year long, no sounds of silk or bamboo alarm.
My house stands near Peng River, low and damp and wet,
Surrounded by yellow reeds and bitter bamboo set.
What do I hear at dawn and dusk within these walls?
Cuckoos bleeding their voices; apes calling mournful calls.
On spring river mornings, flower-dawn and autumn moon,
Often I take my wine and pour it, lonely soon.
Are there no mountain songs or village pipes to hear?
Their harsh and jarring noise is impossible to cheer.
Tonight I hear your pipa speak its eloquent tongue,
Like fairy music making my ears bright and sung.
Do not refuse to sit and play one more refrain;
For you, I will compose this Song of the Pipa vein.

Moved by my words, she stood for a long while in thought,
Then sat again, tightening strings, emotions caught.
The melody sounded sad, unlike what played before,
The whole audience listened, tears streaming down the floor.
Who in the room shed most tears, soaking through their shirts?
The Magistrate of Jiangzhou, whose blue robe holds its hurts."}

by Bai Juyi

By night I saw off a guest at the mouth of the Xunyang River;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn chill.
The host dismounted; his guest was already on the boat.
We raised our cups to drink, but there was no music.
Though drunk, we found no joy; sorrow hung over the parting.
As we parted, the vast river soaked up the moonlight.
Suddenly, from the water, came the sound of a pipa.
The host forgot to return; the guest delayed departure.
Following the sound, I asked softly who was playing,
But the pipa stopped, and she wished to speak yet hesitated.
I moved my boat closer to invite her to come out;
More wine was poured, the lamps were brought back, and the feast resumed.
Amid countless calls and pleas, she finally emerged,
Still holding the pipa half-covering her face.
She turned the tuning pegs and plucked two or three strings;
Before the tune formed, feeling was already present.
Each string suppressed, each note filled with longing,
Seeming to tell of a life unable to fulfill its ambitions.
With lowered brows, she played casually, continuously,
Telling fully of boundless matters within her heart.
Lightly pressing, slowly rolling, sweeping then picking,
First playing "Rainbow Skirt," then the "Sixth Mode."
The thick strings rumbled like sudden rain;
The thin strings whispered like hushed secrets.
Rumbling and whispering mixed together in playing,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Smooth as an oriole’s song beneath blossoms;
Choked as a spring flowing under ice.
When the cold ice made the strings stiff and silent,
And silence blocked all sound for a pause,
There arose elsewhere hidden sorrows and unspoken resentments.
At this moment, silence surpassed sound.
Then, suddenly, silver jars burst and water sprayed out;
Iron cavalry charged forth, swords and spears clashing.
The tune ended: she drew the pick across the center,
A single cry from four strings, like silk tearing.
Boats to the east and west fell silently quiet,
All that remained visible was the white autumn moon mid-river.
Ponderous, she put down the pick into the strings,
Adjusted her clothes, rose, and composed her features.
She said herself: "Originally I was a girl of the capital,
My home lay below Shrimp蟆陵 (Xiamaling).
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa;
My name was listed first among the Imperial Music Bureau.
After finishing a piece, even great masters would admire her skill;
When adorned, often rival beauties would envy her grace.
Young nobles from Five Tombs vied to offer gifts;
For one song, bolts of red silk counted beyond measure.
Inlaid hairpins and silver combs broke keeping time;
Blood-red skirts stained by spilling wine.
This year laughter followed next year’s mirth;
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed idly away.
Her brother went off to soldier; her aunt died;
Evenings departed, mornings arrived, beauty faded.
The door grew desolate; horsemen rarely came.
Growing old, she married a merchant's wife.
The merchant values profit lightly regarding separation;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He left; she guards an empty boat at the river mouth.
The moon circles the boat; the river water is cold.
Deep in night, suddenly dreaming of youthful days,
She wakes crying, tears staining makeup red on her cheeks.
Hearing the pipa, I had already sighed;
Hearing these words again, I lament anew.
Both are castaways drifting to Heaven’s edge;
Meeting now, why need we have known each other before?
Since last year, I left the imperial capital,
Demoted, lying ill in Xunyang City.
Xunyang’s location is remote—no music here;
Throughout the year, not heard any pipe or string tones.
Living near Pén River, land low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo surround my house.
What do I hear here morning and evening?
Dusky cuckoos bleed cries; apes wail mournfully.
On spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moonlit nights,
Often take wine and drink alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village pipes?
They are harsh and coarse, difficult to listen to.
Tonight hearing your pipa speech,
It seems like listening to fairy music—ears momentarily clear.
Do not refuse to sit again and play another piece;
For you, I shall compose 'The Ballad of the Pipa.'
Moved by these words, she stood long;
Returned to seat, tightened strings; notes grew urgent.
Mournful unlike previous sounds,
All seated once more covered faces weeping.
Who among them shed most tears?
The Prefect of Jiangzhou’s blue robe became wet."}

夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。

By night I bid farewell to a guest by the Xunyang River shore,
Where maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in the autumn breeze.
The host dismounts from his horse, the guest waits upon his boat;
We raise our cups to drink, yet have no music to ease the meeting.
Tipsy but joyless, we face the sorrow of parting;
As we depart, the vast river swallows the moonlight.
Suddenly, across the water, comes the sound of a pipa;
The host forgets to return home, the guest delays departure.
Following the sound, I ask softly: who plays so well?
The pipa falls silent; the player wishes to speak but hesitates.
I move my boat closer to invite her out,
Pour fresh wine, relight the lamps, and resume the feast.
After calling many times, she finally appears,
Still holding the pipa half-covering her face.
She turns the tuning pegs and plucks a few strings,
Before the melody forms, emotion already flows.
Each string is muted, each note laden with thought,
Seeming to tell of a life unfulfilled, ambitions thwarted.
With lowered brows, she plays casually, continuously,
Telling all the endless affairs within her heart.
Lightly pressing, slowly twisting, sweeping then plucking,
First 'Rainbow Robe', then 'Six Strings' she renders.
The thick strings rumble like sudden rain,
The thin strings whisper like private talk.
Rumbling and whispering intermingle, mixed together,
Like pearls large and small falling onto a jade plate.
Sweet as orioles singing under blossoms, flowing smoothly,
Choked as spring water running beneath ice, struggling.
The icy spring grows cold and sluggish, the strings freeze and stop;
When the flow halts and cannot pass, the sound temporarily ceases.
Then arises a hidden sorrow, a secret resentment—
At this moment, silence speaks louder than any note.
Suddenly, like a silver vase bursting, water spurts forth;
Like iron cavalry charging out, swords clash loudly.
The tune ends; she draws the plectrum across the center,
All four strings ring once, like tearing silk.
East and west boats fall into quiet speechlessness;
Only the white autumn moon shines on the heart of the river.
She contemplates deeply, puts the plectrum among the strings,
Straightens her dress, rises, and composes her face.
She says herself: 'Originally a girl from the capital,
My home lay beneath the Shrimp蟆 Hill.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa;
My name was listed in the first troupe of the Imperial Music Bureau.
After finishing a piece, even skilled masters admired me;
Once made up, every beauty envied my looks.
Young men of Five Tombs vied to give me gifts;
For one song, red silks were paid without count.
Gold-inlaid hairpins snapped keeping time;
Blood-red skirts stained by spilled wine.
This year laughter, next year still laughter;
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed by idly.
My younger brother joined the army, my aunt died;
Days turned to nights, my beauty faded away.
The gate grew desolate; horses and carriages became rare.
In later years, I married a merchant’s wife.
The merchant values profit over reunion;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
Going and coming, I guard my empty boat at the river mouth;
Around the ship, bright moonlight; below, cold river waters.
Late at night, I suddenly dream of youthful days;
Waking in tears, makeup streaked red down my cheeks.'
Hearing the pipa, I had already sighed;
Listening further to these words, my sighs grow heavier.
We are both wanderers fallen far from grace;
Since we meet now, why need we have known each other before?
Last year I left the imperial capital,
Banished to lie sick in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, devoid of music;
All year round, I hear not the sound of silk and bamboo.
Near the Pen River, land low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo surround my dwelling.
What do I hear here morning and evening?
Cuckoos crying blood, apes wailing mournfully.
Spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moonlit nights—
Often I take wine and pour it alone.
Are there no mountain songs and village flutes?
Their harsh noises are unbearable to listen to.
Tonight hearing your pipa language,
It is like listening to celestial music; my ears awake clear.
Do not refuse to sit again and play one more tune;
For you, I shall compose the 'Song of the Pipa'.
Moved by my words, she stands long in silence;
Returning to sit, she tightens the strings; they play faster.
The melancholy differs from sounds heard before;
The whole audience hears anew and covers their faces, weeping.
Who among those present sheds the most tears?
The blue robe of the Sima of Jiangzhou is wet."}

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。

寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。

弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。

五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。

座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "The Song of the Pipa

At night I bid farewell to a friend by the Yangtze at Xunyang,
Maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in the autumn chill.
I dismount; my guest is already on board;
We raise our cups to drink, but lack the music of pipes and strings.
Drunken yet joyless, we grieve as parting approaches;
In the moment of leaving, the vast river soaks the moon.
Suddenly, from across the water, the sound of a pipa rises;
The host forgets to return home, and the guest delays his departure.
Following the sound, I ask softly who plays;
The pipa falls silent, as if the player wishes to speak but hesitates.
I move my boat closer to invite her out;
More wine is added, lamps are brought back, and the feast resumes.
After a thousand calls and ten thousand summons, she finally appears,
Still holding the pipa before her, half-hiding her face.
She turns the pegs and plucks the strings a few times;
Before the tune begins, emotion already flows.
Each string sighs and restrains, every note carries deep thought,
As if telling of a life frustrated by fate.
Eyes lowered, fingers moving freely, she plays on,
Expressing all the endless sorrow within her heart.
Light chords, slow twists, sweeping strokes, then picks—
First "Rainbow Shirt," then "Six Melodies."
The thick strings rumble like a sudden downpour,
The thin strings whisper like private talk.
Rumbling and whispering intertwine,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Smooth as orioles singing beneath blossoms,
Then choking like springs trapped under ice.
Ice-cold and stagnant, the strings seem to freeze;
Frozen and blocked, the sound abruptly stops.
A new sadness and hidden resentment arise;
Here, silence surpasses all sound.
Then suddenly, like a silver vase breaking with water bursting forth,
Like iron cavalry charging with swords clashing loud.
When the song ends, she draws the pick across the center;
All four strings strike together, tearing silk with a sharp snap.
Boats to the east and west fall silent;
Only the white autumn moon reflects in the river’s heart.
Pondering deeply, she places the pick among the strings,
Straightens her clothes and stands up, composing her expression.
She says, "Once I was a girl from the capital city,
My home lay near Shama Ling.
By thirteen, I had mastered the pipa;
My name belonged to the first troupe of the imperial academy.
When I finished a piece, even the great musicians bowed in admiration;
When I dressed, every courtesan grew jealous.
Young men of the Five Tombs fought to wrap me in brocade,
For one song, red silk was given beyond count.
Gold-inlaid combs snapped while beating time,
Blood-red skirts stained by overturned wine.
Year after year passed in laughter and joy,
Autumn moons and spring breezes treated casually.
Then my brother went off to war, and my aunt died;
Days turned to nights, and my beauty faded away.
The front gate became cold, horsemen rare;
Too old now, I married a merchant as his wife.
Merchants value profit over love, indifferent to separation;
Last month he bought tea and left for Fuliang.
He comes and goes, leaving me alone guarding an empty boat,
Surrounded only by bright moonlight and chilling river waters.
Deep in the night, I dream suddenly of youthful days,
Crying in my sleep, makeup streaked red with tears.
Hearing the pipa, I sighed long ago;
Now hearing these words, again I lament deeply.
Both of us are fallen souls wandering to the ends of the earth;
Since we meet here, why must we have known each other before?
"I left the imperial capital last year,
Banished to lie sick in the city of Xunyang.
This place is remote, without any music;
All year round, I never hear the sound of strings or flutes.
Living near the Pen River, where land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear there day and night?
Cuckoos bleeding from their cries, monkeys wailing in grief.
On spring rivers’ flowering mornings and autumn nights beneath the moon,
Often I take wine and pour it alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
They are harsh and jarring, hard to bear listening to.
Tonight, hearing your pipa speech,
It is like listening to celestial music; my ears are suddenly clear.
Please, sit again and play another tune;
For you, I will compose this 'Song of the Pipa.'"
Moved by my words, she stood for a long time,
Then sat down again, tightening the strings, playing faster.
Sorrowful sounds, unlike those heard before;
Everyone in the room, hearing them anew, covered faces and wept.
Who shed the most tears among those seated?
The Magistrate of Jiangzhou, his blue robe soaked wet."}

Pondering deeply, she places the pick among the strings,
Straightens her clothes and stands up, composing her expression.

My home lay near Shama Ling.
By thirteen, I had mastered the pipa;
My name belonged to the first troupe of the imperial academy.
When I finished a piece, even the great musicians bowed in admiration;
When I dressed, every courtesan grew jealous.
Young men of the Five Tombs fought to wrap me in brocade,
For one song, countless bolts of red silk were given.
Gold-inlaid combs snapped in time to the beat,
Blood-red skirts stained by spilling wine.
Year after year passed in laughter and joy,
Autumn moons and spring breezes treated casually.
Then my brother went off to war, and my aunt died;
Days turned to nights, and my beauty faded away.
The front gate became cold, horsemen rare;
Too old now, I married a merchant as his wife.

Last month he bought tea and left for Fuliang.

Surrounded only by bright moonlight and chilling river waters.
Deep in the night, I dream suddenly of youthful days,
Crying in my sleep, makeup streaked red with tears.

Now hearing these words, again I lament deeply.

Since we meet here, why must we have known each other before?

Then sat down again, tightening the strings, playing faster.

At night I saw a guest off by the Xunyang River's head,
Where maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn wind.
I dismounted, my guest on board; we raised our cups to drink,
But no strings or pipes were there to fill the air with sound.
Drunk yet joyless, gloom hung heavy as parting drew near;
We bade adieu amid vast waters where the moon lay submerged.
Suddenly, from out upon the water came pipa music sweet;
I forgot my homecoming, and my friend delayed his start.
Seeking the source, I asked softly who might be playing so;
The pipa ceased, but she seemed reluctant, slow to speak her name.
We moved our boats close together and invited her to meet us;
More wine was poured, lamps refilled, and the banquet resumed.
After thousands of calls and pleas, at last she came forth,
Still holding her pipa, half-covering her face shyly.
She turned the pegs and tested the strings two or three notes;
Before the melody formed, emotion already flowed.
Each string choked back sorrow, each note carried longing,
As if telling aloud of ambitions thwarted in life.
Head lowered, moving casually through continuous strokes,
She sang all the endless things buried deep in her heart.
Lightly pressing, slowly twisting, sweeping then plucking—
First "Rainbow Garment," then "Six Strings" followed next.
Thick strings rumbled like sudden rainstorm’s fury,
Thin strings whispered like private murmurs’ tender tone.
Rumbling, whispering—notes mixed intricately together,
Like pearls large and small falling onto a jade plate.
Smoothly gliding like warblers singing beneath blossoms,
Muffled groaning like spring water flowing under ice.
Ice-cold springs grew sluggish; strings froze, cut short—
Silence fell when they could not flow; sounds paused briefly.
Yet hidden sorrows and secret resentments stirred anew;
In that moment, silence surpassed even speech itself.
Then suddenly silver bottles burst open, water spurted;
Iron cavalry charged forth with clashing swords and spears.
The song ended; she swept the plectrum across the center—
One final chord rang sharp like tearing silk apart.
Boats east and west stood silent, no word spoken;
Only seen: autumn moon bright upon river's heart.
Lost in thought, she set down her plectrum between strings;
Adjusting clothes, rising, composing her solemn countenance.
She said she had once been a girl from the capital city,
Her home nestled below Shrimp Hill Lane's old ground.
By age thirteen she mastered the pipa fully trained;
Her name listed first among Imperial Academy girls.
After songs, masters praised; after makeup, courtesans envied.
Noble youths of Five Tombs vied lavishing gifts upon her;
For one piece, endless bolts of crimson silk poured forth.
Gold-inlaid hairpins broke tapping rhythm’s beat;
Blood-red skirts stained overturned wine during revelry.
This year laughing, next again, idle months slipped away—
Autumn moons and spring winds passed without regard.
Then brother joined army; aunt died; days fled swiftly on;
Beauty faded as morning turned into evening light.

A merchant’s wife became. He prized profit over love.
Last month he left for Fuliang to trade tea; gone long.

Crying in dream, tears streaked painted cheeks red.

Why must strangers need prior acquaintance before meeting?
Since last year left Emperor’s City exiled sick here too,
Xunyang remote land void music entire years never heard.
Near Penjiang dwelling low damp yellow reeds bitter bamboo.
What heard dusk dawn cuckoo blood crying apes mournful scream.
Spring rivers flower mornings autumn moons nights often took wine pour lonely self.

At the moment of farewell, the vast river was steeped in moonlight.
Suddenly, from the water came the sound of a pipa;
The host forgot to return home, and the guest did not set sail.
Following the sound, I quietly asked who was playing;
The pipa music stopped, as if the player hesitated to speak.
We moved our boats close together and invited her out;
More wine was added, lamps turned back, and the feast resumed.
After a thousand calls and ten thousand entreaties, she finally emerged,
Still holding the pipa against half her face to conceal it.
She adjusted the tuning pegs and plucked two or three strings;
Before the melody had formed, emotion was already present.
Each string was suppressed, each note full of melancholy,
As if telling of a life unfulfilled in ambition.
Lowering her brows, she played casually and continuously,
Expressing all the infinite matters within her heart.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, then brushing and picking,
First playing "Rainbow Garments," then later "Six Strings."
The thicker strings rumbled like a sudden heavy rain;
The thinner ones whispered softly like private conversation.
Rumbling and whispering mingled and alternated,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
The song became smooth like orioles singing under flowers,
Then choked and difficult like spring water flowing beneath ice.
When the cold springs froze stiff and the strings ceased to vibrate,
The flow blocked and silent, the sound paused for a moment.
A hidden sorrow and secret resentment arose anew;
At this time, silence surpassed any possible sound.
Then suddenly, like a silver bottle bursting with water spurting forth,
Or armored cavalry charging with the clash of swords and spears.
When the tune ended, she used her plectrum to sweep across the center;
With one final strike, the four strings sounded like tearing silk.
To the east and west, ships stood silent without word;
Only the white autumn moon in the middle of the river was seen.
Lost in thought, she placed her plectrum among the strings;
She straightened her clothes and rose with a serious expression.
She said that originally she was a girl from the capital city,
Living near the Xiama Ling district.
By age thirteen, she had mastered the pipa;
Her name belonged to the first section of the imperial music academy.
After finishing a piece, even expert musicians admired her skill;
Once made up, every courtesan like Qiuniang grew jealous.
The young nobles of Five Tombs competed to offer red silk headbands;
For one song, countless bolts of red silk were given.
Gold-ornamented hairpins and silver combs broke while beating time;
Blood-red skirts were stained by spilled wine.
Year after year passed in laughter and merriment;
Autumn moons and spring breezes were treated lightly.
But then her brother joined the army and her aunt died;
Evenings went and mornings came, and her beauty faded.
Her door became desolate, few horses came to visit;
Getting old, she married a merchant as his wife.
Merchants care more for profit than for farewell;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
Leaving and returning, she guards an empty boat at the river mouth;
Surrounding the boat is bright moonlight and cold river water.
In the deep night, she suddenly dreams of youthful days;
She wakes crying, makeup tears streaming down her flushed face.
Hearing the pipa, I had already sighed deeply;
And hearing these words, I sighed again heavily.
Both are lost souls wandering to the ends of the earth;
In meeting now, why should we have known each other before?

Banished and sick, lying low in Xunyang City.

All year long, I hear no sounds of silk and bamboo.

It is like listening to fairy music; my ears become clear.
Do not refuse to sit further and play another tune;
For you, I will rewrite the "Song of the Pipa."
Moved by my words, she stood for a long time;
Then sat down again, tightening the strings, which played faster.

座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "The Song of the Pipa

By the Xun River at night, I bid my guest farewell;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustle in the chill of autumn.
The host dismounts, while the guest remains on his boat;
We raise our cups to drink, but there are no pipes or strings.
Drunk yet joyless, we face a sorrowful parting;
As we part, vast mists hang low, moonlight sinking into the river.

Suddenly, from over the water, comes the sound of a pipa;
The host forgets to return home, the guest delays setting sail.
Following the sound, I ask quietly who is playing;
The pipa pauses, hesitant, before words begin.
I move my boat closer, inviting her to appear,
Refill the wine, trim the lamps, and restart the feast.
After a thousand calls and ten thousand entreaties, she finally emerges,
Still holding her pipa, half-covering her face.

She turns the pegs and plucks the strings two or three times;
Before a melody forms, emotion already stirs.
Each string suppresses deep sighs, each note carries thought,
Seeming to recount a life of unfulfilled ambition.
With lowered brows, she plays continuously, fingers roaming freely,
Pouring out the endless tales hidden within her heart.

Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, sweeping then picking again,
First she plays the "Rainbow Garment," then follows with the "Six Melodies."
The thick strings rumble like a sudden downpour;
The thin strings whisper like lovers talking in private.
Loud and soft notes intertwine in complex harmony,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.

Now fluid and sweet, like warblers singing among flowers;
Now choked and difficult, like springs struggling beneath ice.
When cold brooks stagnate and strings cease to vibrate,
The silence breaks off, leaving only a temporary halt.
Then another sorrow arises, a buried resentment born—
At this moment, silence surpasses even the loudest sound.

Abruptly, like a silver vase shattering, water bursts forth;
Like iron cavalry charging, clashing swords and spears ring out.
As the song ends, she draws her plectrum across the center of the strings,
And all four chords sound at once, like tearing silk.
Eastward boats and westward barges fall silent, listening intently;
Only the autumn moon on the river’s middle glows white.

Hesitating, she places her plectrum between the strings,
Straightens her dress, stands up, and composes her expression.
She says: "I was originally a girl from the capital city,
Living near Xia Ma Ling.
By thirteen, I had mastered the pipa;
My name belonged to the first section of the Imperial Music Bureau.
After finishing a tune, I could make great masters admire me;
Once dressed, I often drew the envy of beautiful rivals.

Young nobles from the Five Mausoleums vied to shower her with silk rewards,
For one song, they gave red damask beyond counting.
Jeweled hairpins shattered as guests beat time with them;
Blood-red skirts stained by spilled wine.
Year after year passed in laughter and joy,
Wasting splendid nights under autumn moons and spring breezes.

But then, my brother joined the army, and my aunt died;
Beauty faded as days turned into years.
My door became desolate, horses rare;
Growing older, I married a merchant’s wife.
Merchants value profit above all else, caring little for separation;
Last month, he went to Fuliang to buy tea.

He left, and I stayed at the river mouth guarding an empty boat,
Surrounded by bright moonlight and cold river waters.
Late at night, I suddenly dreamed of my youth’s affairs,
Weeping in dreams, tears staining my makeup red.

I heard the pipa and sighed deeply already,
And hearing these words, I lamented twice as much.
We are both fallen souls drifting to the end of the earth—
Why must we have known each other before meeting?

Since last year, I left the imperial capital,
Banished here to Jiujiang, bedridden with illness.
Jiujiang is remote, devoid of music;
All year long, I hear not the slightest sound of silk or bamboo.
Living near the Pen River, where land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.

What do I hear morning or evening in this place?
Cuckoos crying blood and apes wailing in grief.
On spring river mornings or autumn moonlit nights,
Often, I take wine and pour it alone.

Surely there are mountain songs and village flutes?
But crude and grating sounds, painful to the ear.
Tonight, upon hearing your pipa’s language,
It is like listening to celestial music; my ears are suddenly clear.

Please do not refuse to sit again and play one more piece;
For you, I shall compose 'The Song of the Pipa.'"

Moved by my words, she stood silently for a long time,
Then sat back down, tightening the strings, playing faster.
Her sounds were sad, unlike those before;
Everyone in the audience covered their faces, weeping anew.

Who among us wept the most?
The blue robe of the Jiangzhou Prefect is wet with tears."}

By the Xunyang River, at night, I bid a guest farewell;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustle in autumn's chill.
The host dismounts; his guest is by the boat awaiting;
We raise our cups to drink, but lack both flute and string.
Drunkenness fails to bring joy; sad is parting's sting,
And when we leave, vast moonlight bathes the river's flow.
Suddenly, music from the water strikes my ear;
The host forgets to go; the guest delays departure.
We seek the sound, asking softly: who plays here?
The pipa pauses, hesitant to speak aloud.
We move our boats close in, invite her out to show;
Add wine, relight lamps, resume the banquet now.
After much calling, she comes forth at last,
Still holding the pipa, half hiding her face.
She turns the pegs, plucks strings, two or three notes,
Before the melody begins, emotion springs.
Each string suppresses sighs; each note conveys grief,
As if telling of a life unfulfilled, thwarted.
Lowering brows, fingers dance on, playing on,
Expressing all the endless sorrows deep inside.
Lightly gathered, slowly twisted, swept, then picked,
First 'Rainbow Garments', then 'Six Strings' follow next.
The thick strings thunder like a sudden rainstorm;
The thin strings whisper like private conversation.
Thunders and whispers intertwine, mixed play,
Like pearls large and small falling into jade plates.
Smooth as orioles singing beneath blooming flowers;
Choked as spring ice flowing under frozen streams.
Ice-cold, sluggish, strings freeze, sound stops midway;
Blocked, silent, yet feeling grows within.
Hidden sorrow, secret hate are born anew;
At this moment, silence surpasses speech.
A silver vase bursts, water splashes forth;
Iron cavalry charges, swords and spears clash loud.
The song ends; she lifts the pick, strikes centrally,
One final note from four strings, like silk tearing.
East ships and west boats fall silent, no one speaks;
Only the white autumn moon shines in midstream.
Lost in thought, she puts down the plectrum, adjusts dress,
Stands up, composed, with solemn countenance shown.
She says: 'I was originally a girl from the capital,
Living near Xiama Ridge. At thirteen years old,
I mastered the pipa, joining the top tier of teaching.
When songs ended, skilled masters would admire me;
When made up, the beautiful Qiuniang envied me.
The young men of Wuling vied to give gifts;
One song earned countless bolts of red silk cloth.
Jeweled combs broke keeping time; blood-red dresses stained
With spilled wine. One year of laughter followed another;
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed lightly away.
My brother joined the army; my aunt died; days went by,
Age dimmed my beauty. Few horses came to my door.
Getting older, I married a merchant wife. He values profit, cares little for separation;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea. Left alone at the river mouth guarding an empty boat,
The bright moon circles, cold river waters surround.
Late at night, suddenly dreaming of youthful affairs,
I cry in dreams, tears staining makeup on cheeks.'
Hearing the pipa, I already sighed deeply;
Hearing these words, I sigh again heavily.
Both of us are drifters at the edge of the world;
Meeting now, why need we have known before?
Since last year I left the imperial capital,
Demoted and sick, living in Xunyang city.
Xunyang is remote, devoid of music;
All year long, not heard string or bamboo sounds.
Near Pengjiang River, land low and damp around home,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow wild nearby.
What do we hear morning and evening? Only cuckoos crying blood, apes wailing mournfully.
On spring river flowers mornings, autumn moon nights,
Often take wine, pour it alone. Are there no mountain songs and village flutes? They are harsh, discordant, hard to listen to.
Tonight hearing your pipa words, it seems celestial music clearing deafened ears.
Do not refuse to sit and play another piece;
For you, I compose 'Song of the Pipa'.
Touched by my words, she stood for a long while;
Sat back down, tightened strings, tempo sped up.
Mournful, unlike previous tunes, full of sadness;
Everyone present listened again, covering faces weeping.
Who shed most tears among those seated here?
The green robe of the Jiazhou Prefect was wet."}
