We raise our cups, yet no flutes or strings attend.
Drunk but joyless, we face parting’s chill;
At farewell, vast mist—the river soaks the moon.

Then—unexpected: pipasong rises from the water.
The host forgets to return; the guest delays departure.
Following the sound, I ask softly in the dark: Who plays?
The pipa halts; someone wishes to speak, then hesitates.

I move my ship closer, invite a meeting.
Fresh wine poured, lamps trimmed, the feast reopens.
Called and called again, she finally emerges,
Clutching her pipa, half-hidden behind it.

Turning the pegs, plucking two or three strings—
Before the tune forms, feeling is already there.
Each string suppressed, every note laden with thought,
As if telling of a life unfulfilled by ambition.

Low brows, hands moving freely, playing on and on,
Voicing all the endless sorrows within her heart.
Light presses, slow twists, brushes and picks—
First *Nishang*, then *Liuyao*.

The thick strings roar like sudden rain;
The thin strings whisper like private talk.
Roaring and whispering, mixed together—
Big pearls, small pearls falling into a jade plate.

Smooth as warblers’ song beneath flowers;
Choked as spring water struggling under ice.
Ice-cold, sluggish, the strings freeze and stop;
Frozen, blocked—the sound briefly ceases.

Yet hidden sorrow and secret hate stir anew;
In this silence, stillness speaks louder than sound.

Suddenly, a silver bottle bursts—water splashes out!
Iron cavalry charges—clash of swords and spears!
At the music’s end, the pick sweeps across the center;
Four strings ring once, sharp as tearing silk.

Boats east and west fall silent;
Only the white autumn moon remains in the river’s heart.

She pauses, inserts the pick between the strings,
Straightens her clothes, gathers composure.
“I was born a woman of the capital,” she says,
“My home near Toad Ridge.”

“Learned the pipa at thirteen,
Registered in the First Hall of the Music Bureau.
After each piece, even skilled masters bowed;
When made up, I caused beauty queens envy.

Young men of Five Mausoleums competed for me,
A single song earned countless bolts of red silk.
Gold-ornamented hairpins shattered keeping time,
Blood-red skirts stained with spilled wine.

Year after year of laughter,
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed casually.
My brother joined the army; my aunt died.
Evenings fade, mornings come, beauty fades.

Door grown cold, horses rare;
Age came; I married a merchant wife.
He loves profit, cares little for parting;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.

Leaving me here, guarding an empty boat at the river mouth,
Moonlight surrounds the hull, the river water bitter cold.
Late at night, suddenly dreaming of youth,
I wake crying, makeup running red down my cheeks.”

Hearing the pipa, I sigh deeply;
Hearing these words, I lament again.
Both are wanderers fallen to earth’s edge—
Meeting now, why must we have known before?

Since last year I left the imperial capital,
Exiled, sick, lying low in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, without music;
All year long, no silk-and-bamboo sounds heard.

Living near the Pen River, land low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo surround my house.
What do I hear morning and evening?
Cuckoos bleeding cries, apes wailing mournfully.

Spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn nights—
Often I take wine, pouring alone.
Are there mountain songs and village flutes?
Gurgling, croaking—hard to listen to.

Tonight hearing your pipa’s language,
It’s as if celestial music clears my ears.
Please don’t refuse; sit again, play one more piece—
For you, I will compose the Ballad of the Pipa.

Moved by these words, she stood long in silence,
Then sat back, tightened the strings; notes grew urgent.
Mournful, unlike the earlier tone;
Everyone in the hall listened, wiping tears.

Who among those present wept the most?
The Blue-Robed Magistrate of Jiangzhou, wet robe soaking through."}

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。

寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。

五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。

门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。

住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。

春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。

座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "The Song of the Pipa

By the river at Xunyang, seeing off a friend by night,
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in autumn's chill.
The host dismounted; the guest sat on his boat.
I raised my wine cup to drink—but no strings or pipes were there.
Drunk yet joyless, sorrowful as we parted;
Parting into vast mist, the moon submerged in the river.
Suddenly, from over the water, came the sound of a pipa.
The host forgot to return; the guest delayed his voyage.
Following the sound, I asked quietly: "Who is playing?"
The pipa music paused, hesitant to speak.
I moved my boat close, invited her to appear;
Added more wine, brought back the lamp, and reopened the feast.
Called a thousand times, urged ten thousand voices,
she finally emerged, still holding the pipa before half her face.
She turned the pegs and plucked the strings, two or three notes—
Before a melody formed, emotion was already present.
Each string muffled, each note laden with thought,
As if telling of a life unfulfilled.
Brow lowered, fingers moving freely, she played on,
Expressing all the boundless things within her heart.
Lightly pressing, slowly rolling, sweeping then plucking,
First the "Rainbow Garment," then the "Six Strings."
The thick strings rumbled like sudden rain,
The thin strings whispered like secrets shared.
Rumbling and whispering, intertwined and strung together,
Like large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Smooth and clear like the warbling of an oriole beneath flowers,
Choked and sobbing like spring water clogging under ice.
Ice-like springs, cold and stagnant; the strings froze and stopped,
Stopped and blocked, the sound momentarily ceased.
But another hidden sorrow, dark resentment, arose—
At this moment, silence surpassed sound.
Then suddenly, like a silver vase breaking, water burst forth,
Like armored cavalry charging, the clash of swords and spears.
The music ended; she drew the pick across the center of the strings.
A single cry from the four strings, like silk tearing.
Boats to the east and ships to the west fell silent.
All that remained was the white autumn moon in the middle of the river.
Lost in thought, she placed the pick between the strings,
Straightened her clothes, stood up, composing her expression.
She said: "I was originally a girl of the capital,
Living by the Shrimp Hill Mound.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa,
My name entered the first division of the Imperial Music Bureau.
When I finished a tune, even the finest musicians admired me;
When I completed my makeup, even the most beautiful women envied me.
Young men from the Five Tombs competed to offer me gifts,
For one song, they gave me red silk beyond counting.
Gold-inlay hairpins and silver combs were broken keeping time,
Blood-red skirts stained by spilled wine.
This year’s laughter repeated next year’s,
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed casually away.
My brother went to join the army; my aunt died.
Evenings pass, mornings come; my beauty faded.
The gate became desolate; horses and carriages grew scarce.
Getting old, I married a merchant’s wife.
The merchant values profit above all, cares little for parting.
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
After he left, I guarded the empty boat at the river mouth,
Surrounded by bright moonlight, the river water cold.
Deep in the night, I suddenly dreamed of my youth,
In the dream I wept, tears staining my rouge.
I heard the pipa and sighed,
Heard these words and lamented anew.
We are both wandering souls cast down to the edge of the world—
Why must we have known each other before meeting?
Since last year, I left the Imperial Capital,
Demoted and bedridden in the city of Xunyang.
Xunyang is remote, devoid of music;
All year long, I hear not the sound of silk strings or bamboo pipes.
Living near the Pen River, where the land is low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my home.
What do I hear here, morning and evening?
The cuckoo crying blood, apes wailing mournfully.
On spring rivers and flower mornings, on autumn nights and full moons,
Often I take wine and pour it out alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
They are harsh and grating, difficult to listen to.
Tonight, hearing your pipa language,
It is like listening to celestial music; my ears are suddenly cleared.
Do not refuse to sit again and play another piece;
For you, I will compose the 'Song of the Pipa.'
Moved by my words, she stood for a long time.
Then she returned to her seat, tightened the strings, playing faster.
The melancholy sounds differed from those before.
Hearing them again, the whole company covered their faces, weeping.
Who among them shed the most tears?
The blue robe of the Jiangzhou Assistant Governor was soaked."}

By Bai Juyi

At night I bid farewell to a guest by the Xunyang River bank,
Amidst maple leaves and reed flowers, autumn’s chill blows bleak.
The host dismounts; the guest remains on board his boat;
We raise our cups, but lack the music of strings and pipes.
Drunk yet joyless, we grieve at parting imminent;
As we part, vast is the river, moonlight soaking deep.
Suddenly, over the water, sounds of a pipa are heard;
The host forgets to return, the guest delays his departure.
Following the sound, in darkness, I ask who plays so well;
The pipa pauses, as if the player hesitates to speak.
We move our boats closer, inviting her to meet us;
Wine is refilled, lamps brought back, the feast resumed.
After many calls and entreaties, she finally emerges,
Still holding her pipa, half concealing her face.
She turns the pegs and plucks a few preliminary strings;
Before the melody forms, emotion already flows.
Each string restrained, each sound laden with thought,
Seeming to recount a life of thwarted ambition.
Eyes lowered, fingers moving freely, she plays on,
Telling all the endless sorrows within her heart.
Softly gathered, slowly twisted, swept then picked anew:
First the "Rainbow Feather," then the "Six Strings" tune.
The thick strings roar like sudden heavy rain;
The thin strings whisper like quiet private talk.
Roaring and whispering intermingle in the playing,
Like large and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Now smooth as orioles singing beneath the blossoms,
Now choked as spring water flowing under ice.
Ice-cold springs stagnate, the strings seem frozen tight;
Frozen and blocked, the sound briefly ceases.
But hidden grief and dark resentment arise anew—
At this moment, silence surpasses all sound.
Then, suddenly, like a silver vase bursting, water sprays;
Or iron cavalry charging, swords clashing loudly.
The song ends; she draws her plectrum across the center;
One final strum from the four strings rips like tearing silk.
Boats east and west fall silent, no words spoken;
Only the white autumn moon shines on the river’s heart.
Pondering, she inserts her plectrum between the strings,
Straightens her clothes, rises, with composed countenance.
She says: "I was originally a girl from the capital,
My home located near Shama Mound.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa;
My name ranked first among the Imperial Music Academy.
After my songs finished, even skilled masters admired me;
When I made up my face, other beauties grew envious.
Young men from Five Vaults vied to offer me silks;
For one song, red gauze was given without counting.
Jeweled combs broke as time was beaten out;
Blood-red skirts stained with spilled wine.
Year after year of laughter passed in vain,
Spending autumn moons and spring breezes carelessly.
My brother joined the army; my aunt died;
Days turned, nights came, and my beauty faded.
The door became desolate, horses rare;
Getting old, I married a merchant's wife.
The merchant values profit above love of companionship;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He left, and I guard an empty boat at the river mouth,
Surrounded by bright moonlight and cold river waters.
In the deep night, I dream abruptly of youthful days,
Crying in sleep, tears staining my rouge down my cheeks."
Hearing the pipa, I had already sighed deeply;
Hearing these words, I sigh again with profound grief.
We are both people cast adrift at the world's edge;
Meeting now, why must we have known each other before?
Since last year, I left the imperial capital,
Exiled in Xunyang city, sick and bedridden.
Xunyang is remote, lacking music;
All year round, I hear no sound of strings or flutes.
Living near Pen River, the land is low and damp;
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my home.
What do I hear here, morning and evening?
Dusky cuckoos crying blood, and gibbons wailing mournfully.
On spring rivers under flower mornings, or autumn nights under moon,
Often I take my wine and pour it alone.
Are there not folk songs and village pipes?
Yes, but their harsh, jarring tones are hard to bear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa melodies,
It is like hearing celestial music; my ears are momentarily clear.
Do not refuse to sit and play another piece;
For you, I will compose the "Song of the Pipa."
Moved by my words, she stood for a long while,
Then sat back down, tightening strings that played faster.
The melancholy tone differed from earlier sounds;
The whole audience, hearing it again, covered faces and wept.
Who among them shed the most tears?
It was the Prefect of Jiangzhou, whose blue robe was wet."}

We traced the sound, asking softly who played so well,
The pipa ceased; she hesitated before breaking her spell.
We moved our boats closer to invite her sight,
Added wine, relit lamps, renewed the feast tonight.
After countless calls, at last she emerged to view,
Still holding her pipa, half-hiding her face from us.
She turned the pegs and plucked two or three strings true,
Before the tune began, emotion poured anew.
Each note suppressed, each sound heavy with longing,
As if telling of a life where hope failed belonging.
Brows lowered, fingers moving with easy grace,
She spoke all the sorrows hidden deep in place.

First "Rainbow Robes," then "Six-String Whirl" were cast.

The thin ones whispered like private, tender powers.
Rumbling whispers intertwined, complex and deep,
Like large and small pearls into a jade plate they sweep.
Clear as orioles singing smooth beneath flowers bright,
Choked as spring water struggling through ice in the night.

The music paused, suspended in the glow.
A new kind of hidden sorrow started to rise,
In that silence, more was heard than in cries.
Then like a silver jar bursting, water spurts out,
Like iron cavalry charging, swords clash and shout.
The song ended; she drew her pick across the center string,
One sharp tear like silk ripping, making hearts ring.
East and west boats fell silent, words unspoken,
Only the white autumn moon over the river was broken.
She pondered, placed her pick between the strings,
Straightened her clothes, composed herself with rings.

My home lay below Shrimp Frog Hill, in old times worn.
By thirteen, I mastered the pipa's art,
Named first among the Imperial Music Department.
Once I finished playing, even masters bowed low,
When I dressed up, courtesans watched me glow.
Young nobles fought with treasures to win my favor,
For one song, red silk bolts beyond measure.
Gold-inlaid combs broke keeping time with beats,
Blood-red skirts stained with spilled wine's sweets.
Year after year of laughter, carefree days,
Autumn moons and spring winds passed in lazy ways.
But when my brother joined the army and aunt died,
Time stole my beauty, fading pride.
My door grew cold, horses rare, visitors few,
Aged now, I married a merchant, true.
He values profit more than love's embrace,
Last month he went to Fuliang for tea's chase.
Leaving me alone at the river mouth, guarding an empty boat,
Surrounded by bright moonlight, cold water floats.
Deep in the night, I dreamed of youth's delight,
Woke crying, makeup tears streaming down right.
Hearing her pipa, I sighed with grief,
Hearing her words, my sorrow grew brief.
Both are wanderers fallen far from home,
Why need we have known each other to roam?
Since last year I left the Imperial Capital,
Banished to Jiujiang, sick and pitiful.
Jiujiang is remote, devoid of music's charm,
All year long, no string or wind plays warm.
I live near the Pen River, land damp and low,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo surround my abode.
What do I hear at dawn and dusk? Cuckoos bleed,
Gibbons wail, filling air with need.
Spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moon nights,
I often take wine, drinking alone in sights.
Are there no mountain songs or village pipes?
Their harsh sounds grate against these ears alike.
Tonight I heard your pipa's language pure,
Like celestial music, my ears regained cure.
Do not refuse; sit again, play another song,
I will compose this 'Pipa Ballad,' strong.
Touched by my words, she stood for a long while,
Then sat down quickly, plucking with fierce style.
Melancholy now, unlike earlier sweet,
The whole audience listened, weeping at feet.
Who shed the most tears in the crowd? I ask,
The Sima of Jiangzhou's blue robe is soaked with task."}

East boats and west bargens fell into silence; Only the white autumn moon remained in the river’s heart. She paused, inserted the pick among the strings, Straightened her clothes, rose with composed dignity. She said: "I was born a girl in the capital city, My family lived near Xiama Ling. At thirteen I mastered the pipa skillfully, Renowned among the first troupe of the Imperial Conservatory. After performances even great masters admired me; When made up, courtesans envied my beauty. Young nobles from Five Tombs fought over gifts for me, Each song earning countless bolts of red silk. Hairpins with jeweled heads shattered keeping rhythm; Red skirts stained by spilled wine during revelry. Year after year laughter continued happily; Autumn moons and spring breezes passed idly away. Brother left for army, aunt died; Days and nights aged my beauty. Few visitors came, horses rare before my door; Getting old, I married a merchant wife. Merchants care more for profit than farewell; Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea. He leaves and returns; I guard an empty boat at the river mouth, Encircled by bright moonlight, cold waters around. Deep in night dreams of youthful days; Tears wet my makeup, running down my cheeks. {"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。

醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。

五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。

座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "The Song of the Pipa

By the Xunyang River, I saw off a guest at night;
Maple leaves and reed flowers trembled in autumn's chill.
My horse had stepped down; my guests aboard their boat,
We raised our cups, yet lacked the music to fill the air.
Though tipsy, joy was scarce as parting loomed ahead,
The moon hung low, drowned in the vast, misty river.
Suddenly, from the water, a pipa’s voice arose—
I forgot to go home; they delayed their departure.
Tracing the sound, I asked softly: who plays?
The pipa paused, hesitant before answering.
We drew our boats close, inviting her to meet us,
Refilled the wine, trimmed the lamps, resumed the feast.
After ten thousand calls, she finally appeared,
Still holding the pipa half-covering her face.
She turned the pegs, plucked two or three strings—
Before any melody formed, emotion already stirred.
Each string sighed, each note conveyed longing,
As if telling of a life denied its due respect.
Brows lowered, fingers moved with casual grace,
Pouring out the endless sorrows of her heart.
Lightly pressing, slowly twisting, sweeping then picking,
First came 'Rainbow Garments,' then 'Six-Strand Elegy.'
The thick strings thundered like sudden rain;
The thin ones whispered like lovers’ private talk.
Thick and thin intertwined, complex and rich—
Large pearls and small falling onto a jade plate.
Birdsongs slid through flowers, clear and sweet;
Spring streams choked under ice, muffled and slow.
Ice-cold waters stalled the strings into silence,
In that stillness, hidden grief began to bloom.
At this moment, silence spoke louder than sound.
Like a silver vase bursting, water spraying high;
Like armored cavalry charging, blades clashing loud.
The song ended as the plectrum swept across the center strings,
One final crash like silk tearing apart.
East and west boats fell silent, no word exchanged;
Only the autumn moon shone white on the river’s heart.
Lost in thought, she placed the plectrum between the strings,
Straightened her robes, composed her solemn face.
She said: "Born in the capital, near Shrimp Hill I lived;
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa, joined the top troupe.
Even masters praised when my songs concluded,
And rivals envied my beauty upon dressing.
Young nobles vied to scatter brocade gifts for me,
For one tune alone, countless red silks flowed.
Silver combs broke keeping time with drums,
Blood-red skirts stained by spilled wine.
Year after year, laughter carried me along,
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed idly by.
Then brothers left for war, aunties died away,
Days turned to nights, fading my youthful charm.
Once bustling gates grew cold, horses rare,
Now married, I live as a merchant’s wife.
He cares more for profit than for parting pains,
Last month he went to Fuliang to trade tea.
He leaves; I guard our empty boat at the dock,
Moonlight circling the ship, river cold beneath.
Late at night, dreams of youth return unbidden,
Tears soak my makeup, streaming down in red.
Hearing the pipa, I sighed deeply already,
Hearing these words, I wept anew, broken.
We are both wanderers lost beyond the horizon,
Why must we have known each other before meeting?
Since last year, leaving the imperial capital behind,
Exiled sick, I lay in Xunyang City’s gloom.
Remote lands here know no music’s touch,
All year long, not a flute or zither sounds.
Near Pen River’s banks, damp earth surrounds me,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo choke my home.
What do I hear at dawn and dusk?
Cuckoos bleeding cries, apes mourning aloud.
On spring river mornings, autumn moonlit nights,
Often I take wine and pour it to myself alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
Their hoarse, jarring tones are unbearable.
Tonight, hearing your pipa speak,
It is like celestial music clearing my ears.
Do not refuse; sit again, play one more tune,
I will write this ballad for you: The Song of the Pipa.
Moved by my words, she stood long in silence,
Then sat back, tightened strings, playing faster now.
Sorrowful notes unlike those heard before,
The whole audience wept, faces hidden in tears.
Who among them shed most tears tonight?
The Blue-Clad Magistrate of Jiangzhou, soaked through."}

By the Qanshui River, I saw my friend off at night; Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the chill of autumn.
My horse dismounted, my guest remained on his boat; I raised my wine to drink, but found no music to accompany it.
Though drunk, joy was absent as we faced our sad parting; When we parted, a vast moon floated upon the river's surface.
Suddenly, from over the water, came the sound of a pipa; The host forgot to return home, the guest delayed his departure.
Following the sound, I asked softly who played; The pipa paused, the player hesitated before speaking.
I moved my boat closer and invited her to meet me; We added more wine, relit the lamps, and resumed the feast.
After many calls and entreaties, she finally appeared, Yet still held her pipa half-covering her face.
She turned the pegs and plucked the strings a few times; Before the melody formed, emotion already flowed.
Each string suppressed sorrow, each note carried longing; As if telling of a lifetime of unfulfilled ambitions.
With lowered brows, she played casually yet skillfully, Expressing all the boundless matters within her heart.
Lightly pressing, slowly twisting, sweeping and picking, First playing 'Rainbow Garments,' then 'Six-String Melody.'
The thick strings sounded like heavy raindrops rushing down; The thin strings whispered like intimate secrets shared.
Thick and thin sounds mingled intricately together; Like pearls large and small falling onto a jade plate.
Then came the chirping of orioles sliding beneath blossoms; And the choked sobbing of springs trapped under ice.
The cold spring froze, the strings stopped dead; Stuck and silent, the music ceased for a moment.
But hidden sorrows and secret regrets arose anew; At that moment, silence surpassed speech.
Like a silver vase suddenly bursting with water splashing out; Or armored cavalry charging forth with swords clashing loudly.
When the piece ended, she swept the plectrum across the center; Four strings sounded once, like tearing silk.
To the east and west boats fell into quiet awe; Only the white autumn moon shone in the middle of the river.
Lost in thought, she placed the plectrum between the strings; Straightened her clothes, rose, and composed her expression.
She said: "I was originally a girl from the capital city; My family lived near Shama Hill.""At thirteen I mastered the pipa;
My name ranked first among the Imperial Music Academy's troupe.
After finishing a tune, even skilled masters would admire me; After putting on makeup, the famous courtesan Qiuniang envied me.
The young nobles of Wuling vied to offer me gifts; For one song, countless pieces of red silk were given.
Gold-inlaid combs broke keeping time to the rhythm; Blood-red skirts stained by spilt wine during revelry.
This year laughter continued into next; Autumn moons and spring winds passed casually away.
But then my brother joined the army, my aunt died; Days faded into nights, and my beauty withered.
Before my door grew lonely, horses few; Aging, I married a merchant's wife.
The merchant valued profit over farewell; Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
Leaving me alone at the river mouth guarding an empty boat; Around the ship bright moonlight, cold river waters lap.
Deep in the night, I suddenly dreamed of youthful days; In dreams I wept, make-up tears staining my red cheeks.
Hearing the pipa, I already sighed deeply; Hearing these words, I groaned again with grief.
We are both lost souls drifting at heaven's edge; Having met now, why should it matter if we knew each other before?
Since last year I left the imperial capital; Banished and ill, lying idle in Qanshui City.
Qanshui is remote and lacks music; All year long I never hear stringed instruments.
Living near Penjiang where land is low and damp; Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear there morning and evening? Cuckoos bleeding with cries, apes wailing mournfully.
Spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moonlit nights; Often I take wine and pour it alone.
Are there truly no mountain songs or village flutes? Yes, but their harsh cacophony is unbearable to listen to.
Tonight hearing your pipa song, It is like hearing celestial music, ears suddenly clear.
Please don't refuse to sit longer and play another piece; For you, I will compose this Ballad of the Pipa.
Moved by my words, she stood for a long while; Then sat back down, tightened strings, speed increasing.
The melancholy tone differed from earlier notes; The whole audience listened again, covering faces and weeping.
Who shed the most tears among those present? The Magistrate of Jiangzhou, his blue robe soaked through."}

By Bai Juyi

On the banks of Xunyang River, I bid a guest farewell at night,
Amid maple leaves and reeds rustling in the autumn chill.
The host dismounts to meet his guest who waits aboard the boat;
We raise our cups, yet no flutes or strings are here to play.
Tipsy but joyless, we face a sorrowful parting,
As moonlight drowns in the vast, misty river.
Suddenly, from the water rises the sound of a pipa,
And the host forgets to go home; the guest delays his departure.
Following the music, I ask softly who is playing,
The pipa pauses, hesitant, as if she wishes to speak.
I move my boat closer and invite her to come out,
Refill the wine, trim the lamps, and resume the banquet.
After countless calls, she finally appears,
Still holding the pipa, half hiding her face.
She turns the pegs and plucks two or three strings,
Before the melody forms, emotion already flows.
Each string suppresses its sound with deep thought,
As if telling tales of a life unfulfilled.
With lowered brows, she casually continues to play,
Revealing the endless sorrows within her heart.
Lightly pressing, slowly twisting, sweeping, then picking,
First "Rainbow Garment," then "Six Strings" follows.
The thick strings thunder like sudden rain,
The thin strings whisper like private words.
Thick and thin sounds intertwine and mix,
Like pearls large and small falling onto a jade plate.
Clear birdsong glides smoothly through flowers below,
Muffled streams struggle under ice.
Ice-cold springs stagnate, strings seem to freeze,
When blocked and silent, the sound temporarily ceases.
New hidden grief and secret resentment arise—
In this silence, sound speaks louder than noise.
Then, like a silver vase bursting, water sprays forth,
Or armored cavalry charging, with swords clashing loud.
The song ends; she draws the plectrum across the center,
All four strings ring once, like tearing silk.
Boats east and west fall into quiet stillness,
Only the white autumn moon reflects in the river's heart.
Lost in thought, she inserts the plectrum among the strings,
Adjusts her clothes, stands up, composing her face.
She says: "I was originally a girl from the capital,
My home near Shrimp Mound Hill.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa,
My name belonged to the first rank in the Music Bureau.
After playing songs, even great masters admired me,
Once made up, even renowned beauties grew jealous.
The young nobles of Five Tombs vied to give me gifts,
For one song, I received red silk beyond counting.
Gold-inlaid combs broke keeping time to the beat,
Blood-red skirts stained by spilled wine.
Year after year, laughter followed laughter,
Wasting autumn moons and spring breezes carelessly.
Then my brother joined the army, my aunt died,
Days passed, nights came, my beauty faded.
The door became lonely, few horses remained outside,
Aging, I married a merchant as his wife.
Merchants value profit over love of farewell,
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He left, and I stayed guarding an empty boat at the river mouth,
Surrounded by bright moon and cold river waters.
Deep at night, I suddenly dreamed of youthful days,
Waking from dreams, tears mixed with rouge ran down my face.
Hearing her pipa, I already sighed,
Hearing these words, I sighed again deeply.
Both of us are wanderers lost at the edge of Heaven,
Meeting now, why must we have known each other before?
Since last year, I left the Imperial Capital,
Banished and lying ill in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, without music,
All year long, I hear not the sound of silk and bamboo.
Living near Pen River on low, damp ground,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboos grow around my house.
What do I hear day and night here?
Cuckoos crying blood and apes wailing sadly.
During spring rivers, flower mornings, and autumn moonlit nights,
Often I take wine and drink alone.
Are there truly no mountain songs or village flutes?
Their crude and harsh sounds are hard to listen to.
Tonight, hearing you play the pipa,
It is like hearing fairy music that clears my ears.
Please don't refuse; sit again and play another tune,
For you, I will write this 'Song of the Pipa.'
Moved by my words, she stood for a long while,
Then sat back and tightened the strings, which played faster.
Sorrowful, unlike the previous sounds,
The whole audience heard again and covered their faces, weeping.
Who among them shed the most tears?
The Sima of Jiangzhou, whose blue robe was wet."}

By the Yangtze at Xunyang, I bid a guest farewell by night,
When autumn winds rustled through maple leaves and reeds so slight.
I dismounted to the boat where my guest was bound to stay;
We raised our cups, but no music came to grace the play.
Though drunk on wine, joy failed us as parting drew near,
And we saw only the moon drowned in the river’s clear.
Suddenly, from the water, pipa strings began to sing;
I forgot my return, he his departure, captivated by its ring.
We traced the sound, asking softly who could be the player,
But the music stopped; hesitation hung in the air.
We moved our boats close together, inviting her to show,
Refilled our cups, lit the lamps, renewed the feast below.
After many calls and entreaties, she finally emerged,
Still holding the pipa, half-hiding her face, reserved.
She turned the pegs and plucked two or three tentative notes,
Before a melody formed, her sorrow already floats.
Each string restrained, each note laden with thought deep,
As if telling of a lifetime’s failures, silent and steep.
Brow lowered, fingers moving freely, one after another,
Expressing endless matters within, like wind in clover.
Lightly gathered, slowly twisted, strummed and picked again,
First "Rainbow Garments," then "Six Melodies" in the chain.
The big strings thundered loudly like a sudden rainstorm’s crash,
The small strings whispered gently like lovers’ soft flash.
Thundering and whispering mingled in complex play,
Like pearls large and small falling onto jade plate’s array.
Cuckoo-like birds sang sweetly beneath flowers, smooth and bright,
Then choked sobs like spring water flowing under ice, tight.
Ice-cold springs, stiffened strings, music ceased for a breath,
A new hidden grief arose, silencing death before life.
At this moment, silence surpassed the sound’s own claim,
Then suddenly a silver vase burst, water spurring flame.
Iron cavalry charged forth, blades clashing, spears ringing,
The song ended; with a final stroke, the silk tore, stinging.
Four strings struck as one, like tearing cloth’s sharp cry,
East ships and west barges fell silent, under the sky.
Only the moon’s white reflection upon the river’s heart remained,
While she paused, put down the plectrum, in the strings constrained.
Adjusting her clothes, she stood up, composing her face,
Telling her story, revealing her past’s trace.
"I was born a girl in the capital’s grand domain,
My home lay near Xiama Ling, amidst wealth and fame’s reign.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa’s intricate art,
Named first among the Imperial Music Troupe’s smart.
After finishing a tune, skilled masters bowed to my skill,
My makeup finished, even famed beauties felt ill.
Young men of Five Mounds vied to wrap me in brocade heads,
For one song, red silk bolts piled high, unknown counts spread.
Jeweled hairpins and silver combs broke keeping time’s beat,
Blood-red skirts stained with spilled wine, wild and fleet.
This year of laughter passed into next year’s delight,
Autumn moons and spring breezes spent carelessly in flight.
My brother joined the army, my aunt died away,
As twilight faded into dawn, beauty lost its day.
The gate grew cold, horse hooves rare, visitors few,
Growing old, I married a merchant, true to his cue.
He valued profit more than separation’s pain,
Last month to Fuliang he went, buying tea again.
When he returns, I guard the empty boat at river mouth,
Moonlight circles the ship, cold waters flow south.
Late at night, dreams of youth come crashing back to start,
Crying in sleep, tears ruin makeup, staining the heart."
Hearing the pipa, I sighed deeply, overcome with grief,
Hearing her words, I added sighs beyond relief.
Both are wanderers fallen to the ends of earth’s expanse,
Meeting now, why should we need prior acquaintance?
Since last year I left the Emperor’s Capital City,
Exiled here to Xunyang, sick, alone, pity.
Xunyang is remote, no music fills the air,
All year long, no strings or flutes can be heard there.
Living near Pen River, land low and damp, wet ground,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo surround my abode found.
What do I hear morning and evening in this place?
Cuckoos bleeding cries, apes wailing with sad grace.
Spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moon nights’ glow,
Often take out wine, drink alone, feelings slow.
Are there no mountain songs or village flute’s tune?
Hoarse and harsh sounds, painful to listen soon.
Tonight hearing your pipa speak its language pure,
Like celestial music, my ears brighten, cure.
Do not refuse to sit again and play one more song,
For you I’ll compose this Ballad of the Pipa, strong.
Moved by my words, she stood long in silence profound,
Then sat down, tightened strings, playing faster, bound.
Mournful and desolate, nothing like the former sound,
Everyone present covered faces, tears pouring round.
Who shed most tears among them? Ask if you must know:
The Magistrate of Jiangzhou, his blue robe wet in woe."}

Author: Bai Juyi

By night I see off a friend on the Xunyang River shore,
Maple leaves and reeds rustle in the autumn chill.
The host dismounts; the guest is already aboard;
We raise our cups, yet there are no flutes or strings to cheer.
Drunkenness brings no joy as we face a sorrowful parting,
The river vast and moonlit at the moment of farewell.
Suddenly, from the water, comes the sound of a pipa;
The host forgets to return, the guest delays his departure.
Following the music, I ask softly who plays.
The pipa stops, as if wanting to speak but hesitating.
I move my boat closer and invite her to come forth;
Fresh wine is poured, lamps turned up, the feast resumed.
Though called upon thousands of times, she finally emerges,
Still holding the pipa, half concealing her face.
She turns the pegs and plucks a few strings,
Before a tune forms, emotion is already present.
Each string suppressed, each note full of longing,
As if telling of a life unfulfilled.
Head bowed, fingers moving with ease, she continues playing,
Expressing all the endless sorrows within her heart.
Lightly pinching, slowly twisting, brushing and picking again,
First playing 'Rainbow Skirt', then 'Six Strings'.
Thick strings boom like sudden rain, thin ones whisper like secret talk.
Boom and whisper interweave in complex play,
Like pearls large and small falling into a jade plate.
Birdsong trills smoothly beneath flowers, stream sobbs hard under ice.
Ice-cold spring slows the strings, sound seems to cease.
Ceasing, blocked, the music pauses for a moment.
New hidden sorrow and dark resentment arise;
At this moment, silence surpasses sound.
Like a silver vase bursting, water spurts out;
Like iron cavalry charging, swords clash and ring.
The piece ends; she draws the plectrum across the center,
One final sound from four strings, like tearing silk.
Boats east and west fall silent, no words remain;
Only the white autumn moon shines over the river's heart.
In deep thought, she places the plectrum among the strings,
Straightens her clothes, rises, and assumes a composed look.
She says she was originally a girl from the capital,
Living near Xiama Ling (Toad Hill).
By thirteen she had mastered the pipa,
Her name listed in the first section of the Imperial Music Bureau.
When her songs ended, even skilled masters admired her craft;
After makeup, courtesans envied her beauty.
Young nobles from Five Tombs competed to offer gifts;
For one song, red gauze rolls numbered beyond measure.
Gold-inlaid combs shattered keeping the rhythm;
Blood-red skirts stained by spilled wine.
Year after year of laughter and joy passed casually,
With autumn moons and spring breezes taken for granted.
Then her brother joined the army, her aunt died,
And day by day, morning by evening, her looks faded.
Lonely before her gate, horsemen few;
Aging, she married a merchant's wife.
The merchant values profit over love, caring little for parting;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
Since he left, she guards an empty boat at the river mouth,
Surrounded by bright moonlight, cold river waters.
Late at night she suddenly dreams of her youth,
Wakes crying, tears staining her rouge down her cheeks.
I heard the pipa and sighed already;
Hearing these words, I sigh again deeply.
Both are wanderers fallen from grace in a far-off land;
What need to have known each other before meeting?
Since last year I left the imperial capital,
Exiled and ill, lying low in Xunyang City.
Xunyang is remote, lacking music;
All year round, not a string or bamboo sound is heard.
Living near Pen River, the land is low and wet;
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear here, dawn and dusk?
Cuckoos bleeding cries, gibbons wailing mournfully.
On spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moon nights,
Often I take wine and pour it alone.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
They are harsh and grating, difficult to listen to.
Tonight hearing your pipa speech is like hearing celestial music;
My ears clear temporarily.
Please do not refuse to sit again and play another tune;
For you, I will compose this 'Song of the Pipa'.
Moved by my words, she stood silently for a long time;
Then sat back and played faster, strings urgent.
The melancholy differed from earlier sounds;
The whole audience listened again, wiping away tears.
Who in the seat shed the most tears?
The blue robe of the Sima (Prefectural Secretary) of Jiangzhou is wet."}

The parting vast, the river bled with moonlight.

The host forgets to leave, the guest delays his sail.

The pipa stops, and words are slow to come.
He moves his boat near, invites her to show her face;
More wine is poured, lamps trimmed, the feast rekindled.
After a thousand calls she finally steps out,
Still cradling her pipa, half hiding her face.
She turns the pegs, plucks the strings, a note or two—
Before the tune is formed, the feeling comes.
Each string a sigh, each note a longing deep,
As if recounting a life of thwarted hopes.

Telling all the endless things within her heart.
Her fingers press, roll, sweep, and flick—
First *Rainbow Skirt*, then *Six Small Things*.

The thin strings whisper like secret talk.

Like pearls, great and small, dropped on jade.

Like a choked spring, struggling under ice.

Congealed, they stop—the sound is briefly stilled.

In this silence, silence speaks more than sound.
A silver vase shatters, water bursts forth;
Armored horsemen charge, blades and spears clash.
The tune ends with a stroke across the strings;
Four strings snap as one, like tearing silk.
Boats east and west, all silent, hushed;
Only the white autumn moon on the river's heart.

Smooths her clothes, rises, her face composed.

First in the ranks of the Music Bureau.

When I dressed up, the courtesans envied me.
The young lords of Wuling fought to give me gifts;
For one song, red silk, countless bolts.
Ornamented combs beat time till they broke;
Wine stained my blood-red skirts, again and again.
Joy year after year, carefree and light;
Autumn moons, spring breezes, casually passed.
My brother left for the army, my aunt died;
Dusk came and went, my beauty faded.

Growing old, I married a merchant.

Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.

The moon shines bright, the water cold.

{"source": {"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}, "translation": "On the banks of the Xunyang River, I bid a guest farewell by night,
Maple leaves and reeds rustling in the chill of autumn's might.
The host dismounts from horse while the guest sits aboard his boat;
We raise our wine to drink, but hear no flute or lute’s soft note.
Drunk yet not joyful, we face parting sad and deep,
The moon drowned in the vast river makes us want to weep.
Suddenly, across the water, a pipa’s sound is heard,
The host forgets to go home, the guest stays put undeterred.
We seek the source, asking softly who plays such strains,
The music stops; she wants to speak but hesitates with pains.
We move our boats close together, invite her to appear,
Add more wine, trim the lamps, and start the feast anew here.
Called out many times, she finally emerges shy,
Still holding her pipa, half-covering her face and eye.
She turns the pegs and plucks three strings, few notes so true,
Before a melody forms, emotion shines through.
Each string suppressed, every sound carries thought,
As if telling a life of ambition thwarted and caught.
Brows lowered, fingers moving gently, one after another,
She tells the endless sorrow hidden in her heart’s cover.
Lightly pinching, slowly rolling, sweeping then picking tight,
First 'Rainbow Robe', then 'Six Beats' fill the night.
The thick strings roar like heavy rain pouring down fast,
The thin strings whisper like private talks held past.
Loud and soft, mixed together, they interweave,
Large and small pearls falling onto a jade plate leave.
Smooth as orioles singing among flowers bright,
Choking as springs flowing under ice at night.
Cold and rough, the stream freezes, strings seem to cease,
Frozen still, no sound comes, only silence’s peace.
Other secret sorrows and hidden hatreds arise,
At this moment, silence speaks better than any cries.
Then suddenly, a silver vase bursts, water spurts out loud,
Iron cavalry charges forth, swords and spears clash proud.
The song ends; she draws the plectrum across the center string,
One sharp sound rips silk, making hearts quiver and sing.
East boats and west barges fall silent, no word is said,
Only the white moon in the middle of the river spread.
She pauses, puts the plectrum between the strings’ hold,
Straightens her clothes, composes herself, becoming cold.
She says: 'I was originally a girl from the capital city,
My family lived below Shrimp Mound Hill, amidst beauty.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa, skillful and keen,
Named first in the Teaching Bureau’s finest scene.
After playing tunes, even great masters were impressed,
When made up, courtesans often felt distressed.
Young nobles from Five Tombs fought over me with gifts,
For one song, countless red silks came in swift shifts.
Gold-inlaid hairpins broke keeping time’s beat,
Blood-red skirts stained by spilled wine, never neat.
This year laughter returned, next year too, passing by,
Autumn moons and spring winds wasted, neither high nor low.
My brother joined the army, my aunt passed away,
Days went by, mornings came, youth faded day by day.
Front door deserted, horses rare, visitors few,
In old age, I became a merchant’s wife, through.
The merchant values profit more than love’s bond,
Last month he went to Fuliang for tea beyond.
He left me alone guarding an empty boat at the mouth,
Moonlight surrounds the ship, river water cold south.
Deep in night, I dream of youthful days gone by,
Wake crying, makeup tears running red down the sky.'
Hearing the pipa, I sighed already deeply moved,
Hearing these words, I murmured again, grief improved.
'We are both people lost at the edge of the world,
Meeting each other now, why did we need old bonds unfurled?'
Since last year, I left the imperial capital behind,
Banished and sick, living in Xunyang, weary mind.
Xunyang is remote, devoid of musical grace,
All year round, no strings or pipes touch this place.
I live near Pen River where land is low and wet,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboos grow around my set.
What do I hear morning and evening within?
Cuckoo bleeding its voice, apes wailing their din.
Spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moonlit nights,
Often take wine alone, pouring cups in sights.
Are there no village songs and mountain flutes played?
Hoarse and chaotic sounds, difficult for ears displayed.
Tonight hearing your pipa’s language pure and clear,
Like listening to fairy music, ears brighten near.
Do not refuse to sit and play one more tune,
For you, I compose this 'Song of the Pipa' soon.
Moved by my words, she stood for a long while still,
Then sat back down, tightened strings, growing shrill.
Sad and mournful, unlike the previous sound,
Everyone present hid faces, tears streaming down.
Who among them shed most tears, drowning in grief?
The Sima of Jiangzhou, his blue robe soaked beneath."}

By Bai Juyi

At night by the Xunyang River I saw off a guest;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn chill.
The host dismounted, his guest was already on the boat;
We raised our cups to drink but had no music to accompany us.
Intoxicated yet unable to find joy, we parted in sorrow;
As we left, the vast river was steeped in moonlight.
Suddenly I heard the sound of a pipa over the water;
The host forgot to return home, the guest did not set sail.
Following the sound, I asked quietly who was playing,
But the pipa stopped, and the player hesitated to speak.
I moved my boat closer to invite her out, added wine, turned up the lamps, and resumed the banquet.
After a thousand calls and ten thousand summons, she finally came out,
Still holding the pipa half-covering her face.
She turned the pegs and plucked the strings two or three times,
Before any tune was formed, feeling was already present.
Each string murmured with suppressed emotion, each note carried longing,
As if telling of a lifetime unfulfilled ambition.
She lowered her brows and casually continued to play,
Expressing all the boundless matters in her heart.
Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, wiping then strumming,
First playing 'Rainbow Garment', then 'Six Melodies'.
The thick strings sounded noisy like rushing rain,
The thin strings whispered softly like private talk.
Noisy and soft sounds mingled together as she played,
Large pearls and small pearls falling onto a jade plate.
Sweetly chirping like an oriole under flowers, smooth and flowing,
Muffled and choked like a spring freezing hard under ice.
The cold ice-like spring stagnated, the strings froze and broke off,
When stuck and unable to pass, the sound temporarily ceased.
A hidden sorrow and dark resentment arose,
At this moment, silence surpassed sound.
Then suddenly a silver vase burst, water splashing forth,
Iron cavalry charging out, swords and spears clashing.
The song ended; she drew the plectrum across the center,
In one stroke of the four strings, it sounded like tearing silk.
East boats and west ships were silent without word,
Only seeing the white autumn moon in the center of the river.
She pondered, placed the plectrum among the strings,
Straightened her clothes and rose with a composed expression.
She said herself that originally she was a girl from the capital city,
Her home was below Toad Mound.
At thirteen she learned to master the pipa,
Her name belonged to the first section of the Imperial Music Bureau.
After finishing a tune, she once made even great masters admire her skill;
Once made up, she was often envied by beautiful courtesans.
The young men of the Five Tombs fought over gifts for her,
For one song, she received countless rolls of red silk.
Jeweled hairpins and silver combs broke as they beat time,
Blood-red skirts were stained by spilled wine.
This year laughing and rejoicing, next year again,
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed idly by.
Her brother went off to join the army, her aunt died,
Day after day, morning after evening, her beauty faded.
Before her door became desolate, visitors on horseback grew rare,
Growing older, she married a merchant's wife.
The merchant valued profit above all and cared little about partings;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He left, and at the river mouth I guard an empty boat,
Around the boat shines bright moonlight, the river water is cold.
Deep in the night I suddenly dream of events from when I was young,
Waking weeping, makeup tears streak down in red lines.
Hearing the pipa I sighed already,
And hearing these words, I lamented again deeply.
Both of us are people adrift at the ends of the earth,
Since we have met now, why does it matter if we knew each other before?
I left the imperial capital last year,
Demoted and lying ill in the city of Xunyang.
Xunyang is remote and has no music;
All year round I do not hear the sound of silk and bamboo instruments.
Living near the Pen River, the land is low and damp,
Yellow rushes and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What objects do I hear here morning and evening?
Dusky cuckoos bleeding their cries, gibbons wailing mournfully.
On spring rivers, flower mornings, and autumn moon nights,
Often I take wine and pour it alone.
Is there really no mountain songs or village pipes?
They are harsh and cacophonous, difficult to listen to.
Tonight I hear your pipa speech,
Like listening to celestial music, my ears are momentarily cleared.
Do not refuse to sit again and play another piece;
For you, I shall compose anew this Ballad of the Pipa.
Touched by my words, she stood for a long while,
Then sat back down and tightened the strings, which played faster.
Sorrowful sounds unlike those before,
The whole room listened again and all covered their faces to weep.
Who in the audience shed the most tears?
The blue robe of the Jiangzhou Prefect was soaked wet."}

夜来幽梦忽还乡，小轩窗，正梳妆。

Your lone tomb lies a thousand li away,

My face worn by wind and dust, my temples like frost.

Last night, in a shadowy dream, I suddenly returned home,
At the small window, you were dressing your hair.
We looked at each other, speechless,
Only tears falling in thousand lines.
I surmise where my heart breaks most keenly:
Under the bright moon’s light, on the short pine-covered hill."}

We looked at each other, speechless,
Only tears flowing down in endless streams.
I surmise where my heart breaks most keenly year after year:

{"source": {"title": "蝶恋花·伫倚危楼风细细", "author": "柳永", "text": "伫倚危楼风细细，望极春愁，黯黯生天际。
草色烟光残照里，无言谁会凭阑意。
拟把疏狂图一醉，对酒当歌，强乐还无味。
衣带渐宽终不悔，为伊消得人憔悴。"}, "translation": "I linger, leaning on the high tower’s rail,
As slender breezes softly blow;
Gazing far, spring sorrow grows dim and dark,
Rising from the sky’s far margin.

In smoky light and fading sun,
Grass blends with twilight’s haze;
Silent I stand—what can be done?
No one knows my heart’s sad ways.

I’d cast off restraint to seek one drunken bliss,
To sing and drink, yet find no ease;
Forced joy tastes hollow, empty, amiss,
Leaving only weary sighs.

My belt grows loose, but I don’t rue,
Though wasted thin for Her alone;
I bear this pain, I see it through,
Without a single regret shown."}
